Page 39
[Surat al-Furqan]
Seventy-seven verses, Meccan
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan) upon His servant, that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He has not taken a son, and He has no partner in dominion, and He created everything and determined it with precise determination﴾.
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
The words of the Exalted: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant, that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He has not taken a son, and He has no partner in dominion, and He created everything and determined it with precise determination﴾.
Know that Allah, glorified and exalted be He, spoke in this surah about tawhid (the oneness of God), prophethood, and the states of the Resurrection. Then He concluded it with mention of the attributes of the sincere, certain servants. Since establishing the Creator and establishing the attributes of His majesty must precede everything, Allah opened this surah with that, saying: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾. And in it are several issues:

The first issue: Al-Zajjaj said: "Tabaraka" is from the form tafa"ala of al-barakah (blessing), and al-barakah is the abundance and increase of good. In it there are two meanings:
One: His good increases and multiplies, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿If you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34].
The second: He is exalted above everything in His essence, attributes and actions, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. As for His exaltedness above everything in His essence, it may mean that He is exalted by the necessity of His existence and His eternity above the possibility of annihilation and change, and it may mean that He is exalted by His singularity and oneness above resembling any of the possible things. As for His exaltedness above everything in His attributes, it may mean that He is exalted above His knowledge being necessary or acquired, or conception or assent; and in His power, above needing matter, duration, a model, or the bringing about of a purpose or attainment. As for His actions, He is exalted above existence, continuance, and the good condition of existence being from anyone but Him.
Others said: The root of the word indicates permanence, and it is derived from the kneeling of a camel, and from the settling of birds upon water, and a pond (birkah) is so named because water remains in it. The meaning is that He, glorified and exalted be He, is permanent in His essence, eternal and everlasting, unable to change, and permanent in His attributes, unable to alter. Since He, glorified and exalted, is the Creator of the aspects of benefits and interests and the Sustainer of them, it is necessary to describe Him, glorified and exalted, as Blessed and Exalted.

Page 40
The second issue: The people of language said: The word "alladhi" (the one who) is laid down to point to a thing when one attempts to define it by a known proposition. At this point a difficulty arises: the people did not know that He, glorified be He, is the One who sent down the Criterion, so how is the word "alladhi" appropriate here? The answer: when the proof that the Qur'an is miraculous was established, its being from Allah became evident according to the proof; because of the strength and clarity of the proof, He, glorified and exalted, treated it as something known.

The third issue: There is no dispute that al-Furqan is the Qur'an. It was described thus because He, glorified be He, distinguished by it between truth and falsehood regarding the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and between the lawful and the unlawful; or because He distinguished it in its revelation, as He said: ﴿And a Qur'an We have divided, that you might recite it to the people at intervals﴾ [al-Isra: 106]. This interpretation is closer, because He said: "Nazzala al-Furqan," and the word nazzala indicates distribution, whereas the word anzala indicates gathering; for this reason He said in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3]. Know that when He, glorified and exalted, first said ﴿Tabaraka﴾, whose meaning is abundance of good and blessing, and then mentioned the matter of the Qur'an immediately after it, this indicates that the Qur'an is the source of all good things and the most general of blessings. Yet the Qur'an is nothing but a wellspring of knowledge, insights and wisdom; so this indicates that knowledge is the most noble of created things and the greatest of things in good and blessing.

* * *

The fourth issue: There is no dispute that by "the servant" here is meant Muhammad (ﷺ). It is related from Ibn al-Zubayr that "His servants" means the Messenger of Allah and his community, as He said: ﴿We have sent down to you﴾ [al-Anbiya: 10], ﴿Say: We believe in Allah and in what has been sent down to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 136]. As for His saying: ﴿that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾, the meaning is that this servant should be a warner to the worlds. As for the view of one who said that it refers back to the Criterion, so that the warning is attributed to it just as guidance is attributed to it in His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides﴾ [al-Isra: 9], this is far-fetched; because the one who warns (munthir and nadhir) is an attribute of the agent of fear, and when the Qur'an is described by it, it is metaphorical, and carrying speech on its literal meaning when possible is obligatory. Then they said: this verse indicates several rulings:
The first: The world (al-'alam) is everything other than Allah, Exalted, and it encompasses all the accountable beings of jinn, humankind and angels. But we are agreed that he (peace be upon him) was not a messenger to the angels, so it is necessary that he was a messenger to jinn and humankind together. By this the view of one who says he was a messenger to some and not others is refuted.
The second: The word ﴿lil-'alamin﴾ encompasses all created things, so the verse indicates that he is a messenger to creation until the Day of Resurrection, and therefore he must be the Seal of the Prophets and Messengers.
The third: The Mu'tazilah said: The verse indicates that He, glorified be He, willed faith and the performance of acts of obedience from all, because He sent him to all in order that he be a warner to all, and He willed from all that they occupy themselves with good and turn away from evil. Our companions opposed them with His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and humans﴾ [al-A'raf: 179], and the rest of the verse.
The fourth: One may say: just as His saying "Tabaraka" indicates abundance of good and blessing, what is mentioned after it must be something that causes abundance of good and benefits, and warning causes grief and fear, so how does this suit this context? The answer: this warning operates like the discipline of a child; just as the more thorough the discipline of a child, the greater the kindness toward him, because that leads in the future to great benefits, so here, the more abundant the warning, the greater the return of creatures to Allah, and so the otherworldly happiness is more complete and greater. This serves as a reminder that no attention is to be paid to immediate benefits, because when He, glorified be He, described Himself as the One who gives abundant good, He mentioned only the benefits of religion and mentioned absolutely nothing of the benefits of this world.

Page 41
Then He, glorified be He, described His essence with four kinds of attributes of greatness:
The first of them is His saying: ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. This serves as an indication of the proof of His existence, glorified be He; because there is no way to establish Him except through the dependence of His acts upon Him. So placing this attribute before the other attributes is like a necessary matter. His saying: ﴿to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is an indication of these created things' need of Him, glorified be He, both in the time of their origination and the time of their continuance, in their quiddity and in their existence, and that He, glorified be He, is the One who disposes of them as He wills.
The second: His saying: ﴿He has not taken a son﴾. Thus He made clear that He is the one worshipped forever, and it is not valid that anyone other than Him be worshipped or inherit dominion from Him. So this attribute serves as an affirmation of His saying ﴿Blessed﴾ and of His saying ﴿to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. This serves as a refutation of the Christians.
The third: His saying: ﴿and He has no partner in dominion﴾. The meaning is that He alone is the sole deity. When the servant knows this, his fear and hope toward everything are cut off, and his heart is preoccupied with nothing but His mercy and kindness. This also refutes the Dualists, those who worship the stars, and those who worship idols.
The fourth: His saying: ﴿and He created everything and determined it with precise determination﴾. Here there are questions:
The first: Does His saying ﴿and He created everything﴾ indicate that He, glorified be He, is the Creator of the acts of the servants? The answer: Yes, for two reasons:
The first: His saying ﴿and He created everything﴾ encompasses all things, so it encompasses the acts of the servants.
The second: After He negated a partner, He mentioned this. The implication is that when He negated a partner, it was as if someone said: "Here are peoples who acknowledge the negation of partners and equals, yet they say that they create the acts of their own selves." So Allah mentioned this verse to be a helpful aid in refuting them. The Qadi said: The verse does not indicate this, for several reasons:
One of them: He, glorified be He, explicitly stated that the servant is a creator in His saying: ﴿And when you were creating from clay the likeness of a bird﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110], and He said: ﴿So blessed be Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14].
The second: He, glorified be He, praised Himself by this, so it is not permissible that He intend by it the creation of corruption.
The third: He, glorified be He, praised Himself by saying that He determined it with determination, and it is not permissible that by this He intends anything but goodness and wisdom and nothing else. Thus it is established by these aspects that there must be interpretation if the verse indicated it by its apparent meaning, so how much more so when it does not indicate it at all, because creation is an expression for determination, so it encompasses only what determination appears in, and that appears only in bodies, not in accidents. The answer:
As for His saying ﴿and when you create﴾ and His saying ﴿the best of creators﴾, they are countered by His saying: ﴿Allah is the Creator of everything﴾ [az-Zumar: 62] and by His saying: ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah?﴾ [Fatir: 3]. As for his statement that it is not permissible to praise oneself by the creation of corruption, we say: why is it not permissible that praise may occur by it, in view of the measures of power and because the attribute of bringing into existence from nonexistence and of annihilating from existence belongs to Him alone? As for his statement that creation encompasses only bodies, we say: if that were so, His saying ﴿and He created everything﴾ would be an error, because it requires the attribution of creation to all things, whereas it is not valid by reason to attribute it to them.
The second question: Creation contains the meaning of determination. So His saying ﴿and He created everything and determined it with precise determination﴾ means: "and He determined everything and determined it with precise determination." The answer: the meaning is that He brought every thing into being in a manner that observes in it determination and proportion, and so determined it with precise determination and prepared it for what suits it. An example: He created man in this determined, proportioned shape that you see, and determined him for the obligations and interests attached to him in matters of religion and the world. Likewise every animal and inanimate thing that He brought forth in a proportioned natural form determined by the patterns of wisdom and management: He determined it for a certain matter and a certain benefit, in accordance with what He determined, not deviating from it.
The third question: Does His saying ﴿then determined it with precise determination﴾ indicate your doctrine?
The answer: Yes, and that is from several aspects:

Page 42
One of them: determination on our part returns to conjecture and reckoning, whereas for Him, glorified be He, it has no meaning except knowledge of it and reporting about it. This is agreed between us and the Mu'tazilah. So when He knew of a particular thing that it will not occur, if that thing were to occur it would follow that His knowledge would turn into ignorance and His report of truth into falsehood, and that is impossible; and what leads to the impossible is impossible. Therefore the occurrence of that thing is impossible, and the impossible is not willed; so that thing is not willed, though it is commanded. Thus it is established that command and will do not entail one another, and it becomes clear that the one who is happy is the one who was made happy in his mother's womb, and the wretched is the one who was made wretched in his mother's womb.

Second: If, when the capacity and the pure motive are present, the act becomes necessary, then the servant's act would necessitate the act of God, the Exalted, and in that case the view of the Mu'tazila (al-Mu'tazilah) is refuted. If it is not necessary, then either it is independent of a determining factor (al-murajjih), in which case a possible thing has come into being without a determining factor, and allowing this closes the door to proving the Creator; or it is not independent of a determining factor, in which case the discussion returns to that determining factor, and it does not end except upon arriving at the Necessarily Existent (wajib al-wujud).

Third: If the act of the servant occurred by his power, then nothing would occur except what he intended to bring into existence and produce. But a human being intends only knowledge and truth, so nothing would result for him except ignorance and falsehood. Yet if the matter were by his power, it would not be so. If it is said: it is only because he believed a doubt (shubha) which caused him that ignorance, we say: if he believed that doubt because of another doubt, an infinite regress (tasalsul) would follow, and that is impossible. Therefore it is necessary to arrive at a first ignorance, which entered the human heart not because of a prior ignorance, but which the human being himself originated from the start without any cause. And that is impossible, because a human being never willingly accepts ignorance for himself, nor seeks to acquire ignorance for himself; rather he seeks only knowledge. Therefore it is necessary that nothing comes to him except what he intended and willed. Since it is not so, we know that everything is by an all-pervading decree (qada' sari) and an effective destiny (qadar nafidh), and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And He created everything and determined it with precise determination﴾ (Qur'an 25:2).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verse 3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Yet they have taken, besides Him, gods that create nothing, while they themselves are created; and they control neither harm nor benefit for themselves, nor do they control death or life or resurrection.﴾

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, described Himself with attributes of majesty, might and loftiness, He followed this with refuting the doctrine of the idol-worshippers and explaining its deficiencies from several aspects:

The first: they do not create things, whereas the deity must be capable of creating and bringing into existence.

The second: they are created, and the created is in need, whereas the deity must be self-sufficient.

The third: they do not control harm or benefit for themselves, and whoever is so does not control benefit for others either, and whoever is so there is no benefit in worshipping him.

The fourth: they do not control death, life or resurrection, meaning they are not able to give life or cause death during the time of legal accountability (taklif), and again during the time of recompense. And whoever is like this, how can he be called a god, and how is it proper to worship him, when the one who rightly deserves worship is the one who bestows these specific blessings?

Here there are some questions:

The first: His saying ﴿Yet they have taken, besides Him, gods﴾: does it apply only to idol-worshippers, or does it include Christians, star-worshippers and angel-worshippers?

The answer: al-Qadi said: It is far-fetched that Christians should be included, because they did not take gods besides God in the plural. So the closer view is that it refers to idol-worshippers, though it is permissible that it include those who worshipped the angels, because their object of worship is plural.

Someone may say: His saying ﴿have taken﴾ is in the plural form, and His saying "gods" is plural, and when plural is matched with plural, singular is matched with singular. Therefore the fact that the object of worship of the Christians is one does not prevent their inclusion under this expression.

* * *

The second question: some of our companions (the Ash'aris) argued with His saying ﴿Yet they have taken, besides Him, gods that create nothing, while they themselves are created﴾ that the act of the servant is created by God, Exalted is He. They said: God, Exalted is He, censured these disbelievers in that they worshipped what creates nothing, and this indicates that whoever creates deserves to be worshipped. So if the servant were a creator, he would be a worshipped god. Al-Ka'bi answered this by saying: We do not apply the name "Creator" except to God, Exalted is He.

Some of our companions said regarding creation: it is bringing into existence without effort, thought or toil, and this belongs only to God, Exalted is He. Then he said: He, Exalted is He, has said about the idols: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk?﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:195). Does this indicate that everyone who has feet deserves to be worshipped? If they say no, it is said: then likewise is what you mentioned. And He, Exalted is He, has said: ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾ (Al-Mu'minun 23:14). All of this is the speech of al-Ka'bi.

The answer: As for his saying that the name "Creator" is not applied to the servant, we say: rather, it must be applied, because "khalq" in the language means measuring (taqdir), and measuring returns to conjecture and reckoning. Therefore the name "Creator" must be literally applicable to the servant and figuratively to God, Exalted is He. How, then, can you prevent the application of the word "Creator" to the servant? As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk?﴾, the defect fell upon them through their incapacity, so it is certainly the case that whoever is shown to be incapable in some respect is not fit to be worshipped. As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾, the discussion of it has already preceded.

Know that the argument of our companions with this verse is not strong, because it is possible that the defect arises only from the combination of two matters:

One of them: they are not creators.

The second: they are created.

The servant, although he is a creator, is nonetheless created, so it follows that he is not a worshipped god.

The third question: does this verse indicate resurrection?

The answer: Yes, because He, Exalted is He, mentioned resurrection (nushur). Its meaning is that the one worshipped must be capable of conveying reward to the obedient and punishment to the disobedient. Whoever is not like this must not be fit for divinity.

[Page 43]

[Page 44]

The Almighty said: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "This is nothing but a fabrication which he has invented, and other people have helped him with it. Indeed, they have come with injustice and falsehood."﴾ ﴿And they say, "Tales of the ancients, which he has had written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening."﴾ ﴿Say, "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth. Indeed He is ever Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ ﴿And they say, "What is this Messenger that he eats food and walks about in the markets? Why has an angel not been sent down to him to be a warner along with him?"﴾ ﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him, or he have a garden from which he eats." And the wrongdoers say, "You follow none but a man under a spell."﴾ ﴿Look how they have coined similitudes for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.﴾

Know that He, glorified is He, first spoke about monotheism (tawhid), second about refuting the worshippers of idols, and third, in this verse, He spoke about the question of prophethood. And He, glorified is He, related their doubts (shubah, objections) in denying the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ):

The First Doubt: their saying, ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication which he has invented, and other people have helped him with it.﴾ A similar statement is His, the Exalted: ﴿Only a human is teaching him﴾ [An-Nahl: 103]. Know that it may be that they mean by this that he lied in himself, and it may be that they mean that he lied in attributing it to God, the Exalted. Then here there are two discussions:

The first: Abu Muslim said: al-iftira' (fabrication) is an form of iftaʿala from farayt, and it is said in the sense of cutting a hide: faraytu al-adim (I cut the hide). When the intention is to cut off corruption, it is said: afraytu, iftaraytu, khalaqtu, ikhtalaqtu. And it is said of one who insults a man with what is not in him: iftara ʿalayhi (he fabricated against him).

The second discussion: al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and he is the one who said this statement.

﴿And other people have helped him with it﴾ means: ʿAddas, the freed slave of Huwaytib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzza, Yasar, the slave of Amir ibn al-Hadrami, and Jabr, the freed slave of Amir. These three were from the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), and they used to read the Torah and narrate stories from it. When they embraced Islam, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would look after them, for this reason al-Nadr said what he said.

Know that God, the Exalted, answered this doubt with His saying: ﴿Indeed, they have come with injustice and falsehood.﴾ And in this there are discussions:

The first: this amount is sufficient as an answer to the mentioned doubt, because every intelligent person knows that he (peace be upon him) challenged them with the Qur'an, and they were at the pinnacle of eloquence, and they went to every extreme in their eagerness to nullify his affair, to the point that this drove them to what they described him with in these verses. Had they been able to oppose him, they would have done so, and that would have been closer to achieving their aim in it than what they put forward in this verse and others. And if Muhammad (peace be upon him) had been helped in that by someone else, it would also have been possible for them to seek help from others, because Muhammad (ﷺ) is like those deniers in knowledge of the language and in the capacity to seek help. When they did not do that, in this situation, it became known that the Qur'an had reached the peak of eloquence and had arrived at the limit of inimitability (iʿjaz). And since this proof has been presented many times and repeatedly in the Qur'an, and by means of it the falsity of this objection became evident, it became clear that repeating this objection after these clear proofs has been presented can only be due to persistence in ignorance and obstinacy. Therefore God sufficed in the answer with His saying: ﴿Indeed, they have come with injustice and falsehood.﴾

The second discussion: al-Kisa'i said: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, they have come with injustice and falsehood﴾ means: they came with injustice and lying. It is like His saying: ﴿You have indeed brought a monstrous thing﴾ [Maryam: 89], where it is in the accusative because of the occurrence of the coming upon it. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning: they came with injustice and falsehood.

The third discussion: God, the Exalted, described their speech as being injustice and as being falsehood. As for it being injustice, it is because they attributed this vile act to one who was innocent of it; they placed a thing in other than its place, and that is injustice. As for falsehood, it is because they lied in it. Abu Muslim said: the injustice is their denial of the Messenger and their rejection of him, and the falsehood is their lying about him.

[Page 45]

The Second Doubt of theirs: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "Tales of the ancients, which he has had written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening."﴾ And in this there are discussions:

The first discussion: al-asatir are what the earlier generations wrote down, such as the stories of Rustam and Isfandiyar. It is the plural ofus'tar or ustura, like uhdutha (a story). ﴿Had written down﴾ (iktataba): he had them copied by Muhammad from the People of the Book, meaning ʿAmir, Yasar and Jabr. The meaning of iktataba here is that he ordered that they be written for him, just as it is said ihtajama and iftasada when he ordered that to be done. ﴿They are dictated to him﴾ means: they are read to him. The meaning is that they were written for him while he was illiterate, so they are cast upon him from his book so that he may memorize them, because the form of casting upon one who memorizes is like the form of casting upon one who writes.

As for His saying: ﴿morning and evening﴾, al-Dahhak said: what is dictated to him in the morning he recites to you in the evening, and what is dictated to him in the evening he recites to you in the morning.

The second discussion: al-Hasan said: His saying, ﴿they are dictated to him morning and evening﴾ is the word of God, which He mentioned as an answer to their statement, as if He, the Exalted, said: these verses are dictated to him by revelation from moment to moment, so how is it attributed to him that they are the tales of the ancients? As for the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun), they agreed that this is part of the statement of the people, and they meant by it that the People of the Book dictated these things to him at these times. And there is no doubt that this view is closer, for several reasons:

The first: the strong connection of this speech with what precedes it, for it is as if they said: he had the tales of the ancients written down, so they are dictated to him.

The second: that this is what is meant by their saying: ﴿And other people have helped him with it.﴾

The third: that after this He, the Exalted, answered their speech with His saying: ﴿Say, "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret..."﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: al-Hasan's view is only correct if the hamza is opened for the interrogative which carries the meaning of denial, and al-Hasan should stop at "the ancients." God answered this doubt with His saying: ﴿Say, "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth. Indeed He is ever Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ And in this there are discussions:

The first discussion: explaining how this can be an answer to that doubt. Its explanation is what we have previously mentioned: that he (peace be upon him) challenged them to produce an equal, and their inability to do so became evident. Had he (peace be upon him) brought the Qur'an by seeking help from someone, it would have been obligatory upon them too to seek help from someone and bring something like this Qur'an. When they were unable to do so, it was established that it is the revelation of God and His speech. Therefore He said: ﴿Say, "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret,"﴾ because the one capable of composing the words of the Qur'an must necessarily be one who knows all knowable things, both apparent and hidden, in several respects:

The first: such eloquence can only come from one who knows all knowable things.

The second: the Qur'an includes information about the unseen, and that can only come from one who knows all knowable things.

The third: the Qur'an is free from defect, and that can only come from one who knows, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [An-Nisa': 82].

The fourth: its inclusion of rulings which are conducive to the welfare of the world and the order of the servants, and that can only come from one who knows all knowable things.

The fifth: its inclusion of various kinds of knowledge, and that can only come from one who knows all knowable things. So when the Qur'an indicates in these respects that it is nothing but the speech of one who knows all knowable things, for this reason He sufficed in answering their doubts with His saying: ﴿Say, "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret."﴾

The second discussion: they differed about what is meant by al-sirr (the secret). Some of them said: the meaning is that the One who knows every secret in the heavens and the earth is the one who is able to send down the like of this Book. Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that it was sent down by one who knows the secret, so if he had lied about Him, He would have taken vengeance upon him, because of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 44]. Others said: the meaning is

[Page 46]

that He knows every secret hidden in the heavens and the earth, and among it is what you conceal of plotting against His Messenger, while you know that what he says is true by necessity; likewise the inner reality of the affair of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his innocence of what you accuse him of. He, glorified is He, will requite you and him for what He knows of you and of him.

The third discussion: He mentioned the Forgiving, the Merciful in this place for two reasons:

The first: Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that He only sent it down for the sake of warning, so it is necessary that He be Forgiving and Merciful, not hasty in punishment.

The second: it is an alert that they deserved, by their scheming, that He pour the punishment upon them in a pouring, but what averted that from them is that He is Forgiving and Merciful, granting respite and not hastening.

The Third Doubt: and it is in the extreme of weakness. They mentioned five attributes of his, and claimed that they undermine the prophethood:

The first of them: their saying: ﴿What is this Messenger that he eats food﴾.

The second: their saying: ﴿and walks about in the markets﴾, meaning: since he is like that, from where does he get superiority over us, when he is like us in these matters?

The third: their saying: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him to be a warner along with him?﴾, who would confirm him, or bear witness for him and refute those who oppose him.

The fourth: their saying: ﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him﴾, meaning from the sky, so that he may spend it and not need to go about seeking a livelihood.

The fifth: their saying: ﴿or he have a garden from which he eats.﴾ Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: "na'kulu minha" (we eat from it) with the nun, and the rest read it with the ya' (ya'kulu). The meaning: if you do not have a treasure, then at least you should be like one of the landowners (dahaqin), so that you would have a garden from which you eat.

The sixth: their saying: ﴿You follow none but a man under a spell.﴾ This story has already been mentioned at the end of Surat Bani Isra'il. God, the Exalted, answered this doubt in several ways:

The first of them: His saying: ﴿Look how they have coined similitudes for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.﴾ And in this there are discussions:

The first: how can this be an answer to that doubt? Its explanation is that what distinguishes the Messenger from others is the miracle (mu'jiza), and these things they mentioned do not detract from the miracle in any way, so none of them is detrimental to prophethood. It is as if He, the Exalted, said: look how the people busied themselves with coining these similitudes which have no benefit, because when they went astray and wanted to discredit your prophethood, they found no way at all to discredit it, since the attack on it can only be by what undermines the miracles he claimed, not by this kind of speech.

There is another aspect to it, which is that when they went astray, no capacity remained in them to accept the truth. This is valid only according to our school, and its explanation by reason is clear: a person is either equally inclined toward truth and falsehood, or his inclination toward one of them is stronger than his inclination toward the other. If it is the first, then the state of equality makes preponderance impossible, so the act is impossible. If it is the second, then in the state of preponderance of one of the two sides, the occurrence of the other side is impossible. Thus it is established that in the state of the preponderance of misguidance in his heart, it became impossible for him to accept the truth, and what is impossible is not within one's power. Thus it is established that when they went astray, they were not capable.

Know that He, glorified is He, first spoke about monotheism (tawhid), second about refuting the worshippers of idols, and third, in this verse, He spoke about the question of prophethood. And He, glorified is He, related their doubts (shubah, objections) in denying the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ):

The First Doubt: their saying, ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication which he has invented, and other people have helped him with it.﴾ A similar statement is His, the Exalted: ﴿Only a human is teaching him﴾ [An-Nahl: 103]. Know that it may be that they mean by this that he lied in himself, and it may be that they mean that he lied in attributing it to God, the Exalted. Then here there are two discussions:

The first: Abu Muslim said: al-iftira' (fabrication) is an form of iftaʿala from farayt, and it is said in the sense of cutting a hide: faraytu al-adim (I cut the hide). When the intention is to cut off corruption, it is said: afraytu, iftaraytu, khalaqtu, ikhtalaqtu. And it is said of one who insults a man with what is not in him: iftara ʿalayhi (he fabricated against him).

The second discussion: al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and he is the one who said this statement.

﴿And other people have helped him with it﴾ means: ʿAddas, the freed slave of Huwaytib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzza, Yasar, the slave of Amir ibn al-Hadrami, and Jabr, the freed slave of Amir. These three were from the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), and they used to read the Torah and narrate stories from it. When they embraced Islam, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would look after them, for this reason al-Nadr said what he said.

Know that God, the Exalted, answered this doubt with His saying: ﴿Indeed, they have come with injustice and falsehood.﴾ And in this there are discussions:

The first: this amount is sufficient as an answer to the mentioned doubt, because every intelligent person knows that he (peace be upon him) challenged them with the Qur'an, and they were at the pinnacle of eloquence, and they went to every extreme in their eagerness to nullify his affair, to the point that this drove them to what they described him with in these verses. Had they been able to oppose him, they would have done so, and that would have been closer to achieving their aim in it than what they put forward in this verse and others. And if Muhammad (peace be upon him) had been helped in that by someone else, it would also have been possible for them to seek help from others, because Muhammad (ﷺ) is like those deniers in knowledge of the language and in the capacity to seek help. When they did not do that, in this situation, it became known that the Qur'an had reached the peak of eloquence and had arrived at the limit of inimitability (iʿjaz). And since this proof has been presented many times and repeatedly in the Qur'an, and by means of it the falsity of this objection became evident, it became clear that repeating this objection after these clear proofs has been presented can only be due to persistence in ignorance and obstinacy. Therefore God sufficed in the answer with His saying: ﴿Indeed, they have come with injustice and falsehood.﴾

The second discussion: al-Kisa'i said: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, they have come with injustice and falsehood﴾ means: they came with injustice and lying. It is like His saying: ﴿You have indeed brought a monstrous thing﴾ [Maryam: 89], where it is in the accusative because of the occurrence of the coming upon it. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning: they came with injustice and falsehood.

The third discussion: God, the Exalted, described their speech as being injustice and as being falsehood. As for it being injustice, it is because they attributed this vile act to one who was innocent of it; they placed a thing in other than its place, and that is injustice. As for falsehood, it is because they lied in it. Abu Muslim said: the injustice is their denial of the Messenger and their rejection of him, and the falsehood is their lying about him.

[Page 45]

The Second Doubt of theirs: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "Tales of the ancients, which he has had written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening."﴾ And in this there are discussions:

The first discussion: al-asatir are what the earlier generations wrote down, such as the stories of Rustam and Isfandiyar. It is the plural ofus'tar or ustura, like uhdutha (a story). ﴿Had written down﴾ (iktataba): he had them copied by Muhammad from the People of the Book, meaning ʿAmir, Yasar and Jabr. The meaning of iktataba here is that he ordered that they be written for him, just as it is said ihtajama and iftasada when he ordered that to be done. ﴿They are dictated to him﴾ means: they are read to him. The meaning is that they were written for him while he was illiterate, so they are cast upon him from his book so that he may memorize them, because the form of casting upon one who memorizes is like the form of casting upon one who writes.

As for His saying: ﴿morning and evening﴾, al-Dahhak said: what is dictated to him in the morning he recites to you in the evening, and what is dictated to him in the evening he recites to you in the morning.

The second discussion: al-Hasan said: His saying, ﴿they are dictated to him morning and evening﴾ is the word of God, which He mentioned as an answer to their statement, as if He, the Exalted, said: these verses are dictated to him by revelation from moment to moment, so how is it attributed to him that they are the tales of the ancients? As for the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun), they agreed that this is part of the statement of the people, and they meant by it that the People of the Book dictated these things to him at these times. And there is no doubt that this view is closer, for several reasons:

The first: the strong connection of this speech with what precedes it, for it is as if they said: he had the tales of the ancients written down, so they are dictated to him.

The second: that this is what is meant by their saying: ﴿And other people have helped him with it.﴾

The third: that after this He, the Exalted, answered their speech with His saying: ﴿Say, "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret..."﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: al-Hasan's view is only correct if the hamza is opened for the interrogative which carries the meaning of denial, and al-Hasan should stop at "the ancients." God answered this doubt with His saying: ﴿Say, "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth. Indeed He is ever Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ And in this there are discussions:

The first discussion: explaining how this can be an answer to that doubt. Its explanation is what we have previously mentioned: that he (peace be upon him) challenged them to produce an equal, and their inability to do so became evident. Had he (peace be upon him) brought the Qur'an by seeking help from someone, it would have been obligatory upon them too to seek help from someone and bring something like this Qur'an. When they were unable to do so, it was established that it is the revelation of God and His speech. Therefore He said: ﴿Say, "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret,"﴾ because the one capable of composing the words of the Qur'an must necessarily be one who knows all knowable things, both apparent and hidden, in several respects:

The first: such eloquence can only come from one who knows all knowable things.

The second: the Qur'an includes information about the unseen, and that can only come from one who knows all knowable things.

The third: the Qur'an is free from defect, and that can only come from one who knows, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [An-Nisa': 82].

The fourth: its inclusion of rulings which are conducive to the welfare of the world and the order of the servants, and that can only come from one who knows all knowable things.

The fifth: its inclusion of various kinds of knowledge, and that can only come from one who knows all knowable things. So when the Qur'an indicates in these respects that it is nothing but the speech of one who knows all knowable things, for this reason He sufficed in answering their doubts with His saying: ﴿Say, "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret."﴾

The second discussion: they differed about what is meant by al-sirr (the secret). Some of them said: the meaning is that the One who knows every secret in the heavens and the earth is the one who is able to send down the like of this Book. Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that it was sent down by one who knows the secret, so if he had lied about Him, He would have taken vengeance upon him, because of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 44]. Others said: the meaning is

[Page 46]

that He knows every secret hidden in the heavens and the earth, and among it is what you conceal of plotting against His Messenger, while you know that what he says is true by necessity; likewise the inner reality of the affair of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his innocence of what you accuse him of. He, glorified is He, will requite you and him for what He knows of you and of him.

The third discussion: He mentioned the Forgiving, the Merciful in this place for two reasons:

The first: Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that He only sent it down for the sake of warning, so it is necessary that He be Forgiving and Merciful, not hasty in punishment.

The second: it is an alert that they deserved, by their scheming, that He pour the punishment upon them in a pouring, but what averted that from them is that He is Forgiving and Merciful, granting respite and not hastening.

The Third Doubt: and it is in the extreme of weakness. They mentioned five attributes of his, and claimed that they undermine the prophethood:

The first of them: their saying: ﴿What is this Messenger that he eats food﴾.

The second: their saying: ﴿and walks about in the markets﴾, meaning: since he is like that, from where does he get superiority over us, when he is like us in these matters?

The third: their saying: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him to be a warner along with him?﴾, who would confirm him, or bear witness for him and refute those who oppose him.

The fourth: their saying: ﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him﴾, meaning from the sky, so that he may spend it and not need to go about seeking a livelihood.

The fifth: their saying: ﴿or he have a garden from which he eats.﴾ Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: "na'kulu minha" (we eat from it) with the nun, and the rest read it with the ya' (ya'kulu). The meaning: if you do not have a treasure, then at least you should be like one of the landowners (dahaqin), so that you would have a garden from which you eat.

The sixth: their saying: ﴿You follow none but a man under a spell.﴾ This story has already been mentioned at the end of Surat Bani Isra'il. God, the Exalted, answered this doubt in several ways:

The first of them: His saying: ﴿Look how they have coined similitudes for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.﴾ And in this there are discussions:

The first: how can this be an answer to that doubt? Its explanation is that what distinguishes the Messenger from others is the miracle (mu'jiza), and these things they mentioned do not detract from the miracle in any way, so none of them is detrimental to prophethood. It is as if He, the Exalted, said: look how the people busied themselves with coining these similitudes which have no benefit, because when they went astray and wanted to discredit your prophethood, they found no way at all to discredit it, since the attack on it can only be by what undermines the miracles he claimed, not by this kind of speech.

Thus it is established that in the state of the preponderance of misguidance in his heart, it became impossible for him to accept the truth, and what is impossible is not within one's power. Thus it is established that when they went astray, they were not capable.

And if Muhammad (peace be upon him) had been helped in that by someone else, it would also have been possible for them to seek help from others, because Muhammad (ﷺ) is like those deniers in knowledge of the language and in the capacity to seek help. When they did not do that, in this situation, it became known that the Qur'an had reached the peak of eloquence and had arrived at the limit of inimitability (iʿjaz). And since this proof has been presented many times and repeatedly in the Qur'an, and by means of it the falsity of this objection became evident, it became clear that repeating this objection after these clear proofs has been presented can only be due to persistence in ignorance and obstinacy. Therefore God sufficed in the answer with His saying: ﴿Indeed, they have come with injustice and falsehood.﴾

The second discussion: al-Kisa'i said: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, they have come with injustice and falsehood﴾ means: they came with injustice and lying. It is like His saying: ﴿You have indeed brought a monstrous thing﴾ [Maryam: 89], where it is in the accusative because of the occurrence of the coming upon it. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning: they came with injustice and falsehood.

The third discussion: God, the Exalted, described their speech as being injustice and as being falsehood. As for it being injustice, it is because they attributed this vile act to one who was innocent of it; they placed a thing in other than its place, and that is injustice. As for falsehood, it is because they lied in it. Abu Muslim said: the injustice is their denial of the Messenger and their rejection of him, and the falsehood is their lying about him.

[Page 45]

The Second Doubt of theirs: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "Tales of the ancients, which he has had written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening."﴾ And in this there are discussions:

The first discussion: al-asatir are what the earlier generations wrote down, such as the stories of Rustam and Isfandiyar. It is the plural ofus'tar or ustura, like uhdutha (a story). ﴿Had written down﴾ (iktataba): he had them copied by Muhammad from the People of the Book, meaning ʿAmir, Yasar and Jabr. The meaning of iktataba here is that he ordered that they be written for him, just as it is said ihtajama and iftasada when he ordered that to be done. ﴿They are dictated to him﴾ means: they are read to him. The meaning is that they were written for him while he was illiterate, so they are cast upon him from his book so that he may memorize them, because the form of casting upon one who memorizes is like the form of casting upon one who writes.

As for His saying: ﴿morning and evening﴾, al-Dahhak said: what is dictated to him in the morning he recites to you in the evening, and what is dictated to him in the evening he recites to you in the morning.

The second discussion: al-Hasan said: His saying, ﴿they are dictated to him morning and evening﴾ is the word of God, which He mentioned as an answer to their statement, as if He, the Exalted, said: these verses are dictated to him by revelation from moment to moment, so how is it attributed to him that they are the tales of the ancients? As for the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun), they agreed that this is part of the statement of the people, and they meant by it that the People of the Book dictated these things to him at these times. And there is no doubt that this view is closer, for several reasons:

The first: the strong connection of this speech with what precedes it, for it is as if they said: he had the tales of the ancients written down, so they are dictated to him.

The second: that this is what is meant by their saying: ﴿And other people have helped him with it.﴾

The third: that after this He, the Exalted, answered their speech with His saying: ﴿Say, "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret..."﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: al-Hasan's view is only correct if the hamza is opened for the interrogative which carries the meaning of denial, and al-Hasan should stop at "the ancients." God answered this doubt with His saying: ﴿Say, "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth. Indeed He is ever Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ And in this there are discussions:

The first discussion: explaining how this can be an answer to that doubt. Its explanation is what we have previously mentioned: that he (peace be upon him) challenged them to produce an equal, and their inability to do so became evident. Had he (peace be upon him) brought the Qur'an by seeking help from someone, it would have been obligatory upon them too to seek help from someone and bring something like this Qur'an. When they were unable to do so, it was established that it is the revelation of God and His speech. Therefore He said: ﴿Say, "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret,"﴾ because the one capable of composing the words of the Qur'an must necessarily be one who knows all knowable things, both apparent and hidden, in several respects:

The first: such eloquence can only come from one who knows all knowable things.

The second: the Qur'an includes information about the unseen, and that can only come from one who knows all knowable things.

The third: the Qur'an is free from defect, and that can only come from one who knows, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [An-Nisa': 82].

The fourth: its inclusion of rulings which are conducive to the welfare of the world and the order of the servants, and that can only come from one who knows all knowable things.

The fifth: its inclusion of various kinds of knowledge, and that can only come from one who knows all knowable things. So when the Qur'an indicates in these respects that it is nothing but the speech of one who knows all knowable things, for this reason He sufficed in answering their doubts with His saying: ﴿Say, "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret."﴾

The second discussion: they differed about what is meant by al-sirr (the secret). Some of them said: the meaning is that the One who knows every secret in the heavens and the earth is the one who is able to send down the like of this Book. Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that it was sent down by one who knows the secret, so if he had lied about Him, He would have taken vengeance upon him, because of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 44]. Others said: the meaning is

[Page 46]

that He knows every secret hidden in the heavens and the earth, and among it is what you conceal of plotting against His Messenger, while you know that what he says is true by necessity; likewise the inner reality of the affair of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his innocence of what you accuse him of. He, glorified is He, will requite you and him for what He knows of you and of him.

The third discussion: He mentioned the Forgiving, the Merciful in this place for two reasons:

The first: Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that He only sent it down for the sake of warning, so it is necessary that He be Forgiving and Merciful, not hasty in punishment.

The second: it is an alert that they deserved, by their scheming, that He pour the punishment upon them in a pouring, but what averted that from them is that He is Forgiving and Merciful, granting respite and not hastening.

The Third Doubt: and it is in the extreme of weakness. They mentioned five attributes of his, and claimed that they undermine the prophethood:

The first of them: their saying: ﴿What is this Messenger that he eats food﴾.

The second: their saying: ﴿and walks about in the markets﴾, meaning: since he is like that, from where does he get superiority over us, when he is like us in these matters?

The third: their saying: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him to be a warner along with him?﴾, who would confirm him, or bear witness for him and refute those who oppose him.

The fourth: their saying: ﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him﴾, meaning from the sky, so that he may spend it and not need to go about seeking a livelihood.

The fifth: their saying: ﴿or he have a garden from which he eats.﴾ Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: "na'kulu minha" (we eat from it) with the nun, and the rest read it with the ya' (ya'kulu). The meaning: if you do not have a treasure, then at least you should be like one of the landowners (dahaqin), so that you would have a garden from which you eat.

The sixth: their saying: ﴿You follow none but a man under a spell.﴾ This story has already been mentioned at the end of Surat Bani Isra'il. God, the Exalted, answered this doubt in several ways:

The first of them: His saying: ﴿Look how they have coined similitudes for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.﴾ And in this there are discussions:

The first: how can this be an answer to that doubt? Its explanation is that what distinguishes the Messenger from others is the miracle (mu'jiza), and these things they mentioned do not detract from the miracle in any way, so none of them is detrimental to prophethood. It is as if He, the Exalted, said: look how the people busied themselves with coining these similitudes which have no benefit, because when they went astray and wanted to discredit your prophethood, they found no way at all to discredit it, since the attack on it can only be by what undermines the miracles he claimed, not by this kind of speech.

There is another aspect to it, which is that when they went astray, no capacity remained in them to accept the truth. This is valid only according to our school, and its explanation by reason is clear: a person is either equally inclined toward truth and falsehood, or his inclination toward one of them is stronger than his inclination toward the other. If it is the first, then the state of equality makes preponderance impossible, so the act is impossible. If it is the second, then in the state of preponderance of one of the two sides, the occurrence of the other side is impossible. Thus it is established that in the state of the preponderance of misguidance in his heart, it became impossible for him to accept the truth, and what is impossible is not within one's power. Thus it is established that when they went astray, they were not capable.

[Page 44]

The Almighty said: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "This is nothing but a fabrication which he has invented, and other people have helped him with it. The second discussion: al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and he is the one who said this statement.
