أَمَّا قَوْلُهُ: ﴿لَا تَدْعُوا الْيَوْمَ ثُبُورًا وَاحِدًا﴾ أَيْ: يُقَالُ لَهُمْ ذَلِكَ، وَهُمْ أَحِقَّاءُ بِأَنْ يُقَالَ لَهُمْ ذَلِكَ، وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ ثَمَّ قَوْلٌ. وَمَعْنَى ﴿وَادْعُوا ثُبُورًا كَثِيرًا﴾ أَنَّكُمْ وَقَعْتُمْ فِيمَا لَيْسَ ثُبُورُكُمْ مِنْهُ وَاحِدًا، إِنَّمَا هُوَ ثُبُورٌ كَثِيرٌ، إِمَّا لِأَنَّ العَذَابَ أَنْوَاعٌ وَأَلْوَانٌ، لِكُلِّ نَوْعٍ مِنْهَا ثُبُورٌ لِشِدَّتِهِ وَفَظَاعَتِهِ، أَوْ لِأَنَّهُمْ كُلَّمَا نَضِجَتْ جُلُودُهُمْ بُدِّلُوا غَيْرَهَا، أَوْ لِأَنَّ ذَلِكَ العَذَابَ دَائِمٌ خَالِصٌ عَنِ الشَّوْبِ، فَلَهُمْ فِي كُلِّ وَقْتٍ مِنَ الأَوْقَاتِ الَّتِي لَا نِهَايَةَ لَهَا ثُبُورٌ، أَوْ لِأَنَّهُمْ رُبَّمَا يَجِدُونَ بِسَبَبِ ذَلِكَ القَوْلِ نَوْعًا مِنَ الخِفَّةِ، فَإِنَّ المُعَذَّبَ إِذَا صَاحَ وَبَكَى وَجَدَ بِسَبَبِهِ نَوْعًا مِنَ الخِفَّةِ فَيُزْجَرُونَ عَنْ ذَلِكَ، وَيُخْبَرُونَ بِأَنَّ هَذَا الثُّبُورَ سَيَزْدَادُ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ لِيَزْدَادَ حُزْنُهُمْ وَغَمُّهُمْ، نَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ مِنْهُ. قَالَ al-Kalbi (الكَلْبِيُّ): نَزَلَ هَذَا كُلُّهُ فِي حَقِّ أَبِي جَهْلٍ وَالكُفَّارِ الَّذِينَ ذَكَرُوا تِلْكَ الشُّبُهَاتِ.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verse 15–16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which has been promised to the God-fearing? It shall be for them a reward and a destination."﴾ ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, abiding forever. It is a promise incumbent upon your Lord, one to be asked for.﴾ In the verse there are issues:

The First Issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, described the state of the punishment prepared for those who deny the Hour, He followed it with what reinforces the regret and remorse. So He said to His Messenger: ﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity"﴾, [that they should seek it] through belief and obedience. If it is asked: How can it be said, "Is the punishment better, or the Garden of Eternity?" Is it permissible for a rational person to say, "Is sugar sweeter, or patience?" We say: This is fitting in the context of rebuke, as when a master gives his slave wealth, and he rebels, refuses and is arrogant, so he beats him a painful beating, and says by way of reproach: "Is this better, or that?"

The Second Issue: Our companions argued with His saying, ﴿those who are God-fearing have been promised﴾, that reward is not obligatory upon God, exalted is He; for whoever says, "The sultan promised so-and-so that he would give him such-and-such," that is understood as favor. As for if that giving were obligatory, one would not say that he promised him it. As for the Mu'tazilah, they also argued with it for their doctrine, saying: Because He, glorified is He, established that promise for those described with the attribute of God-consciousness, and the linking of a judgment to an attribute indicates causation. So this indicates that this promise came about being caused by the attribute of God-consciousness, and favor is not specific to the God-fearing, so what is specific to them must be obligatory.

صفحة ٥١
The Third Issue: Abu Muslim said: The Garden of Eternity is the one whose bliss does not end. "Khuld" and "khulud" are the same, like "shukr" and "shukur"; God, exalted is He, said: ﴿We do not want from you any reward or thanks﴾ [al-Insan: 9]. If it is said: "Paradise" is a name for the abode of reward, and it is everlasting, so what is the benefit of His saying ﴿the Garden of Eternity﴾? We say: The idafah (construct) may be for distinction, and it may be for explaining an attribute of perfection, as one says: "God is the Creator, the Originator"; and what is here is of this kind.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿It shall be for them a reward and a destination﴾, there are issues:
The First Issue: The Mu'tazilah argued with this verse to establish entitlement in two respects:

The first: The term "reward" applies only to what is deserved; as for a promise by pure favor, it is not called a reward.

The second: If the meaning of "reward" were what they arrive at merely by the promise, then there would be no difference between His saying ﴿a reward﴾ and His saying ﴿and a destination﴾, and that would be repetition without benefit.

Our companions, may God have mercy on them, said: There is no dispute that it is a ﴿reward﴾; the dispute is whether its being a reward was established by the promise or by entitlement, and there is nothing in the verse that indicates a specific one.

The Second Issue: The Mu'tazilah said: The verse indicates that God, exalted is He, does not pardon the one who commits a major sin, in two respects:

The first: The one who commits a major sin deserves punishment, so he must not be deserving of reward; for reward is lasting benefit pure of any admixture of harm, and punishment is lasting harm pure of any admixture of benefit, and combining the two is impossible; and what is impossible to exist, its entitlement is impossible to occur. So whenever the entitlement to punishment is established, the entitlement to reward must cease. We say: If God pardoned the one who commits a major sin, then either He would bring him out of the Fire and not admit him to Paradise, and that is false by consensus, for they agreed that accountable people on the Day of Resurrection are either among the people of Paradise or the people of the Fire, since He, exalted is He, said: ﴿A party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura: 7]; or He would bring him out of the Fire and admit him to Paradise, and that is false, for Paradise is the right of the God-fearing, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It shall be for them a reward and a destination﴾, so He made Paradise for them and specific to them, and showed that it was for them only because it is a reward for them for their deeds, so it was their right, and giving a person's right to another is not permissible. And since the divisions have been refuted, it is established that pardon is not permissible. Our companions answered: Why is it not permissible to say: the God-fearing are content with God's admitting the people of pardon into Paradise? Then their entry into it is not impossible.

The second respect: They said: In the usage of the Shariah, "the God-fearing" is specific to those who guard against disbelief and major sins; and although we differ as to whether the one who commits a major sin is called a believer or not, we agree that he is not called God-fearing. Then He said in describing Paradise: it was for them a reward and a destination, and this is restrictive, meaning it is a destination for the God-fearing and not for others; and if that is so, the one who commits a major sin must not enter it. We say: At most, what this amounts to is that this generality is explicit regarding the threat, so we specify it by the verses of promise.

The Third Issue: One may say: Paradise will become a reward and a destination for the God-fearing, but after it has become so, why did God say: ﴿it was for them a reward and a destination﴾? Its answer is in two respects:

The first: What God has promised, in its realization, is as if it already was.

The second: It was written on the Preserved Tablet, before God created them by vast periods of time, that Paradise is their reward and their destination.

* * *

صفحة ٥٢
As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, abiding forever﴾, it is similar to His saying: ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire﴾ [Fussilat: 31], and there are issues:

The First Issue: One may say: The people of the lower ranks, when they witness the higher ranks, must desire them; so if they ask their Lord for them, then if He gives them to them, no difference remains between the deficient and the complete in rank; and if He does not give them, that impugns His saying ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish﴾. Also, if a father has a son in the ranks of the Fire and in the most severe punishment, and he wishes that God deliver him from that punishment, he must ask his Lord to deliver him from it; if God does so, that impugns that the punishment of the disbeliever is everlasting; and if He does not, that impugns His saying ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire﴾ [Fussilat: 31] and His saying ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish﴾ [Qaf: 35]. Its answer: God removes that thought from the hearts of the people of Paradise; rather, each one of them being occupied with the pleasures he has becomes a preoccupation that prevents him from turning to the state of others.

The Second Issue: The condition of the bliss of Paradise is that it be everlasting; for if it ended, it would be tainted with some kind of grief. For this reason al-Mutanabbi said:

The greatest grief to me is joy whose possessor is certain it will pass away.
For this reason He took its eternity into account, saying: ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, abiding forever﴾.

The Third Issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish﴾ is like an alert that the attainment of all desires in their entirety occurs only in Paradise; as for other than it, that does not occur, rather in this world its comforts must be mixed with wounds. For this reason, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever seeks what has not been created for him wearies himself and is not provided; it was said: And what is that, O Messenger of God? He said: The joy of a day."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿It is a promise incumbent upon your Lord, one to be asked for﴾, there are issues:

The First Issue: The word "ʿalā" (incumbent) indicates obligation. He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever vows and names it, upon him is the fulfillment of what he named." So His saying ﴿incumbent upon your Lord﴾ indicates that this is obligatory upon God, exalted is He. And the obligatory is that which, if not done, its abandoner would deserve blame by his act; or it is that whose non-existence is impossible. If obligation is by the first explanation, its abandonment would be impossible, for since its abandonment entails deserving blame, and God's deserving blame is impossible, and what entails the impossible is impossible, that abandonment would be impossible, and the impossible is not within power; so God would not be able not to do it, and it would follow that He is compelled to the act. And if obligation is by the second explanation, namely that the obligatory is what whose non-existence is impossible, then the doctrine of compulsion follows necessarily, and God would not be capable. If it is said: It is established by the judgment of the promise, we say: If He did not do it, His true report would turn into falsehood and His knowledge into ignorance, and that is impossible; and what leads to the impossible is impossible; so abandonment is impossible, and it follows that He is compelled to the act; and one compelled to an act is not capable, nor deserving of praise and commendation.

The completion of the objection and its answer: The doing of a thing precedes the report about its doing and the knowledge of its doing; so that act is an act not by way of compulsion, and so He was capable and deserving of praise and commendation.

The Second Issue: His saying ﴿promise﴾ indicates that Paradise came about by the judgment of the promise, not by the judgment of entitlement, and this has been established previously.

صفحة ٥٣
The Third Issue: His saying ﴿one to be asked for﴾: they mentioned several meanings concerning it:
One of them: The responsible people asked Him by their saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 194].

The second: The responsible people asked Him through the language of their state; for when they bore severe hardship in obeying Him, that stood in place of a request. Al-Mutanabbi said:

Within the soul are needs, and in you is shrewdness; my silence is speech in its presence, and address.

The third: The angels asked God for that by their saying: ﴿Our Lord, and admit them to Gardens of Eternity﴾ [Ghafir: 8].

The fourth: ﴿a promise to be asked for﴾, meaning obligatory; it is said: "I will certainly give you a thousand, a promise to be asked for," meaning obligatory even if you do not ask. This was said by al-Farra'. The other meanings are closer to this, since they are closer to the literal reality, whereas what al-Farra' said is metaphorical.

The fifth: "to be asked for" meaning that it is his right that he be asked, since it is a right and obligatory, either by the judgment of entitlement according to the Mu'tazilah, or by the judgment of the promise according to the People of the Sunnah.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verse 17:**

God's words: ﴿And on the Day He gathers them and what they worship besides God, and He says, "Did you lead these servants of Mine astray, or did they themselves stray from the way?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "Glory be to You! It was not for us to take any protectors besides You, but You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the Reminder, and they were a people doomed to perish."﴾ ﴿Indeed they have denied you in what you say, so you cannot avert [the punishment] nor gain help. And whoever among you does wrong, We shall make him taste a great punishment.﴾ ﴿We did not send any messengers before you except that they ate food and walked in the markets, and We made some of you a trial for others. Will you be patient? Your Lord is ever Seeing.﴾

Know that God's words ﴿And on the Day He gathers them﴾ refer back to His words ﴿and they have taken gods besides Him﴾ (25:3). Then there are several issues here:

**First issue: ﴿yaḥshuruhum﴾ (He gathers them).** We say: both are read with the *nūn* and with the *yā'*. It is also read *naḥshuruhum* with a *kasra* on the *shīn*.

**Second issue:** The apparent meaning of His words ﴿and what they worship﴾ is idols, and the apparent meaning of His words ﴿He says, "Did you lead these servants of Mine astray"﴾ is that it refers to those among the living who were worshipped, such as the angels, the Messiah and others, because leading astray and its opposite are possible for them. Because of this, the scholars differed.

Some people understood it to refer to idols. If it is said to them, "An idol is an inanimate object, so how did God address it, and how was it able to answer?", they then mention two views:

The first: God creates life in them, and at that point He addresses them and they return an answer.

The second: that speech is not spoken with the tongue, but is in the manner of the "tongue of the state" (*lisān al-ḥāl*), as some of them mentioned regarding the glorification of dead things and the speech of hands and feet, and as it is said: "Ask the earth, who split your rivers and planted your trees? If it does not answer you in dialogue, it will answer you by reflection."

As for the majority, they claimed that what is meant is the angels, Jesus and Uzayr, peace be upon them. They said: this view is reinforced by God's words ﴿And on the Day He gathers them all, then He will say to the angels, "Was it you whom they used to worship?"﴾ (34:40). And if it is said to them that the word *mā* ("what") is not used for rational beings, they answered it in two ways:

The first: We do not accept that the word *mā* is only for non-rational beings, as evidence that they say *man* ("who") for non-rational beings.

The second: It is intended as a description, as if it were said: "and their object of worship." God's words ﴿By the sky and He who built it﴾ (91:5) and ﴿Nor will you worship what I worship﴾ (109:3) cannot be correct except according to one of these two views. In any case, the objection falls away.

**Third issue:** The summary of the discourse is that God gathers those who were worshipped, then says to them: "Did you put My servants into error, away from the path of truth, or did they stray from it of their own accord?" The Mu'tazilah said: In this there is a clear refutation of those who say that God in reality leads His servants astray, because if the matter were so, the correct answer would have been for them to say: "Our God has a third option besides these two, which is the truth, namely that You led them astray." But when they did not say that, and instead attributed their misguidance to themselves, we know that God does not lead any of His servants astray.

If it is said: We do not accept that the worshipped ones did not address this option; rather they mentioned it, for they said: ﴿but You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the Reminder﴾, and this is an explicit statement that their misguidance came about because of what God did to them, namely that He, glory be to Him, gave them and their fathers the bounties of this world. We say: If the matter were as you say, it would follow that God would become veiled in the hand of those worshipped beings, and it is known that this is not the intent. Rather, the intent is that the unbeliever be shown to be defeated, silenced and held accountable. This is the full statement of the Mu'tazilah's position on the verse.

Our companions answered: The capacity for misguidance, if it is not suited to guidance, then leading astray is from God, the Exalted. And if it is suited to it, then its being a source of leading astray is not preferred over its being a source of guidance, except by a preponderating cause from God, the Exalted. At that point the question returns. As for the apparent meaning of this verse, although it is in their favour, it is opposed by the other apparent meanings that agree with our position.

**Fourth issue:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that this question is from God, the Exalted, although it is possible that it could be from the angels by God's command.

Questions remain about the verse:

**The first question:** What is the benefit of ﴿antum﴾ ("you") and ﴿hum﴾ ("they")? Why was it not said: "Did you lead these servants of Mine astray, or did they stray from the way?" The answer: The question is not about the act and its existence, for if the act did not exist, this reproach would not be directed. Rather, it is about its doer, so it is necessary to mention him and attach to him the interrogative particle, so that it is known that he is the one being asked about.

**The second question:** He, glory be to Him, has been knowing from eternity the state of the one being asked about, so what is the benefit of this question? The answer: This is a question in the manner of rebuke to the polytheists, as He said to Jesus: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides God"?﴾ (5:116). Also, because those worshipped ones, when they disowned themselves and attributed that misguidance to them, the disowning of the worshipped ones toward them became greater in their grief and bewilderment.

**The third question:** He, the Exalted, said ﴿or did they themselves stray from the way?﴾, and the analogical form would be: "they strayed from the way." The answer: The original is that, but when a person is extreme in negligence and lacking in caution, it is said: "he strayed the way."

\* \* \*

As for His words ﴿Glory be to You!﴾: Know that He, glory be to Him, related their answer, and in His words ﴿Glory be to You!﴾ there are several aspects:

First: He expressed wonder at them, since they were astonished at what was said to them, because they are angels and prophets who are protected from sin; how far they are from leading astray, which is specific to Iblis and his party.

Second: They spoke ﴿Glory be to You!﴾ to show that they are those who glorify, sanctify and believe in that, so how would it befit their state that they would lead His servants astray?

Third: By it they intended to declare Him free from equals, whether that equal be an idol, a prophet or an angel.

Fourth: They intended to declare Him free from having the purpose of this question be gaining knowledge or harming one who was innocent of wrongdoing; rather He asked them only to rebuke and censure the unbelievers.

As for His words ﴿It was not for us to take any protectors besides You﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** The well-known reading is ﴿an nattakhidha﴾ with a *fatḥa* on the *nūn* and a *kasra* on the *khā'*. It is reported from Abu Ja'far and Ibn 'Amir that it is read with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* and a *fatḥa* on the *khā'* in the passive form (*mā lam yusammā fā'iluh*, "whose doer is not named"). Al-Zajjaj said: "He erred who read ﴿an nuttakhadha﴾ with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn*, because *min* enters this construction on nouns only when the noun is the first object; it does not enter on the object of the state. You say: 'I did not take any one as a protector (*mā ittakhadhtu min aḥadin waliyyan*)', and it is not permitted to say: 'I did not take anyone as a protector (*mā ittakhadhtu aḥadan min waliyyin*)'." The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: *ittakhadha* is transitive to one object, as in your saying "he took a protector (*ittakhadha waliyyan*)", and to two objects, as in your saying "he took so-and-so as a protector (*ittakhadha fulānan waliyyan*)". God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And God took Abraham as a close friend﴾ (4:125). The first reading is of the one transitive to one object, which is ﴿min awliyā'﴾ ("any protectors"), and the original is ﴿an nattakhidha awliyā'﴾, but *min* was added to emphasize the meaning of negation. The second is of the one transitive to two objects: the first is the one to which the verb is attached (the subject, *nā*), and the second is ﴿min awliyā'﴾, where *min* is partitive, meaning: "we do not take some protectors." The indefiniteness of ﴿awliyā'﴾ is because, as protectors, they are specific protectors, namely the jinn and the idols.

**Second issue:** They mentioned several views in the interpretation of this verse:

The first, which is the most correct and strongest: the meaning is, "If we do not consider it right to take protectors besides You, how would we call others to that?"

The second: "It was not fitting for us to be like the devils in their befriending of the unbelievers, as the unbelievers befriend them." God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So fight the protectors of Satan﴾ (4:76), meaning the unbelievers, and He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the taghut﴾ (2:257). This is from Abu Muslim.

The third: "It was not for us to take protectors besides Your pleasure," meaning, since we knew that You would not be pleased with this, we did not do it. The summary is that the *muḍāf* (the governing noun) was omitted and the *muḍāf ilayh* (the governed noun) was put in its place.

The fourth: The angels said: "They are Your servants, so it is not fitting for Your servants to take any protector or beloved besides Your permission, let alone for one servant to take another servant as a god for himself."

The fifth: On the reading of Abu Ja'far, the difficulty disappears. If it is said: "This reading is not permissible, because they have no part in others taking them as protectors," we say: The meaning is that we are not suited to that, so how would we call them to our worship?

The sixth: This is the statement of the idols, and that they said: "It is not valid for us to be among those who worship, so how can we claim that we are among those who are worshipped?"

**Third issue:** The verse indicates that befriending and enmity are not permissible except by God's permission. So every friendship that is based on the inclination of the soul and the share of natural disposition, that is contrary to the Sharia.

[Page 56]

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the Reminder, and they were a people ruined﴾, there are several issues.

The first issue: the meaning of the verse is that You, our God, bestowed abundant blessings upon them and their fathers, and these blessings necessitate gratitude and faith, not turning away and disbelief. The purpose of this is to show that they went astray by their own choice and not by Our leading them astray. For were it not for their manifest obstinacy, then, with this proof made manifest, it would be impossible to turn away from obeying God, Exalted is He.

Others said: this statement is like an allusion to what Moses, peace be upon him, stated plainly in His saying: ﴿It is but Your trial﴾ [al-A'raf 7:155]. This is because the one who answers says: "My God, You are the One who gave him all his worldly desires, until he became like one drowning in the sea of appetites. His total immersion in them became an obstacle preventing him from turning to Your obedience and occupying himself with Your service. So it is but Your trial."

The second issue: the Reminder (al-dhikr) means the remembrance of God, faith in Him, the Qur'an, and the laws (shara'i'), or whatever brings them good remembrance in this world and the Hereafter.

The third issue: Abu 'Ubayda said: it is said "rajul bur" (a ruined man), "rajulan bur" (two ruined men), and "rijal bur" (ruined men), and likewise for the feminine. Its meaning is "perishing" (halik). It is also said "rajul ba'ir" and "qawm bur," and it is like "ha'ir" and "hur." Al-bawar means destruction (al-halak). Our companions (i.e., the Ash'ari theologians) have argued with this verse on the issue of divine decree and predestination (al-qada' wa'l-qadar). There is no doubt that what is meant by it is: "and they were among those who were judged in the Hereafter to suffer punishment and destruction." Therefore, the one whom God has judged to suffer the punishment of the Hereafter, and has known this, recorded it, and established it in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), and informed the angels of it, if he were to become a believer, then the true report would become false, knowledge would become ignorance, the writing established in the Preserved Tablet would become invalid, and the belief of the angels would become ignorance. All of this is impossible, and what necessitates the impossible is impossible. Therefore the emergence of faith from him is impossible. This shows that the one destined for happiness cannot turn into a wretched one, and the wretched one cannot turn into a happy one.

From another aspect: they mentioned that God gave them the causes of misguidance, namely the granting of worldly desires and the total immersion of the soul in them. The verse indicates that this cause reached a level that necessitates ruin. For mentioning ruin immediately after this cause indicates that the ruin occurred because of that cause. Thus the outcome of the statement returns to this: God, Exalted is He, did to the disbeliever what made him such that it is impossible for him to abandon disbelief. In that case it becomes clear that the happy one does not turn into a wretched one, and the wretched one does not turn into a happy one.

As for His saying: ﴿Then they have denied you in what you say﴾, know that it has been recited as "yaqulun" with the letter ya' and with ta'. The meaning for one who reads with ta' is: "they have denied you by your statement that they are gods," i.e., they denied you in your saying that they are gods. For one who reads with the dotted ya' from beneath, the meaning is that they denied you by your saying "Glory be to You" (subhanaka). An example of this is your saying: "I wrote with the pen."

As for His saying: ﴿so you cannot avert [punishment] or get help﴾, know that it has been recited as "yasta'un" also with ya' and with ta'. That is, "you, O disbelievers, cannot avert the punishment from yourselves." It was also said: al-sarf means repentance; it was also said: it means a stratagem, from their saying: "he is tasarraf," i.e., he schemes. Or the meaning is: "your gods cannot avert the punishment from you, nor can they devise stratagems for you."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And whoever among you wrongs, We will make him taste a great punishment﴾, there are two issues in it.

The first issue: it has been recited as "yudhiqhu" with ya', and in it the pronoun refers either to God, Exalted is He, or to the wrongdoing (al-zulm).

The second issue: the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilite theologians) held fast to this verse in affirming with certainty the threat (wa'id) against the people of major sins. They said: it is established that "man" (من) is general in the context of a conditional, and it is established that the disbeliever is a wrongdoer, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, association is great injustice﴾ [Luqman 31:13], and the sinner (fasiq) is a wrongdoer, by His saying: ﴿And whoever does not repent, it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:11]. Therefore it is established by this verse that the sinner is not pardoned, but will certainly be punished.

* * *

[Page 57]

The answer: we do not concede that the word "man" in the context of a conditional is general, and the discussion of this is mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). Even if we concede that it is general, is that with certainty or with probability? The claim of certainty is disputed. For we observe in common, well-known usage the employment of forms of generality while the intended meaning is the majority, or because the intended ones are specific groups. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:6]. Then, many of those who disbelieved have indeed believed. There is no way to dispel this except to say: His saying "those who disbelieve," although it indicates generality, what is meant by it is the majority, or what is meant by it is specific groups. In either case, it is established that the use of expressions of generality for the most part is a clear custom, and when that is so, the indication of these forms on generality is an apparent indication, not a decisive one, and that does not negate the permissibility of pardon.

Even if we concede that its indication is decisive, we agree that His saying: ﴿And whoever among you wrongs﴾ is conditional upon there being nothing that removes it. At this point we say: this is conceded, but why do you say that nothing removing it exists? For pardon (al-'afw) is, in our view, one of the things that removes it, and that is one of the three mentioned at the beginning of the issue. Even if we concede its indication to what he said, it is nevertheless opposed by the verses of promise, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them will be the Gardens of Paradise as a lodging﴾ [al-Kahf 18:107]. If it is said: the verses of threat take precedence, because the thief has his hand cut off as a deterrent, and one who does not deserve punishment may not have his hand cut off as a deterrent; so when it is established that he deserves punishment, it is established that the entitlement to reward is nullified, because we have explained that combining the two entitlements is impossible. We reply: we do not concede that the thief has his hand cut off as a deterrent. Do you not see that if he repents, his hand is cut off not as a deterrent but as a trial (mihna)? Let us set aside these positions. Nevertheless, His saying: ﴿And whoever among you wrongs﴾ is addressed to specific, identified people. Grant that He will not pardon them; why do you say that He will not pardon others?

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾, there are several issues in it.

The first issue: this is an answer to their saying: ﴿What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan 25:7]. God, Exalted is He, has shown that this is a constant practice of God with all His messengers, so there is no basis for this criticism.

The second issue: the proper form of the statement would be "ala annahum" with a fatha on the alif, because it is in the middle, and the kasra is only suitable at the beginning of a sentence. Because of this, they mentioned several explanations:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: the clause after (illa) is an attribute of a deleted noun, and the meaning is: "And We did not send before you any messenger among the messengers except that they were eating and walking." It was deleted because His saying "among the messengers" is an indication of it. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat 37:164], meaning: "there is none of us but is one who has a known station."

The second: al-Farra' said: it is a relative clause (silah) attached to a deleted noun, and the sense is satisfied by His saying "among the messengers." The meaning is: "except one who they are." Like His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾ [Maryam 19:71], meaning "except one who will pass over it." According to al-Zajjaj, the noun described is deleted; according to al-Farra', the relative noun is what is deleted. It is not permissible, according to the Basrans, to delete the relative noun and leave the relative clause.

The third: Ibn al-Anbari said: "inna" is given a kasra after the exception by supposing a waw, on the reckoning of "illa wa-innahum."

The fourth: some of them said: the meaning is "except it is said: they are..."

The third issue: it has been recited as "yumashsha'un" in the passive voice, meaning: their needs cause them to walk, or the people cause them to walk. Had it been recited as "yamshun," it would have been more appropriate, were it not for the transmitted recitation.

The third issue: it has been recited as "yumashsha'un" in the passive voice, meaning: their needs cause them to walk, or the people cause them to walk. Had it been recited as "yamshun," it would have been more appropriate, were it not for the transmitted recitation.

**[Page 58]**

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾, there are several issues.

**First issue:** There are several opinions on it.

One: This refers to the chiefs of the polytheists and the poor Companions. When a man of noble standing sees a lowly man embrace Islam before him, he is too proud to embrace it himself, so he remains upon his disbelief, lest the lowly man have precedence and merit over him. Its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11]. This is the view of al-Kalbi, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

Two: This applies to all people in general. Abu al-Darda' narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Woe to the scholar because of the ignorant, woe to the ruler because of the subjects, woe to the subjects because of the ruler, woe to the master because of the slave, woe to the strong because of the weak, and to the weak because of the strong, some of you are a trial for others." And he recited this verse.

Three: This applies to those who are tested and those who enjoy well-being. One says: "Why was I not made like him in form and character, in intellect and knowledge, in provision and lifespan?" This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

Four: This is an argument against them concerning the specification of Muhammad with prophethood, although he is equal to them in humanity and its attributes. So He afflicted the messengers through those to whom they were sent, and with various kinds of harm, as He said: ﴿And you will certainly hear much hurtful talk from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with Allah﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 186]. Those to whom the messenger was sent are also harmed by the messenger, due to envy and his becoming obligated to serve and to give up self and wealth after having been a leader who was served. The most fitting interpretation of the verse is that it applies to all of them, because there is a shared measure among all of them.

**Second issue:** Our companions said: the verse indicates qada' and qadar (divine decree and predestination), because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾. Al-Jubba'i (al-Jubba'i, a Mu'tazili scholar) said: this "making" means "informing," as is said of one who stole: "Verily, so-and-so is a thief," meaning he made him a thief. This interpretation is weak, because He, exalted is He, attributed the making to the state of being a trial, not to the judgment that it is so. Rather, reason indicates that the intended meaning is other than what he mentioned. This is because the one who causes the cause is the one who causes the effect. Whoever Allah, exalted is He, created with the temperament of bile and heat, and with the character of anger, and then created within him the perception that informs him of the thing that angers him, the one who did this whole combination is necessarily the one who produced the anger. The same applies to envy and the rest of the characters and actions. At this point it becomes clear that it is He, glorified is He, who made some a trial for others. Even if we grant that what al-Jubba'i said is the intended meaning, namely that "making" means judgment, yet if what is made were to change, it would necessitate the change of Allah's judgment from truth to falsehood, and that is impossible. So the change of that making is impossible, and therefore the change of what is made is also impossible. At this point the doctrine of qada' and qadar becomes evident.

**Third issue:** The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when the people criticized the Messenger (ﷺ), saying that he eats food and walks in the markets, and that he is poor, these words were like fabrications. For when the proof of prophethood was established, none of these things had any effect in discrediting it. So the Prophet (ﷺ) was harmed by them, both because they insulted him and because they uttered crooked, corrupt speech and did not understand a good reply. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, made him patient through all that harm, and He explained that He made some of creation a trial for others.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you be patient? And your Lord is ever Seeing﴾, there are several issues.

**First issue:** The Mu'tazila said: If His saying ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾ were intended as a report, He would not have followed it with ﴿Will you be patient?﴾, because commanding the incapable is not permissible.

**Second issue:** The meaning is: Will you be patient under trials? You know what Allah has promised to those who are patient. ﴿And your Lord is ever Seeing﴾

**[Page 59]**

That is, He is the Knower of who is patient and who is not patient, so He will reward each of them with the reward or punishment they deserve.

**Third issue:** His saying ﴿Will you be patient?﴾ is an interrogative, and what is intended by it is confirmation (taqrir). Its position after the mention of the trial is like the position of "which of you" after the testing in His saying: ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hud: 7].

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verse 21:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Why have the angels not been sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?" Indeed, they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression.﴾ ﴿On the day they see the angels, there will be no good tidings that day for the criminals, and they will say, "A forbidding, forbidden [barrier]."﴾ ﴿And We will advance toward what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust.﴾ ﴿The companions of the Garden, that day, will be better in resting place and finer in place of noontime rest.﴾

Know that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Why have the angels not been sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?"﴾ is the fourth doubt of those who deny the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). Its substance is: Why did God not send down the angels so that they might testify that Muhammad is truthful in his claim? Or why do we not see our Lord, so that He may tell us directly that He sent him to us? The formulation of this doubt is that whoever wants to achieve something, and has two paths to achieving it, one of which certainly leads to it and the other of which may or may not lead to it, then the Wise One, in His wisdom, must choose in achieving that aim the stronger and better path. There is no doubt that the sending down of angels to testify to the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) is more conducive to the aim. So if God, exalted is He, wanted to confirm Muhammad (ﷺ), He would have done that; and since He did not do that, we know that He did not want to confirm him. This is the substance of the doubt. Then there are several issues here:

**The first issue:** al-Farra' said: His saying, ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us﴾, means: those who do not fear meeting Us. Placing "expect" (rajaʾ) in the place of "fear" (khawf) is a Tihamah dialect usage when it is accompanied by denial. A similar example is His saying, ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not expect for God any dignity?﴾ [Nuh: 13], i.e., you do not fear any greatness of His. Al-Qadi said: There is no basis for this, because whenever a statement can be taken in its literal sense, it is not permissible to take it in its figurative sense. It is known that the condition of the idol-worshippers is that, just as they do not fear punishment because they deny the Return, likewise they do not expect to meet Us or Our promise of Paradise and reward for obedience. And it is known that whoever does not expect that does not fear punishment either; so fear follows from this expectation.

**The second issue:** The Mujassimah (anthropomorphists) held on to His saying, ﴿meeting Us﴾, that He is a body. They said: "Meeting" (liqaʾ) means arrival, as one says: "This body met that," i.e., it arrived at it and came into contact with it. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then the water met upon a matter already decreed﴾ [al-Qamar: 12]. So the verse indicates that He, glorified is He, is a body. The answer is given in two ways:

The first is the way of some of our companions (the Ashʿarites). He said: The intended meaning of "meeting" is seeing, because the one who sees, by his seeing, arrives at the reality of the seen object. So "meeting" is called one of the types of seeing, and the other type is contact and touching. Thus the verse, from this perspective, indicates the permissibility of seeing.

The second way, which is the statement of the Mu'tazilah (the Rationalist school): The Qadi said: Interpreting "meeting" as visual sight is ignorance of the language. One says in supplication: "May God meet you with good" (laqqākallāh al-khayr). A speaker may say: "I did not meet the amir," even if he saw him from a distance or was screened from him. And one says of a blind man: "He met the amir" when he was given permission and was not barred. And one may meet someone on a dark night without seeing him. Rather, the intended meaning of "meeting" here is coming to His judgment, where no one else has any judgment, as in ﴿The day when no soul will have power for any soul at all﴾ [al-Infitar: 19], not visual sight. Know that this statement is weak, because we do not interpret "meeting" as visual sight; rather, we interpret it with a shared meaning between visual seeing and contact and touching, namely arrival at a thing. We have already shown that the one who sees arrives by his seeing at the seen object. And a word that is coined for a meaning shared among many meanings applies to each of those meanings. So the statement "May He meet you with good" is correct, and the blind man's statement "I met the amir" is correct, and the sighted man's statement "I met him" in the sense of "I saw him," and "I did not meet him" in the sense of "I did not arrive at him," are all correct. If this is established, then we say: His saying, ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say﴾, is mentioned in the context of censuring them. Therefore, expectation of meeting must be affirmed, and the meaning of "meeting" is shared between physical arrival and arrival by sight. The first has been ruled out, so the second is determined. And his statement that "the intended meaning of meeting is arrival at His judgment" is a diversion of the word from its apparent meaning without evidence. Thus the verse's indication of the validity of seeing is established, indeed of its obligatoriness, indeed that denying it is nothing but the religion of the disbelievers.

**The third issue:** His saying, ﴿Why has not ... been sent down﴾ [lawlā unzila], means: "Why not" (halla unzila). Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: This verse was revealed about Abu Jahl, al-Walid, and their companions, who denied prophethood and resurrection.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression﴾, know that this is the answer to that doubt, and in it there are issues:

**The first issue:** In establishing that it is an answer, there are several aspects:

First: When the Qur'an's being miraculous has become manifest, the proof of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) has been established. After that, the demanding of such signs can only be pure arrogance and obstinacy.

Second: If the descent of the angels had occurred, it too would have been among the miracles, and it would not indicate truthfulness specifically because it is by the descent of an angel, but because of the general fact of its being a miracle. So accepting that miracle and rejecting that other miracle would be preferring one of two equal things over the other without any added benefit or preponderant reason; and this is pure arrogance and obstinacy.

Third: Suppose they were to see the Lord and ask Him about the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ), and He, glorified is He, says: "Yes, he is My messenger." That would add nothing to confirmation beyond the manifestation of a miracle at the hand of Muhammad (ﷺ). Because we have shown that the miracle stands in the place of confirmation by speech, since there is no difference, when one who claims prophethood says: "O God, if I am truthful, then revive this dead man," and God Almighty revives him, though such a thing is not customary, and between God's saying to him: "You are truthful." And since the confirmation obtained by speech or obtained by a miracle is equally a confirmation of the claimant, then specifying one of them is pure arrogance and obstinacy.

Fourth: We believe that God, glorified is He, acts according to what is beneficial, as the Mu'tazilah say; or we say that God, exalted is He, acts according to His will, as our companions say. If it is the first, then it is not permissible for them to specify the miracle, since perhaps the manifestation of that miracle would involve a corruption that only God Almighty knows; and specifying it would be arrogance and transgression, in that when one thinks something is beneficial, he is certain it is beneficial. Whoever says that has believed about himself that he knows all knowable things, and that is great arrogance. If it is the second, which is the statement of our companions, then it is not for the servant to propose conditions to his Lord, for He is the doer of whatever He wills. So proposing would be arrogance, transgression, and going beyond the limit of servanthood to the station of contention and opposition.

Fifth: The purpose of sending prophets is the benefit of creatures. When a great king shows kindness to some weak person out of mercy, and that weak person takes to disputing and contention, saying: "I do not want this; rather I want that," it is fitting to say: This beggar has become arrogant within himself and has transgressed with severe transgression, since he does not know his own worth and the limit of his rank. So it is here too.

Sixth: It is possible that the meaning is that God Almighty said: If I knew that they did not raise this question out of arrogance and severe transgression, I would have granted them their request. But I know that they raised this proposal out of arrogance and obstinacy, so if I granted them their request, they would not benefit from it. Therefore, I will certainly not give them that. This interpretation is recognized from the wording.

Seventh: Perhaps they heard from the People of the Book that God, exalted is He, is not seen in this world, and that He does not send down angels in this world to the common people. Then they conditioned their faith on that, either as obstinacy or as mockery.

* * *

**The second issue:** The Mu'tazilah said: The verse indicates that seeing God, exalted is He, is impermissible, because if seeing Him were permissible, asking for it would not be transgression and arrogance. They said: His saying, ﴿Indeed, they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression﴾ is only because of their asking to see Him; even if they had limited themselves to the descent of the angels, they would not have been addressed with that. The proof of this is that God, exalted is He, mentioned the matter of seeing in another verse separately, and mentioned the enormity of it, namely His saying, ﴿We will never believe you until we see God openly, and the thunderbolt seized you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55]; and He mentioned the descent of the angels separately in another verse, and did not mention enormity, namely their saying, ﴿Why have the angels not been sent down to us?﴾ and "Do we see the angels?" So it is established by this that the arrogance and transgression in this verse only occurred because of asking to see.

Know that the discussion of this has already preceded in surah al-Baqarah. What we want here is that we have shown that His saying, ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say﴾, indicates seeing. As for arrogance and transgression, it is not possible for that to indicate that seeing is impossible; because whoever asks for something impossible is not called one who has transgressed and become arrogant. Do you not see that when they said, ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 138], He did not attribute to them transgression and arrogance for asking for this impossibility, but said: ﴿Indeed, you are a people who are ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 138]. Rather, transgression and arrogance are established only when a person asks for what is not fitting for him from one above him, or what was fitting for him but he asks for it by way of obstinacy. In summary, we have mentioned many aspects in clarifying the meaning of arrogance and transgression, whether seeing is impossible or possible. And among what indicates this is that when Moses asked for seeing, God, exalted is He, did not describe him with arrogance and transgression, because he, peace be upon him, asked for seeing out of longing, whereas these people asked for it as a test and by obstinacy. Therefore He described them with that. Thus the falsity of what the Mu'tazilah said is established.

**The third issue:** He said ﴿within themselves﴾ because they concealed arrogance against the truth, which is disbelief and stubbornness, in their hearts, and they believed it; as He said: ﴿There is nothing in their breasts but pride, which they will never attain﴾ [Ghafir: 56]. And His saying, ﴿and have transgressed with great transgression﴾, means they exceeded the limit in wrongdoing. One says: "So-and-so transgressed." He has described the transgression with greatness, thereby exaggerating its extremity, meaning that they did not dare this great statement except because they had reached the utmost degree of arrogance and the farthest limit of transgression.

Regarding the words of the Most High: ﴿On the day they see the angels, there will be no good news that day for the criminals, and they will say, "A barrier, barred."﴾ This is a response to their statement: ﴿Why were the angels not sent down upon us?﴾ So God, exalted is He, explains that what they asked for will indeed come to pass, but they will meet with what they dislike in it. Here there are several issues:

First issue: They mentioned two views regarding the grammatical case (i'rab) of "yawm" (the day):

The first: The governing element is what is indicated by "no good news" (la bushra), meaning, "On the day they see the angels, they will seek good news; and 'that day' (yawma'idhin) is for emphasis."

The second: The implied sense is: "Remember the day they see the angels."

[Page 62]

Second issue: They differed about which day this is. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means at the time of death. The rest said: he means the Day of Resurrection.

Third issue: It is said of the disbeliever, "no good news," because although the disbeliever is astray and leads others astray, he believes about himself that he was guided and rightly guided, so he would hope for that great reward. Also, they may have done deeds from which they hoped for benefit, such as supporting the oppressed, giving to the poor, and maintaining ties of kinship, but their disbelief nullified these. God, glorified is He, thus explains that at the beginning of the matter they will be addressed with what indicates the utmost despair and disappointment, and that is the utmost in pain. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah what they had not reckoned.﴾ [al-Zumar: 47]

Fourth issue: The proper form of the statement would be: "On the day they see the angels, there is no good news for them." But He said, "no good news for the criminals," and there are two aspects to this:

One: It is an explicit noun placed in the position of a pronoun.

The second: It is general, encompassing them by its generality. The Mu'tazila said: The verse indicates with certainty the threat against sinners (fussaq) and the absence of pardon, because His words, ﴿no good news that day,﴾ are an indefinite noun in the context of negation, so it encompasses all kinds of good news at all times. The evidence is that whoever wishes to deny this proposition would say, "Rather, he has good news at such-and-such a time." Since the affirmation of good news at some time is cited to refute this proposition, we know that His words, ﴿no good news,﴾ require the negation of all kinds of good news at all times. Then God, exalted is He, emphasized this negation with His words: ﴿a barrier, barred,﴾ and pardon from God is among the greatest good news, and escape from the Fire after entering it is among the greatest good news, and the intercession of the Messenger (ﷺ) is among the greatest good news. Therefore it is necessary that none of this be established for any of the criminals. The discussion of holding to the forms of generality has already been presented more than once. The commentators said: What is meant by "the criminals" here is the disbelievers, as evidenced by His words: ﴿Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah, Allah has forbidden him Paradise.﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 72]

Fifth issue: Regarding the explanation of His words, ﴿a barrier, barred.﴾ Sibawayh, in the chapter on verbal nouns (masadir) that are not inflected and are put in the accusative by verbs whose expression is omitted, such as "ma'adhallah" (God forbid) and "qi'dakallah" and "amrakallah," mentioned that this is a phrase they used when encountering a enemy seeking vengeance, or when a calamity struck, and similar situations, placing it in the position of seeking refuge. Sibawayh said: A man says to another who does such-and-such, and he says, "Hijran" (a barrier). It derives from "hajarahu," when he prevented him, because the one seeking refuge asks God to prevent the harm so that it does not reach him. So the meaning is: I ask God to prevent that with prevention and to bar it with barring. Its coming in the form "fi'l" or "fa'l" in the reading of al-Hasan is a variation in it, due to its being specific to one place. If it is said: Since it is established that it is among the verbal nouns, what is the meaning of describing it as "barred"? We say: This attribute came to emphasize the meaning of the barrier, as they said: "dhabl dhabil" (a feeble thing that is feeble), "dhabl" being humiliation, and "mawt ma'it" (dead death) and "haram muharram" (forbidden prohibition).

Sixth issue: They differed regarding who the speakers of "a barrier, barred" are, in three views:

The first view: They are the disbelievers. This is because they used to ask for the descent of the angels and demand it, but when they saw them at death and on the Day of Resurrection, they disliked meeting them and feared them, because they would meet them only with what they dislike. So when they saw them, they said what they used to say when encountering an enemy seeking vengeance and when severe hardship descended.

The second view: The speakers are the angels, and the meaning is: "Forbidden, prohibited for you are forgiveness, Paradise, and good news," meaning God has made that forbidden for you. Then they differed on this view. Some said: When the disbelievers come out of their graves, the guardian angels (hafaza) say to them, "A barrier, barred." Al-Kalbi said: The angels are at the gates of Paradise, giving good news to the believers of Paradise, and they say to the polytheists, "A barrier, barred." 'Atiyya said: When the Day of Resurrection comes, the angels meet the believers with good news,

[Page 63]

and when the disbelievers see that, they say to them, "Give us good news." They say, "A barrier, barred."

The third view: This is the view of al-Qaffal and al-Wahidi, and it is narrated from al-Hasan that the disbelievers, on the Day of Resurrection, when they witness what they fear, seek refuge from it and say, "A barrier, barred," and the angels say, "None is sheltered from the evil of this day."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verses 23–24:

As for His saying, ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds﴾, the Mujassima (anthropomorphists) have used it as evidence, since arrival (qudum) is only valid for bodies. Its answer is that the proof has already been established that arrival is impossible for Him, because arrival is a movement, and whatever is characterized by movement is originated (muhdath). For this reason Khalil (Abraham), peace be upon him, used the setting of the stars as proof of their origination. It is established that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, cannot be originated, so the wording of "arrival" must be interpreted, and this has several aspects:

The first: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds﴾ means: We will intend their deeds. For one who arrives at a thing intends it, so intention is what affects the thing arrived at, and the effect (musabbab) is used for the cause (sabab) metaphorically.

The second: the intended meaning is the arrival of the angels at the place of reckoning in the Hereafter. Since they come by His command, it is permissible to say "And We came" by way of extension (tawassu'). Its parallel is His saying: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 55].

The third: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town, they ruin it﴾ [an-Naml: 34]. When Allah destroyed their deeds and wholly ruined them, they became like the places that a king visits, and therefore He said "And We came."

As for His saying, ﴿to what they did of deeds﴾, it means the deeds they believed to be righteous and thought would bring them closer to Allah, and the meaning is: to whatever deed of any kind they did.

As for His saying, ﴿and We will make it scattered dust﴾, it means: We will nullify it and render it in a state where it cannot be benefited from, like scattered dust that cannot be grasped. Its parallels are His saying: ﴿like a mirage in a level plain﴾ [an-Nur: 39], ﴿like ashes which the wind blows violently on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18], and ﴿like eaten straw﴾ [al-Fil: 5]. Abu 'Ubaydah and az-Zajjaj said: al-Haba' is like dust that enters through a window with the light of the sun. Muqatil said: it is the dust that rises from the hooves of animals.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day will have a better abode and a finer resting place﴾, know that when He, glorified is He, had explained the state of the disbelievers in total loss and complete failure, He described the people of the Garden, as an alert that all good lies in obedience to Allah, the Exalted. Here there are questions:

The first: how can the companions of the Garden have a better abode than the people of the Fire, when there is no good in the Fire, and one does not say of honey that it is sweeter than vinegar? The answer has several aspects:

The first: what has preceded in His saying: ﴿Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity?﴾ [al-Furqan: 15].

The second: it is possible that He means they are in the utmost good, because the abode of the Garden is better than the Fire, like the saying of the poet:

Indeed He who raised the sky built for us a house whose pillars are mightier and higher.

The third: the comparison drawn between the two positions refers to the place, and the place, insofar as it is a place with no evil in it, [is good].

The fourth: this comparison holds under a hypothetical assumption, that is, if they had an abode in which there was good, the abode of the people of the Garden would be better than it.

The second question: the verse indicates that their abode is other than their resting place (maqil), so how is that? The answer has several aspects:

The first: the abode (mustaqarr) is the place of settling, and the resting place (maqil) is the time of the midday rest (qailulah). This is an indication that they are in the best place in terms of place, and in the best time in terms of time.

The second: the abode of the people of the Garden is other than their resting place, for they take their midday rest in Firdaws, then return to their abode.

The third: after finishing the reckoning and going to the Garden, the time becomes the time of midday rest. Ibn Mas'ud said: "The day of Resurrection does not reach midday until the people of the Garden take their midday rest in the Garden, and the people of the Fire in the Fire." Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Then indeed their resting place is toward the Blazing Fire." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: when Allah begins the judgment, He judges between them for the duration between the morning prayer and midday, so the people of the Garden take their rest in the Garden, and the people of the Fire in the Fire. Muqatil said: He eases the reckoning for the people of the Garden until it amounts to half a day of the days of this world, and then they take their rest on that day in the Garden.

The third question: how can there be midday rest in the Garden and the Fire, when you hold that the people of the Garden in the Hereafter do not sleep, and the people of the Fire are forever in a punishment they know, and the people of the Garden are in a bliss they know? The answer: Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And for them is their provision therein morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 62], yet there is no morning and evening in the Garden, by His saying: ﴿They will see therein neither sun nor bitter cold﴾ [al-Insan: 13]. And since there is no sun there, there is no midday nor time of midday rest. Rather, the intent is to show that this place is the most pleasant and best of places, just as the place of midday rest is the most pleasant of places. And Allah knows best.
