For this reason Khalil (Abraham), peace be upon him, used the setting of the stars as proof of their origination. It is established that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, cannot be originated, so the wording of "arrival" must be interpreted, and this has several aspects:

The first: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds﴾ means: We will intend their deeds. For one who arrives at a thing intends it, so intention is what affects the thing arrived at, and the effect (musabbab) is used for the cause (sabab) metaphorically.

The second: the intended meaning is the arrival of the angels at the place of reckoning in the Hereafter. Since they come by His command, it is permissible to say "And We came" by way of extension (tawassu'). Its parallel is His saying: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 55].

The third: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town, they ruin it﴾ [an-Naml: 34]. When Allah destroyed their deeds and wholly ruined them, they became like the places that a king visits, and therefore He said "And We came."

As for His saying, ﴿to what they did of deeds﴾, it means the deeds they believed to be righteous and thought would bring them closer to Allah, and the meaning is: to whatever deed of any kind they did.

As for His saying, ﴿and We will make it scattered dust﴾, it means: We will nullify it and render it in a state where it cannot be benefited from, like scattered dust that cannot be grasped. Its parallels are His saying: ﴿like a mirage in a level plain﴾ [an-Nur: 39], ﴿like ashes which the wind blows violently on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18], and ﴿like eaten straw﴾ [al-Fil: 5]. Abu 'Ubaydah and az-Zajjaj said: al-Haba' is like dust that enters through a window with the light of the sun. Muqatil said: it is the dust that rises from the hooves of animals.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day will have a better abode and a finer resting place﴾, know that when He, glorified is He, had explained the state of the disbelievers in total loss and complete failure, He described the people of the Garden, as an alert that all good lies in obedience to Allah, the Exalted. Here there are questions:

The first: how can the companions of the Garden have a better abode than the people of the Fire, when there is no good in the Fire, and one does not say of honey that it is sweeter than vinegar? The answer has several aspects:

The first: what has preceded in His saying: ﴿Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity?﴾ [al-Furqan: 15].

The second: it is possible that He means they are in the utmost good, because the abode of the Garden is better than the Fire, like the saying of the poet:

Indeed He who raised the sky built for us a house whose pillars are mightier and higher.

The third: the comparison drawn between the two positions refers to the place, and the place, insofar as it is a place with no evil in it, [is good].

The fourth: this comparison holds under a hypothetical assumption, that is, if they had an abode in which there was good, the abode of the people of the Garden would be better than it.

The second question: the verse indicates that their abode is other than their resting place (maqil), so how is that? The answer has several aspects:

The first: the abode (mustaqarr) is the place of settling, and the resting place (maqil) is the time of the midday rest (qailulah). This is an indication that they are in the best place in terms of place, and in the best time in terms of time.

The second: the abode of the people of the Garden is other than their resting place, for they take their midday rest in Firdaws, then return to their abode.

The third: after finishing the reckoning and going to the Garden, the time becomes the time of midday rest. Ibn Mas'ud said: "The day of Resurrection does not reach midday until the people of the Garden take their midday rest in the Garden, and the people of the Fire in the Fire." Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Then indeed their resting place is toward the Blazing Fire." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: when Allah begins the judgment, He judges between them for the duration between the morning prayer and midday, so the people of the Garden take their rest in the Garden, and the people of the Fire in the Fire. Muqatil said: He eases the reckoning for the people of the Garden until it amounts to half a day of the days of this world, and then they take their rest on that day in the Garden.

The third question: how can there be midday rest in the Garden and the Fire, when you hold that the people of the Garden in the Hereafter do not sleep, and the people of the Fire are forever in a punishment they know, and the people of the Garden are in a bliss they know? The answer: Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And for them is their provision therein morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 62], yet there is no morning and evening in the Garden, by His saying: ﴿They will see therein neither sun nor bitter cold﴾ [al-Insan: 13]. And since there is no sun there, there is no midday nor time of midday rest. Rather, the intent is to show that this place is the most pleasant and best of places, just as the place of midday rest is the most pleasant of places. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verse 25:**

[Page 65 is omitted here.]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the day the sky is split open with the clouds, and the angels are sent down in a descent.﴾ ﴿The sovereignty on that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful, and it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿On the day the wrongdoer bites his hands, he will say, "Would that I had taken a way with the Messenger!"﴾ ﴿Woe to me! Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend!﴾ ﴿He led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me. And Satan is ever a forsaker of man.﴾

Know that this speech is built upon what they requested, namely the sending down of the angels. So He, glory be to Him, explained that this will take place on a day that has attributes:

The first attribute: on that day the sky will be split open with the clouds, and concerning this there are several issues:

First issue: His saying, ﴿When the sky breaks apart﴾ [Al-Infitar: 1] indicates splitting, and His saying, ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 210] indicates the clouds. So His saying, ﴿the sky is split open with the clouds﴾ comprises the meaning of both verses. A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And the sky is opened and becomes gateways﴾ [An-Naba': 19], and His saying, ﴿So on that day it will be frail﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 16].

Second issue: Abu 'Amr and the people of Kufa read the shin (ش) here and in Surat Qaf with a single consonant (تَشَقُّ, lightened), while the rest read it with the doubled consonant (تَشَّقَّقُ, intensified). Abu 'Ubayda said: the preferred reading is the lightened form, just as تَسَاءَلُونَ is lightened. As for the one who doubles it, its meaning is تَتَشَقَّقُ (the sky "splits apart" in a gradual, repeated manner).

Third issue: al-Farra' said: the intended meaning of His saying ﴿with the clouds﴾ is "from the clouds" (عَنِ الغَمامِ), because the sky does not split by means of the clouds, but rather split from the clouds. The judge (al-Qadi) said: there is nothing to prevent Him, exalted be He, from making the clouds such that the sky splits by relying upon them, and this is like His saying, ﴿the sky will be split by it﴾ [Al-Muzzammil: 18].

Fifth issue: His saying ﴿and the angels are sent down﴾ is a general form (صِيغَةُ عُمُومٍ), so it encompasses all of them. Also, because the sky is the dwelling place of the angels, when it splits they must descend to the earth. Then Muqatil said: the sky of this world splits, and its inhabitants descend, and they are more numerous than the inhabitants of the world; thus the skies split one after another, then the Karubiyyun (the cherubim) and the bearers of the Throne descend, then the Lord, exalted be He, descends.

And al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: every sky splits, and its inhabitants descend, and they surround the creation and become seven rows around the creation. Know that the descent of the Lord in His essence is definitively false, because descent is a movement, and whatever is characterized by movement is originated, and God cannot be originated.

As for the descent of the angels to the earth, there is an objection to it: it has been established that the earth, in comparison with the lowest heaven, is like a ring in a desert; so how, in comparison with the Kursi (Footstool) and the Throne? So the angels of all these places, how can the earth contain them all? Perhaps Allah, exalted be He, will increase the length and breadth of the earth and bring it to a state that is wide enough for all of them. Among the exegetes there is one who said: the angels will be in the clouds from it (i.e., within it), and Allah, exalted be He, will settle the cloud above the people of the Resurrection, and that cloud will be the dwelling place of the angels.

Al-Hasan said: the cloud is a veil between the sky and the earth; the angels ascend through it with the copying (naskh, transcription) of the deeds of the children of Adam, and the reckoning takes place on the earth.

Sixth issue: As for the descent of the angels, it is evident, and the meaning of ﴿tanzil﴾ (تَنْزِيلًا, "in a descent") is a tawkid (emphasis, a grammatical device intensifying the meaning) of the descent, and an indication of their swiftness in it.

Seventh issue: The alif and lam in ﴿al-ghamam﴾ (الغَمامِ, "the clouds") are not for generality; rather they are for what is already known, and the intended meaning is what was mentioned in His saying: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds and the angels﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 210].

Eighth issue: It was read: "wa-nunazzilu al-mala'ikata" (وَنُنَزِّلُ المَلائِكَةَ), "wa-nunzilu al-mala'ikata" (وَنُنْزِلُ المَلائِكَةَ), "wa-nuzzila al-mala'ikatu" (وَنُزِّلَ المَلائِكَةُ), "wa-nuzzilat al-mala'ikatu" (وَنُزِلَتِ المَلائِكَةُ), "wa-nuzila al-mala'ikatu" (وَنُزِلَ المَلائِكَةُ), with the deletion of the nun that is the first radical of the verb from "nunzilu," which is the reading of the people of Mecca.

The second attribute of that day: His saying, ﴿The dominion that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-Haqq" is an attribute of "al-mulk," and its sense is: "the dominion, the true one, that day belongs to the Most Merciful." It is permissible to read "al-haqqa" in the accusative, with the sense of "I mean," but it has not been transmitted as a reading. The meaning of describing it as true is that it does not cease and does not change. If it is said: "Such dominion has never belonged to anyone but the Most Merciful, so what is the benefit of His saying 'that day'?" We reply: because on that day there is no owner besides Him, neither in appearance nor in reality. Thus kings submit to Him, faces are humbled before Him, and tyrants are abased, unlike other days.

Know that this verse refutes the view of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) that it is obligatory for God to give reward and recompense. For if that were obligatory, He would deserve blame for not doing it, and so He would be fearful lest He not do it, and He would not then be absolute sovereign. Also, His saying ﴿The dominion that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾ indicates that no one else has dominion, and this cannot hold on the Mu'tazilah view. For whoever has a claim against another thereby becomes its owner, and He, glory be to Him, would not be the owner of that claimed thing. For when He, glory be to Him, has a claim against someone, He can pardon it, whereas if another has a claim against someone, he cannot validly release him from it. So servitude here is more complete. Also, whoever disbelieved in God throughout his life, and then at the very end of his life recognized God for a moment and died, if He gave him a thousand thousand years of various rewards, and then afterwards intended not to give him even a moment's reward, He would become foolish, and this is the extreme of servitude and humiliation. How, then, would it befit One whose state is this to be told: ﴿The dominion that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾? Also, every person who performs an act, such that if he had not performed it he would deserve blame, and by that act gains perfection while by abandoning it gains deficiency, is not a king but a needy one who deserves [what he receives]. It is therefore established that His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿The dominion that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾ is not fitting with the principles of the Mu'tazilah.

* * *

The third attribute: His saying, ﴿And it will be a hard day for the disbelievers﴾. The meaning is evident, for He, exalted is He, knows all circumstances and is able to do whatever He wills, whereas everything else is in the noose of helplessness and the bridle of subjugation. Thus it is in the utmost hardship for the disbeliever.

The fourth attribute: His saying, ﴿And the day when the wrongdoer bites his hands﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: the "al" in "al-zalim" (the wrongdoer). Regarding it there are two views: one, that it is generic; two, that it refers to a specific known person. Those who say it refers to a known person are of two opinions:

The first: Ibn Abbas said: "The intended one is Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt ibn Umayyah ibn Abd Shams. Whenever he returned from a journey, he would prepare food and invite his neighbours from the people of Mecca, and he would frequently sit with the Messenger (ﷺ), and he admired his speech. So he prepared food and invited the Messenger (ﷺ). He (ﷺ) said: 'I will not eat of your food until you bear witness to the two testimonies.' So he did, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) ate of his food. This reached Ummayah ibn Khalaf, who said: 'You have turned away, O Uqbah!' He was his close friend. Uqbah said: 'I only did it so that he would eat of my food.' He said: 'I will not be content until you go to him, spit in his face, and tread on his neck.' He did so, and the Messenger (ﷺ) said: 'If I ever meet you outside Mecca, I will strike your head with the sword.' Then there was revealed: ﴿And the day when the wrongdoer bites his hands﴾ in regret. He means Uqbah, who says: 'Oh, would that I had not taken Ummayah as a close friend! He led me astray from the Reminder,' that is, turned me away from the Reminder, which is the Qur'an and faith, after it had come to me along with Muhammad (ﷺ). Uqbah was taken captive on the day of Badr and was killed in cold blood, and no one else among the captives was killed that day except him and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith."

The second: The Rafidah (a Shi'i sect) said: this wrongdoer is a specific man, and that the Muslims changed his name and concealed it, and put so-and-so in place of his name, and mentioned certain virtuous companions of the Messenger of God. Know that applying the wording in its generality is not due to the wording itself, for we have explained in the principles of jurisprudence that "al" when attached to a singular noun does not indicate generality, but indicates it only by a contextual indicator, insofar as the ordering of a ruling upon a description indicates that the description is the cause. This shows that the determining factor in biting the hands is being a wrongdoer, and then the ruling becomes general because its cause is general. This view is preferable to restricting it to a single case, because what we have mentioned requires generality, and its being revealed concerning a particular event does not preclude that the intended meaning is generality, so that this instance and others are included. Also, the purpose of the verse is to deter everyone from wrongdoing, and this is achieved only through generality. As for the claim of the Rafidah, it cannot hold except by impugning the Qur'an and asserting that it has been altered and substituted, and there is no dispute that this is disbelief.

* * *

The second issue: the Mu'tazilah cited His saying ﴿And the day when the wrongdoer bites his hands﴾. They said: "The wrongdoer includes the disbeliever and the sinner, so this shows that God does not pardon the one who commits a major sin." The discussion of this has already passed.

The third issue: His saying ﴿The wrongdoer bites his hands﴾. Al-Dahhak said: "He eats his hands up to the elbows, then they grow back, and he continues like this, every time he eats them they grow back." The people of verification said: this expression indicates grief and distress; it is said: "he bit his fingertips" and "he bit upon his hands."

* * *

The fourth issue: just as we have explained that the wrongdoer is not restricted to one individual but includes all wrongdoers, so too the intended meaning of His saying "so-and-so" is not one individual, but everyone who is obeyed in disobedience to God. Also, His saying ﴿The dominion that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾ indicates that no one else has dominion, and this cannot hold on the Mu'tazilah view. Also, every person who performs an act, such that if he had not performed it he would deserve blame, and by that act gains perfection while by abandoning it gains deficiency, is not a king but a needy one who deserves [what he receives]. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 25, verses 30–31:**

Know that when the disbelievers multiplied their corrupt objections and forms of obstinacy, the chest of the Messenger (ﷺ) became constricted, and he complained to God, Exalted, and said: ﴿O my Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned.﴾ On this there are several issues:

**First issue:** Most exegetes (mufassirun) hold that this is a statement actually made by the Messenger (ﷺ). Abu Muslim said: rather, the intended meaning is that the Messenger, peace be upon him, will say it on the Day of Judgment, like His saying: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these?﴾ [al-Nisa': 41]. The first view is preferable, because it accords with the wording, and because what God, Exalted, mentioned after it, namely: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾ [al-Furqan: 31], is consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), and this consolation is only fitting if that statement was indeed made by him.

**Second issue:** Scholars have mentioned two views regarding *mahjur* (abandoned):

The first: it is from *al-hijran* (forsaking), meaning they abandoned belief in it, did not accept it, and turned away from listening to it.

The second: it is from *ahjara*, meaning "something abandoned in it" (i.e., they abandoned the Qur'an through their speech about it), and the preposition has been omitted. This is confirmed by the saying of God, Exalted: ﴿Acting arrogantly by it, talking nonsense by night﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 67]. Their "abandonment" of it consisted in their saying that it is sorcery, poetry, lies, and *hajr*, that is, raving (*hadhayan*).

It is narrated from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever learns the Qur'an and teaches it, and hangs a copy of the Mushaf without attending to it or looking into it, will come on the Day of Resurrection clinging to it, saying: 'O Lord of the worlds, this servant of Yours took me as abandoned. Judge between me and him.'"

Then God, Exalted, said, consoling and comforting His Messenger, peace be upon him: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals.﴾ By this He showed that he has a model among all the Messengers, so let him be patient with what he meets from his people, as they were patient.

Then there are issues in this:

**First issue:** Our companions (the Ash'arites) have argued from this verse that God created both good and evil, because His saying: ﴿We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾ indicates that this enmity is by God's appointment, and there is no doubt that this enmity is disbelief. Al-Jubba'i said: the meaning of "appointment" is "designation" (*tabyin*). When He showed that they are His enemies, it is permissible to say: "We made them His enemies," just as when a man shows that so-and-so is a thief, one says: "He made him a thief," as one says of a judge: "He declared so-and-so just, declared so-and-so a sinner, and disqualified him." Al-Ka'bi said: when God commanded the prophets to be hostile to the disbelievers, and their hostility to the disbelievers necessitates the disbelievers' hostility toward them, therefore it is permissible to say: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾, because He, glorified is He, is the One who impelled and called him to that which resulted in that enmity. Abu Muslim said: the word *'aduww* (enemy) may mean "distant" rather than "near," since *mu'adah* is "distancing," just as *nasr* is "nearness" and "support." God, Exalted, has indeed distanced between the believers and the disbelievers.

The answer to the first: they never call designation "appointment" at all, because whoever shows to another the existence of the Creator and His eternity is not said to have "appointed" the Creator or "appointed" His eternity.

The answer to the second: what God commanded him to do, does it have an effect in bringing about enmity in their hearts or not? If it has an effect, then the matter is settled, because their enmity toward the Messenger (ﷺ) is disbelief, and when God commands the Messenger with what has an effect on that enmity, He has commanded him with what has an effect on the occurrence of disbelief. If it has no effect whatsoever, then it is entirely unrelated to it, and attributing it to him is impossible. This is the answer to Abu Muslim's statement.

**Second issue:** One may say that the words of Muhammad, peace be upon him: ﴿And the Messenger said: "O my Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned"﴾ are in meaning like the words of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, indeed I have called my people night and day, but my calling has only increased them in flight﴾ [Nuh: 5–6]. Just as the purpose of that was to bring down punishment, so too here. How then is this fitting for one whom God described as mercy in His saying: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107]?

The answer: when Noah, peace be upon him, said that, he prayed against them. But when Muhammad, peace be upon him, said this, he did not pray against them; rather, he waited. When God, Exalted, said: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾, this was like a command to him to be patient over that and to refrain from praying against them. Thus the difference becomes apparent.

**Third issue:** His saying "We have appointed" (*ja'alna*) is the form of the majestic. When the Majestic mentions Himself in every context of exaltation and says that He gives, that gift must be great, as in His saying: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾ [al-Hijr: 87], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾ [al-Kawthar: 1]. How then is it fitting for this form that the gift should be that enmity which is the source of harm in religion and in worldly life? The answer: the creation of enmity is a cause of increased hardship, which necessitates greater reward. And God knows best.

**Fourth issue:** The word *'aduww* may be singular or plural, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 77]. It is reported in the exegesis that the enemy of the Messenger (ﷺ) was Abu Jahl.

As for His saying: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as guide and helper﴾, al-Zajjaj said: the *ba'* (in *bi-rabbika*) is superfluous, meaning "your Lord suffices." *Hadiyan* and *nasiran* are in the accusative as circumstantial accusatives (*hal*). *Hadiyan* means guiding to the interests of religion and worldly life, and *nasiran* means giving victory over the enemies. A parallel is His saying: ﴿O Prophet, God is sufficient for you, and for those of the believers who follow you﴾ [al-Anfal: 64].

**His saying, exalted is He:** ﴿Those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" It is thus, that We may strengthen your heart with it; and We have arranged it in gradual recitation.﴾ ﴿And they bring you no example but We bring you the truth and the best explanation.﴾ ﴿Those who will be gathered upon their faces into Hell, they are the worst in place and the most astray in way.﴾

Know that this is the fifth doubt raised by those who deny the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. The people of Makkah said: "You claim that you are a messenger from Allah. Why do you not bring us the Qur'an all at once, as the Tawrah (Torah) was sent down all at once to Musa (Moses), the Injil (Gospel) to Isa (Jesus), and the Zabur (Psalms) to Dawud (David)?" It is reported from Ibn Jurayj that between its beginning and its end there were twenty-two or twenty-three years. Allah answered with His saying: ﴿It is thus, that We may strengthen your heart with it.﴾ The explanation of this answer is in several aspects:

The first: He ﷺ was not one of those who could read and write. Had it been sent down to him all at once, he would not have been able to retain it, and error and forgetfulness would have been possible for him. The Tawrah was sent down all at once because it was written, and Musa would read it.

The second: whoever has the Book with him may rely on the Book and become lax in memorization. Allah, exalted is He, did not give him the Book in a single installment, but sent it down to him in portions, so that his memorization of it would be more complete, and this would keep him further from laxity and poor retention.

The third: if Allah had sent the Book down all at once upon creation, the laws would all have descended upon creation at one time, and this would have been burdensome for them. But since it was sent down dispersed and in parts, the obligations were sent down little by little, and so bearing them was easier.

The fourth: when he saw Jibril (Gabriel) moment by moment, his heart was strengthened by beholding him, so he was stronger in carrying out what he was charged with, in patience with the incidental afflictions of prophethood, in enduring the harm of his people, and in striving (jihad).

The fifth: when the condition of inimitability was fulfilled in it despite its being revealed in portions, its miraculous nature was established. For if that were within the capacity of humans, they would have been obliged to bring something like it in portions, dispersed.

The sixth: the Qur'an was sent down according to their questions and the events that befell them, so they would increase in insight, because along with its eloquence, the report of unseen matters was joined to it through this means.

The seventh: when the Qur'an was sent down in dispersed portions, and he ﷺ had been challenging them from the beginning of the matter, it was as though he had challenged them with each one of the Qur'an's portions. When they were unable to produce that, their inability to oppose the whole was all the more certain. By this way it was established in his heart that the people were unable to oppose it without doubt.

The eighth: the mission between Allah, exalted is He, and His prophets, and the conveying of His speech to creation, is a great rank. It may be said that if Allah had sent the Qur'an down to Muhammad ﷺ all at once, that rank would have been nullified for Jibril (peace be upon him). But when He sent it down dispersed in portions, that lofty rank remained with him. For this reason Allah, glorified is He and exalted, made it dispersed in portions.

As for His saying, "﴿Thus﴾," there are two views:

The first: it is part of the speech of the polytheists, meaning: "all at once, thus," i.e., like the Tawrah and the Injil. On this view, no supposition is needed in the verse, which would be to say: "We sent it down in portions so that We might strengthen your heart with it."

The second: it is the speech of Allah, exalted is He, mentioned as an answer to them; i.e., "Thus We sent it down in portions." If it is objected that the "that" in "﴿thus﴾" must refer to something preceding it, and what preceded is its being sent down all at once, how then is "thus We sent it down in portions" explained by it? **His saying, exalted is He:** ﴿Those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" It is thus, that We may strengthen your heart with it; and We have arranged it in gradual recitation.﴾ ﴿And they bring you no example but We bring you the truth and the best explanation.﴾ ﴿Those who will be gathered upon their faces into Hell, they are the worst in place and the most astray in way.﴾

Know that this is the fifth doubt raised by those who deny the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. The people of Makkah said: "You claim that you are a messenger from Allah. Why do you not bring us the Qur'an all at once, as the Tawrah (Torah) was sent down all at once to Musa (Moses), the Injil (Gospel) to Isa (Jesus), and the Zabur (Psalms) to Dawud (David)?" The first: He ﷺ was not one of those who could read and write. Had it been sent down to him all at once, he would not have been able to retain it, and error and forgetfulness would have been possible for him. The Tawrah was sent down all at once because it was written, and Musa would read it.

The second: whoever has the Book with him may rely on the Book and become lax in memorization. Allah, exalted is He, did not give him the Book in a single installment, but sent it down to him in portions, so that his memorization of it would be more complete, and this would keep him further from laxity and poor retention.

The third: if Allah had sent the Book down all at once upon creation, the laws would all have descended upon creation at one time, and this would have been burdensome for them. But since it was sent down dispersed and in parts, the obligations were sent down little by little, and so bearing them was easier.

The fourth: when he saw Jibril (Gabriel) moment by moment, his heart was strengthened by beholding him, so he was stronger in carrying out what he was charged with, in patience with the incidental afflictions of prophethood, in enduring the harm of his people, and in striving (jihad).

The fifth: when the condition of inimitability was fulfilled in it despite its being revealed in portions, its miraculous nature was established. For if that were within the capacity of humans, they would have been obliged to bring something like it in portions, dispersed.

The sixth: the Qur'an was sent down according to their questions and the events that befell them, so they would increase in insight, because along with its eloquence, the report of unseen matters was joined to it through this means.

The seventh: when the Qur'an was sent down in dispersed portions, and he ﷺ had been challenging them from the beginning of the matter, it was as though he had challenged them with each one of the Qur'an's portions. When they were unable to produce that, their inability to oppose the whole was all the more certain. By this way it was established in his heart that the people were unable to oppose it without doubt.

The first story is the story of Musa (peace be upon him).

﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book and appointed with him his brother Harun as a minister. So We said, "Go to the people who denied Our signs." Then We utterly destroyed them.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾ [al-Furqan: 31], He followed it with mention of a group of the prophets, and informed him of what befell those among their peoples who denied them. So He said: ﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book and appointed with him his brother Harun as a minister.﴾ The meaning is: O Muhammad, you are not the first whom We sent and who was denied, and to whom We gave the signs and who was rejected. We gave Musa the Torah and strengthened his arm with his brother Harun, yet, despite that, he was rejected. And in this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: His being a minister does not preclude his being a partner with him in prophethood, so there is no basis for the view of one who says that in His words ﴿So We said, "Go"﴾ it is addressed to Musa alone. Rather, it follows the pattern of His words: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 43].

Page 71
If it is said: his being a minister seems incompatible with his being a partner; rather it must be said that when he became a partner he ceased to be a minister. We say: there is no incompatibility between the two attributes, for there is nothing impossible in his sharing in the prophethood while also being a minister, a helper and one who assists him.

The second issue: al-Zajjaj said: the wazir (minister) in the language is the one who is returned to and whose opinion is relied upon for protection, and al-wazar is that by which one seeks protection. From this is His words: ﴿No! There is no refuge﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 11], meaning: there is no escape and no shelter. The qadi said: for this reason He, exalted is He, is not described as having a minister, nor is it said of Him that He is a minister, because seeking refuge in Him for counsel and opinion in this sense is not valid.

The third issue: ﴿We destroyed them﴾ means We destroyed them with a complete destruction. If it is said: the fa' denotes sequence, yet the destruction did not occur immediately after the going of Musa and Harun to them, but after a long period. We say: the sequence here is to be understood with respect to the judgment, not the occurrence. It was also said: He, exalted is He, intended to abridge the story, so He mentioned its two edges, the beginning and the end, because these are the purpose of the story in its full length, namely the establishment of proof through the sending of messengers and the deserving of destruction through their denial.

The fourth issue: His words, exalted is He: ﴿Go to the people who denied Our signs.﴾ If we take the denial of the signs to mean denial of the signs of divinity, there is no difficulty. If we take it to mean denial of the signs of prophethood, then although the wording is in the past tense, the intended meaning is the future.

The second story: the story of Noah, peace be upon him.

﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them, and made them a sign for mankind, and We have prepared for the wrongdoers a painful punishment.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, said ﴿denied the messengers﴾, this is either because they were among the Barahima (Brahmins) who denied all the messengers, or because their denial of one of them was a denial of all of them, since denying one of them is not possible except by discrediting the miracle, and that entails denying all of them. Or it is because, although the intended messenger was Noah, peace be upon him, alone, the expression is used as one says: "So-and-so rides horses."

As for His saying ﴿We drowned them﴾, al-Kalbi said: God sent rain upon them from the sky for forty days, and also brought forth the water of the earth during those forty days, so the earth became one sea. ﴿And We made them﴾, that is, We made their drowning or their story ﴿a sign﴾. ﴿And We have prepared for the wrongdoers﴾, that is, for everyone who follows their path in denying the messengers, ﴿a painful punishment﴾. It is possible that the intended meaning is the people of Noah.

The Third Narrative: the story of ʿĀd, Thamūd and the People of the Well (Ar-Rass).

﴿And ʿĀd and Thamūd and the people of ar-Rass, and many generations between them.﴾ ﴿And to each We presented parables, and each We destroyed with utter destruction.﴾

Page 72

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And ʿĀd and Thamūd and the people of ar-Rass, and many generations between them﴾ ﴿And to each We presented parables, and each We destroyed with utter destruction.﴾ There are several issues concerning this verse.

First issue: ﴿ʿĀdan﴾ (ʿĀd) is conjoined either to "them" in ﴿and We made them﴾, or to "the wrongdoers" (al-ẓālimīn), because the meaning is: "And We promised the wrongdoers."

Second issue: It has been read as (Thamūda) according to the interpretation of the tribe, while as a diptote (Thamūd) it is according to the interpretation of the clan (ḥayy), or because it is the name of the great forefather.

Third issue: Abū ʿUbayda said: ar-Rass is an unlined well (al-biʾr ghayr al-maṭwiyya). Abū Muslim said: there is a place in the lands called ar-Rass, so it is possible that this valley was their dwelling. In the language of the Arabs, ar-Rass means burial, and the word is also applied to digging; it is said: "rusṣa al-mayyit" when the dead person was buried and hidden in the pit. In the exegesis it is said that it is the well. Whatever it was, God Most High has informed us of the destruction of the People of ar-Rass. End quote.

Fourth issue: The exegetes have mentioned several views concerning the People of ar-Rass:

The first: They were a people among the worshippers of idols, owners of wells and livestock. God Most High sent to them Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, who called them to Islam. They persisted in their rebellion and in harming him. While they were around the ar-Rass, God caused the earth to swallow them up along with their dwellings.

The second: ar-Rass is a village at Falaj al-Yamāma. They killed their prophet and were destroyed; they were the remnant of Thamūd.

The third: The Companions of the Prophet, such as Ḥanẓala ibn Ṣafwān, were afflicted by the ʿanqāʾ, which is the greatest of birds, so named for the length of its neck. It used to dwell on their mountain called Fatkh, and would swoop down upon their children and snatch them if hunting became scarce for it. Ḥanẓala invoked God against it, and a thunderbolt struck it. Then they killed Ḥanẓala, and so they were destroyed.

The fourth: They are the People of the Trench (al-Ukhdūd), and ar-Rass is the trench.

The fifth: ar-Rass is Antioch, where they killed Ḥabīb the carpenter. It was also said: they denied him and cast him (rassūhu) into a well, meaning they thrust him into it.

The sixth: It is related from ʿAlī, peace be upon him, that they were a people who worshipped a pine tree, and they were called the People of ar-Rass only because they cast (rassū) their prophet into the earth.

The seventh: The People of ar-Rass were a people who had villages on the bank of a river called ar-Rass in the lands of the East. God Most High sent to them a prophet from the descendants of Yahūdh ibn Yaʿqūb, and they denied him. He remained among them for a time, then complained to God Most High about them. They dug a well, cast him into it, and said: "We hope that our God will be pleased with us." For the whole of their day they would hear the groaning of their prophet, who was saying: "My God and my Lord, You see the narrowness of my place, the severity of my distress, the weakness of my heart and the scarcity of my resources, so hasten the taking of my soul." Until he died. Then God Most High sent a violent wind of intense redness, so the earth beneath them became a blazing brimstone rock, and a black cloud overshadowed them, and their bodies melted as lead melts.

The eighth: Ibn Jarīr related from the Messenger ﷺ that: "God sent a prophet to the people of a town, and none of its people believed in him except a black slave. Then they attacked the Messenger, dug a well for him and threw him into it, then sealed it over with a huge stone. That slave used to gather firewood, buy food and drink with it, lift the stone and lower it to him. This continued for as long as God willed. One day he gathered firewood, and when he wanted to lift it he found sleep and lay down, and God caused his ear to be stopped for seven years while he slept. Then he awoke, stretched, and turned onto his other side, and slept for seven more years. Then he got up and lifted his bundle, thinking he had slept only an hour of the day. He went to the town, sold his bundle, bought food and drink, and went to the pit, but found no one there. His people had already brought him out, believed in him and confirmed him. That prophet used to ask them about the black slave, and they would say: 'We do not know his condition.' Until God took the prophet and took that slave. He, peace be upon him, said: 'That black slave is indeed the first to enter Paradise.'"

Know that the correct view is what Abū Muslim said: that none of these narrations is established by the Qur'an, nor by a report of strong chain. But however they were, God Most High has informed us about them that they were destroyed because of their disbelief.

Fifth issue: al-Nakhaʿī said: a qarn is forty years. ʿAlī, peace be upon him, said: rather seventy years. It was also said: a hundred and twenty.

Sixth issue: His saying ﴿between that﴾ means: between that which has been mentioned. A speaker may mention various things and then refer to them by "that," and a counter may reckon numerous figures and then say: "That is such and such," meaning: that which was counted or enumerated.

The Third Narrative: the story of ʿĀd, Thamūd and the People of the Well (Ar-Rass).

﴿And ʿĀd and Thamūd and the people of ar-Rass, and many generations between them.﴾ ﴿And to each We presented parables, and each We destroyed with utter destruction.﴾

Page 72

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And ʿĀd and Thamūd and the people of ar-Rass, and many generations between them﴾ ﴿And to each We presented parables, and each We destroyed with utter destruction.﴾ There are several issues concerning this verse.

First issue: ﴿ʿĀdan﴾ (ʿĀd) is conjoined either to "them" in ﴿and We made them﴾, or to "the wrongdoers" (al-ẓālimīn), because the meaning is: "And We promised the wrongdoers."

Second issue: It has been read as (Thamūda) according to the interpretation of the tribe, while as a diptote (Thamūd) it is according to the interpretation of the clan (ḥayy), or because it is the name of the great forefather.

Third issue: Abū ʿUbayda said: ar-Rass is an unlined well (al-biʾr ghayr al-maṭwiyya). Abū Muslim said: there is a place in the lands called ar-Rass, so it is possible that this valley was their dwelling. In the language of the Arabs, ar-Rass means burial, and the word is also applied to digging; it is said: "rusṣa al-mayyit" when the dead person was buried and hidden in the pit. In the exegesis it is said that it is the well. Whatever it was, God Most High has informed us of the destruction of the People of ar-Rass. End quote.

Fourth issue: The exegetes have mentioned several views concerning the People of ar-Rass:

The first: They were a people among the worshippers of idols, owners of wells and livestock. God Most High sent to them Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, who called them to Islam. They persisted in their rebellion and in harming him. While they were around the ar-Rass, God caused the earth to swallow them up along with their dwellings.

The second: ar-Rass is a village at Falaj al-Yamāma. They killed their prophet and were destroyed; they were the remnant of Thamūd.

The third: The Companions of the Prophet, such as Ḥanẓala ibn Ṣafwān, were afflicted by the ʿanqāʾ, which is the greatest of birds, so named for the length of its neck. It used to dwell on their mountain called Fatkh, and would swoop down upon their children and snatch them if hunting became scarce for it. Ḥanẓala invoked God against it, and a thunderbolt struck it. Then they killed Ḥanẓala, and so they were destroyed.

The fourth: They are the People of the Trench (al-Ukhdūd), and ar-Rass is the trench.

The fifth: ar-Rass is Antioch, where they killed Ḥabīb the carpenter. It was also said: they denied him and cast him (rassūhu) into a well, meaning they thrust him into it.

The sixth: It is related from ʿAlī, peace be upon him, that they were a people who worshipped a pine tree, and they were called the People of ar-Rass only because they cast (rassū) their prophet into the earth.

The seventh: The People of ar-Rass were a people who had villages on the bank of a river called ar-Rass in the lands of the East. God Most High sent to them a prophet from the descendants of Yahūdh ibn Yaʿqūb, and they denied him. He remained among them for a time, then complained to God Most High about them. They dug a well, cast him into it, and said: "We hope that our God will be pleased with us." For the whole of their day they would hear the groaning of their prophet, who was saying: "My God and my Lord, You see the narrowness of my place, the severity of my distress, the weakness of my heart and the scarcity of my resources, so hasten the taking of my soul." Until he died. Then God Most High sent a violent wind of intense redness, so the earth beneath them became a blazing brimstone rock, and a black cloud overshadowed them, and their bodies melted as lead melts.

The eighth: Ibn Jarīr related from the Messenger ﷺ that: "God sent a prophet to the people of a town, and none of its people believed in him except a black slave. Then they attacked the Messenger, dug a well for him and threw him into it, then sealed it over with a huge stone. That slave used to gather firewood, buy food and drink with it, lift the stone and lower it to him. This continued for as long as God willed. One day he gathered firewood, and when he wanted to lift it he found sleep and lay down, and God caused his ear to be stopped for seven years while he slept. Then he awoke, stretched, and turned onto his other side, and slept for seven more years. Then he got up and lifted his bundle, thinking he had slept only an hour of the day. He went to the town, sold his bundle, bought food and drink, and went to the pit, but found no one there. His people had already brought him out, believed in him and confirmed him. That prophet used to ask them about the black slave, and they would say: 'We do not know his condition.' Until God took the prophet and took that slave. He, peace be upon him, said: 'That black slave is indeed the first to enter Paradise.'"

**The fourth story: the story of Lot (peace be upon him).**

﴿Certainly they have passed by the town that was rained upon with the rain of evil. Have they not been seeing it? Rather, they did not expect resurrection.﴾ ﴿When they see you, they take you only as a mockery: "Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?"﴾ ﴿He nearly led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in worshipping them. But they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in the way.﴾ ﴿Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god? Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or reason? They are only like livestock; rather, they are further astray in the way.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly they have passed by the town that was rained upon with the rain of evil. Have they not been seeing it? Rather, they did not expect resurrection.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, intended by "the town" Sodom (Sadum), one of the towns of the people of Lot (peace be upon him). There were five of them; Allah destroyed four with their inhabitants and one remained. "The rain of evil" means stones. The meaning is that the Quraysh passed many times on their trade journeys to the Levant (al-Sham)

[Page 74]

by that town which had been destroyed by stones from the sky. ﴿Have they not been seeing it?﴾ during their passing, looking at the traces of Allah's punishment and His retribution? ﴿Rather, they were﴾ a disbelieving people ﴿who did not expect resurrection.﴾ Regarding the meaning of ﴿expect﴾ they mentioned several aspects:

The first, which is what al-Qadi said, and it is the strongest: it is to be taken in its literal sense of hope (raja'). This is because a person does not bear the hardships of obligations and the difficulties of reflection and reasoning except out of hope for the reward of the Hereafter. So when he does not believe in the Hereafter, he does not hope for its reward, and therefore he does not bear those difficulties and hardships.

The second: its meaning is "they do not anticipate resurrection and its consequence," so hope is placed in the position of anticipation, because only one who believes anticipates the consequence.

The third: its meaning is "they do not fear," according to the Tihami dialect, and this is weak. The first is the correct view.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When they see you, they take you only as a mockery: "Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?"﴾ ﴿He nearly led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in worshipping them. But they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in the way.﴾ ﴿Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god? Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or reason? They are only like livestock; rather, they are further astray in the way.﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, had explained the extremity of the polytheists in denying His prophethood and in raising doubts about it, He then explained that when they see the Messenger, they take him as a mockery. They do not limit themselves to refusing to believe in him, but add to that mockery and belittling, and some of them say to others: ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: the author of the *al-Kashshaf* said: the first ﴿in﴾ is negative (*nafiyah*), and the second is a lightened form of the heavy (*mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah*), and the *lam* is the one that distinguishes between them (*al-lam al-fariqah*).

The second issue: the answer to (*idha*, "when") is what is implied of speech. That is: "And when they see you mocking, they say: 'Has Allah sent this one as a messenger?'" His saying ﴿they take you﴾ is a parenthetical clause placed between (*idha*) and its answer.

The third issue: ﴿they took him as mockery﴾ means "they mocked him," and the original is "they took him as an object of mockery, or as one mocked."

The fourth issue: know that Allah, exalted is He, informed about the polytheists that whenever they see the Messenger, they do two kinds of actions. One of them is that they mock him, and He explained that mockery by His saying: ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾ and that is great ignorance, because mockery either falls upon his form or upon his attributes.

As for the first, it is false, because peace be upon him was more beautiful than them in form and appearance. And even if it were not so, he, peace be upon him, did not claim to be distinguished from them by form, but by the proof (*hujjah*).

As for the second, it is also false, because peace be upon him claimed to be distinguished from them by the manifestation of the miracle upon him and not upon them, and they were unable to discredit his argument and its evidence. So in reality it is they who deserve to be mocked, but out of their shamelessness they reversed the matter and mocked the Messenger, peace be upon him. This shows that the falsifier at all times has nothing but foolishness and shamelessness.

The second kind: they used to say about him: ﴿He nearly led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in worshipping them.﴾ That indicates several matters:

The first: they called that "misguiding," which shows that they were extreme in exalting their gods and in considering his action of turning them away from them as a grave matter. This indicates that they believed this to be the truth. From this aspect, the view of the adherents of the theological sciences (*ashab al-ma'arif*) is refuted, who say that no one disbelieves except one who knows the proofs; because they were ignorant of it, and then Allah, exalted is He, attributed to them disbelief and error. Their saying ﴿had we not been steadfast in worshipping them﴾ also indicates this.

The second: this statement from them indicates the earnestness of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and his striving to turn them away from worshipping idols. Had it not been so, they would not have said ﴿He nearly led us astray from our gods﴾

[Page 75]

﴿had we not been steadfast in worshipping them.﴾ And so he, peace be upon him, was: at the beginning he exerted himself greatly in presenting proofs and answering doubts, and he bore what they did of kinds of foolishness and bad manners.

The third: this indicates that the people admitted that they had not at all objected to the proofs of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and they opposed them only with pure denial and blind imitation (*taqlid*). Because their saying ﴿had we not been steadfast in worshipping them﴾ is a sign of denial and imitation. And had they mentioned an objection to the proofs of the Messenger, peace be upon him, mentioning that would have been better than merely mentioning denial and insistence, which is the practice of the ignorant. This indicates that the people were overpowered by his argument, peace be upon him, and that all they had was mere shamelessness.

The fourth: the verse indicates that when his argument became manifest against them, peace be upon him, they became like madmen. Because they first mocked him, then described him as one who "nearly led us astray from our gods had we not confronted him with denial and insistence." This last statement indicates that the people had conceded to him the strength of argument and the perfection of intellect, while the first statement, which is ridicule and mockery, is fitting only for the ignorant and the incapable. So when the people combined these two statements, this indicates that they were like those bewildered about his affair: at times, out of shamelessness, they mock him, and at times they describe him with what is fitting only for the perfect scholar. Then, when He, glorified is He, related this statement of theirs, He refuted their way in that from three aspects:

The first of them: His saying: ﴿But they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in the way.﴾ Because when they described him with misguidance in their saying ﴿He nearly led us astray﴾, He explained that it will become clear to them who is the misguider and who is the one astray, at the sight of the punishment from which there is no escape for them. This is a severe warning to them for their blindness and turning away from reasoning and reflection.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god? Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ The meaning is that He, glorified is He, explained that the extent of these people's ignorance and their turning away from proofs was only due to the dominance of imitation over them, and that they took their desires as gods. Whenever desire called them to something, they obeyed it, whether or not evidence forbade it. Then there are several discussions here:

The first: His saying ﴿Have you seen﴾ (*ara'ayta*) is a word that may be used for informing and for asking. Here it is for expressing wonder at the ignorance of one whose description and attribute are such.

The second: His saying ﴿took his god, his desire﴾ means: "he took as his god what he desires," or "a god that he desires." It was also said that it is inverted, meaning "he took his desire as his god." This is weak, because His saying ﴿took his god, his desire﴾ conveys restriction (*hasr*), that is, he took for himself no god except his desire. This meaning does not arise from the inverted reading. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Desire is a god that is worshipped." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "A man among the polytheists would worship an idol, and when he saw something better than it, he would discard it and take the other and worship it."

The third: His saying ﴿Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ means: a protector who guards him from following his desire; that is, you are not such.

The fourth: a parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 22], and His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a compeller﴾ [Qaf: 45], and His saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256]. Al-Kalbi said: "It was abrogated (*nasakhat-ha*) by the verse of fighting."

The third of them: His saying: ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or reason?﴾ Here ﴿or﴾ (*am*) is disjunctive (*munqati'ah*), meaning "rather, do you think?" This indicates that this blame is more severe than the one preceding it, to the point that it required turning away from it to this one, which is that they are deprived of hearing and intellect. Because due to their intense obstinacy, they do not listen to speech, and if they hear it, they do not reflect upon it. So it is as if they had no intellect or hearing at all. At that point He likened them to livestock in their not benefiting from speech, and their not venturing to contemplate and reflect, and their devotion to immediate sensory pleasures, and their turning away from seeking the lasting intellectual felicities. Here there are questions:

[Page 76]

The first question: why did He say ﴿Or do you think that most of them﴾, passing judgment on most and not on all? The answer: because among them there were those who knew God, exalted is He, and understood the truth, but they abandoned Islam merely out of love of leadership, not out of ignorance.

The second question: why were they made more astray than livestock? The answer has several aspects:

The first: livestock submit to their owners and to the one who feeds and tends them, and they distinguish between the one who does good to them and the one who harms them. They seek what benefits them and avoid what harms them. These people do not submit to their Lord, nor do they distinguish between His kindness toward them and the harm of Satan to them, who is their enemy. They do not seek reward, which is the greatest benefit, nor do they guard against punishment, which is the greatest harm.

The second: just as the hearts of livestock are empty of knowledge, they are also empty of ignorance, which is the belief of one who believes contrary to what is the case, together with firm conviction. As for these people, their hearts, though empty of knowledge, are characterized by ignorance, for they do not know, and they do not know that they do not know; rather, they insist that they know.

The third: the lack of knowledge in livestock does not harm anyone, but the ignorance of these people is a source of great harm, because they block people from the path of Allah and seek to make it crooked.

The fourth: livestock know nothing, but they are incapable of seeking. As for these ignorant people, they are not incapable of seeking. One who is deprived of seeking lofty ranks, if he is incapable of it, does not deserve blame as one who is capable of it but abandons it due to his bad choice.

The fifth: beasts do not deserve punishment for lack of knowledge, but these people deserve the greatest punishment for it.

The sixth: according to the view of some people, beasts glorify Allah, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿There is not a thing but it exalts Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra': 44], and He said: ﴿Have you not considered that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens...﴾ up to His saying ﴿and the creatures (al-dawabb)﴾ [al-Hajj: 18], and He said: ﴿And the birds in flight; each has known its prayer and its glorification﴾ [al-Nur: 41]. And if that is the case, then the misguidance of the disbelievers is more severe and greater than the misguidance of these livestock.

The third question: since He, glorified is He, denied them hearing and intellect, how did He blame them for turning away from religion, and how did He send the Messenger to them? For the condition of obligation is intellect. The answer: the intended meaning is not that they do not have intellect, but that they do not benefit from that intellect. This is like the saying of a man to another when he does not understand: "You are only blind and deaf."
