And if that is the case, then the misguidance of the disbelievers is more severe and greater than the misguidance of these livestock.

The third question: since He, glorified is He, denied them hearing and intellect, how did He blame them for turning away from religion, and how did He send the Messenger to them? For the condition of obligation is intellect. The answer: the intended meaning is not that they do not have intellect, but that they do not benefit from that intellect. This is like the saying of a man to another when he does not understand: "You are only blind and deaf."

**The fourth story: the story of Lot (peace be upon him).**

﴿Certainly they have passed by the town that was rained upon with the rain of evil. Have they not been seeing it? Rather, they did not expect resurrection.﴾ ﴿When they see you, they take you only as a mockery: "Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?"﴾ ﴿He nearly led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in worshipping them. But they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in the way.﴾ ﴿Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god? Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or reason? They are only like livestock; rather, they are further astray in the way.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly they have passed by the town that was rained upon with the rain of evil. Have they not been seeing it? Rather, they did not expect resurrection.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, intended by "the town" Sodom (Sadum), one of the towns of the people of Lot (peace be upon him). There were five of them; Allah destroyed four with their inhabitants and one remained. "The rain of evil" means stones. The meaning is that the Quraysh passed many times on their trade journeys to the Levant (al-Sham)

[Page 74]

by that town which had been destroyed by stones from the sky. ﴿Have they not been seeing it?﴾ during their passing, looking at the traces of Allah's punishment and His retribution? ﴿Rather, they were﴾ a disbelieving people ﴿who did not expect resurrection.﴾ Regarding the meaning of ﴿expect﴾ they mentioned several aspects:

The first, which is what al-Qadi said, and it is the strongest: it is to be taken in its literal sense of hope (raja'). This is because a person does not bear the hardships of obligations and the difficulties of reflection and reasoning except out of hope for the reward of the Hereafter. So when he does not believe in the Hereafter, he does not hope for its reward, and therefore he does not bear those difficulties and hardships.

The second: its meaning is "they do not anticipate resurrection and its consequence," so hope is placed in the position of anticipation, because only one who believes anticipates the consequence.

The third: its meaning is "they do not fear," according to the Tihami dialect, and this is weak. The first is the correct view.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When they see you, they take you only as a mockery: "Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?"﴾ ﴿He nearly led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in worshipping them. But they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in the way.﴾ ﴿Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god? Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or reason? They are only like livestock; rather, they are further astray in the way.﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, had explained the extremity of the polytheists in denying His prophethood and in raising doubts about it, He then explained that when they see the Messenger, they take him as a mockery. They do not limit themselves to refusing to believe in him, but add to that mockery and belittling, and some of them say to others: ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: the author of the *al-Kashshaf* said: the first ﴿in﴾ is negative (*nafiyah*), and the second is a lightened form of the heavy (*mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah*), and the *lam* is the one that distinguishes between them (*al-lam al-fariqah*).

The second issue: the answer to (*idha*, "when") is what is implied of speech. That is: "And when they see you mocking, they say: 'Has Allah sent this one as a messenger?'" His saying ﴿they take you﴾ is a parenthetical clause placed between (*idha*) and its answer.

The third issue: ﴿they took him as mockery﴾ means "they mocked him," and the original is "they took him as an object of mockery, or as one mocked."

The fourth issue: know that Allah, exalted is He, informed about the polytheists that whenever they see the Messenger, they do two kinds of actions. One of them is that they mock him, and He explained that mockery by His saying: ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾ and that is great ignorance, because mockery either falls upon his form or upon his attributes.

As for the first, it is false, because peace be upon him was more beautiful than them in form and appearance. And even if it were not so, he, peace be upon him, did not claim to be distinguished from them by form, but by the proof (*hujjah*).

As for the second, it is also false, because peace be upon him claimed to be distinguished from them by the manifestation of the miracle upon him and not upon them, and they were unable to discredit his argument and its evidence. So in reality it is they who deserve to be mocked, but out of their shamelessness they reversed the matter and mocked the Messenger, peace be upon him. This shows that the falsifier at all times has nothing but foolishness and shamelessness.

The second kind: they used to say about him: ﴿He nearly led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in worshipping them.﴾ That indicates several matters:

The first: they called that "misguiding," which shows that they were extreme in exalting their gods and in considering his action of turning them away from them as a grave matter. This indicates that they believed this to be the truth. From this aspect, the view of the adherents of the theological sciences (*ashab al-ma'arif*) is refuted, who say that no one disbelieves except one who knows the proofs; because they were ignorant of it, and then Allah, exalted is He, attributed to them disbelief and error. Their saying ﴿had we not been steadfast in worshipping them﴾ also indicates this.

The second: this statement from them indicates the earnestness of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and his striving to turn them away from worshipping idols. Had it not been so, they would not have said ﴿He nearly led us astray from our gods﴾

[Page 75]

﴿had we not been steadfast in worshipping them.﴾ And so he, peace be upon him, was: at the beginning he exerted himself greatly in presenting proofs and answering doubts, and he bore what they did of kinds of foolishness and bad manners.

The third: this indicates that the people admitted that they had not at all objected to the proofs of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and they opposed them only with pure denial and blind imitation (*taqlid*). Because their saying ﴿had we not been steadfast in worshipping them﴾ is a sign of denial and imitation. And had they mentioned an objection to the proofs of the Messenger, peace be upon him, mentioning that would have been better than merely mentioning denial and insistence, which is the practice of the ignorant. This indicates that the people were overpowered by his argument, peace be upon him, and that all they had was mere shamelessness.

The fourth: the verse indicates that when his argument became manifest against them, peace be upon him, they became like madmen. Because they first mocked him, then described him as one who "nearly led us astray from our gods had we not confronted him with denial and insistence." This last statement indicates that the people had conceded to him the strength of argument and the perfection of intellect, while the first statement, which is ridicule and mockery, is fitting only for the ignorant and the incapable. So when the people combined these two statements, this indicates that they were like those bewildered about his affair: at times, out of shamelessness, they mock him, and at times they describe him with what is fitting only for the perfect scholar. Then, when He, glorified is He, related this statement of theirs, He refuted their way in that from three aspects:

The first of them: His saying: ﴿But they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in the way.﴾ Because when they described him with misguidance in their saying ﴿He nearly led us astray﴾, He explained that it will become clear to them who is the misguider and who is the one astray, at the sight of the punishment from which there is no escape for them. This is a severe warning to them for their blindness and turning away from reasoning and reflection.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god? Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ The meaning is that He, glorified is He, explained that the extent of these people's ignorance and their turning away from proofs was only due to the dominance of imitation over them, and that they took their desires as gods. Whenever desire called them to something, they obeyed it, whether or not evidence forbade it. Then there are several discussions here:

The first: His saying ﴿Have you seen﴾ (*ara'ayta*) is a word that may be used for informing and for asking. Here it is for expressing wonder at the ignorance of one whose description and attribute are such.

The second: His saying ﴿took his god, his desire﴾ means: "he took as his god what he desires," or "a god that he desires." It was also said that it is inverted, meaning "he took his desire as his god." This is weak, because His saying ﴿took his god, his desire﴾ conveys restriction (*hasr*), that is, he took for himself no god except his desire. This meaning does not arise from the inverted reading. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Desire is a god that is worshipped." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "A man among the polytheists would worship an idol, and when he saw something better than it, he would discard it and take the other and worship it."

The third: His saying ﴿Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ means: a protector who guards him from following his desire; that is, you are not such.

The fourth: a parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 22], and His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a compeller﴾ [Qaf: 45], and His saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256]. Al-Kalbi said: "It was abrogated (*nasakhat-ha*) by the verse of fighting."

The third of them: His saying: ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or reason?﴾ Here ﴿or﴾ (*am*) is disjunctive (*munqati'ah*), meaning "rather, do you think?" This indicates that this blame is more severe than the one preceding it, to the point that it required turning away from it to this one, which is that they are deprived of hearing and intellect. Because due to their intense obstinacy, they do not listen to speech, and if they hear it, they do not reflect upon it. So it is as if they had no intellect or hearing at all. At that point He likened them to livestock in their not benefiting from speech, and their not venturing to contemplate and reflect, and their devotion to immediate sensory pleasures, and their turning away from seeking the lasting intellectual felicities. Here there are questions:

[Page 76]

The first question: why did He say ﴿Or do you think that most of them﴾, passing judgment on most and not on all? The answer: because among them there were those who knew God, exalted is He, and understood the truth, but they abandoned Islam merely out of love of leadership, not out of ignorance.

The second question: why were they made more astray than livestock? The answer has several aspects:

The first: livestock submit to their owners and to the one who feeds and tends them, and they distinguish between the one who does good to them and the one who harms them. They seek what benefits them and avoid what harms them. These people do not submit to their Lord, nor do they distinguish between His kindness toward them and the harm of Satan to them, who is their enemy. They do not seek reward, which is the greatest benefit, nor do they guard against punishment, which is the greatest harm.

The second: just as the hearts of livestock are empty of knowledge, they are also empty of ignorance, which is the belief of one who believes contrary to what is the case, together with firm conviction. As for these people, their hearts, though empty of knowledge, are characterized by ignorance, for they do not know, and they do not know that they do not know; rather, they insist that they know.

The third: the lack of knowledge in livestock does not harm anyone, but the ignorance of these people is a source of great harm, because they block people from the path of Allah and seek to make it crooked.

The fourth: livestock know nothing, but they are incapable of seeking. As for these ignorant people, they are not incapable of seeking. One who is deprived of seeking lofty ranks, if he is incapable of it, does not deserve blame as one who is capable of it but abandons it due to his bad choice.

The fifth: beasts do not deserve punishment for lack of knowledge, but these people deserve the greatest punishment for it.

The sixth: according to the view of some people, beasts glorify Allah, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿There is not a thing but it exalts Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra': 44], and He said: ﴿Have you not considered that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens...﴾ up to His saying ﴿and the creatures (al-dawabb)﴾ [al-Hajj: 18], and He said: ﴿And the birds in flight; each has known its prayer and its glorification﴾ [al-Nur: 41]. And if that is the case, then the misguidance of the disbelievers is more severe and greater than the misguidance of these livestock.

The third question: since He, glorified is He, denied them hearing and intellect, how did He blame them for turning away from religion, and how did He send the Messenger to them? For the condition of obligation is intellect. The answer: the intended meaning is not that they do not have intellect, but that they do not benefit from that intellect. This is like the saying of a man to another when he does not understand: "You are only blind and deaf."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verses 45–46:

God says: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord extends the shade? Had He willed, He could have made it stationary. Then We made the sun its guide. Then We withdraw it to Us with an easy withdrawal.﴾ ﴿And it is He who made the night for you as a garment, and sleep as rest, and made the day a resurrection.﴾ ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy, and We send down from the sky pure water,﴾ ﴿that We may give life thereby to a dead land and give it to drink, of what We have created, livestock and many people.﴾

Page 77

Know that when God, exalted is He, had explained the ignorance of those who turn away from the signs of God and the corruption of their path in this, He then mentioned several kinds of signs indicating the existence of the Creator.

The first kind: reasoning from the state of the shade in its increase, its decrease, and its change from one state to another. On this there are several issues.

The first issue: His saying, ﴿Have you not seen﴾ has two interpretations.

One of them: that it is from seeing with the eye.

The second: that it is from seeing with the heart, meaning knowledge. If we take it as seeing with the eye, the meaning is: Have you not seen the shade, how your Lord extended it? Although the wording in the manner of the Arabs is more eloquent. If we take it as knowledge, which is the choice of al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj), the meaning is: Have you not known? And this is preferable, because if we consider the shade among the perceptible things, the effect of God's power in extending it is not visible by agreement, but it is known from the fact that every changing thing is contingent and every contingent thing has an influencer. Therefore, taking this expression as seeing with the heart is preferable to this interpretation.

The second issue: The one addressed by this address, although according to the apparent wording it is the Messenger, peace be upon him, the address is general in meaning, because the purpose of the verse is to explain God's blessings through the shade, and all those under obligation share in the fact that it is necessary to alert them to this blessing and to enable them to reason from it to the existence of the Creator.

The third issue: People have said much about the interpretation of this verse, and the summarized account returns to two views.

The first: that the shade is the matter intermediate between pure light and pure darkness, and it is what lies between the appearance of dawn and the rising of the sun, and likewise the conditions found under ceilings and in the courtyards of walls. This state is the most pleasant of states, because pure darkness is disliked by nature and the senses recoil from it, while pure light, which is the quality emanating from the sun, by its strength dazzles the visual sense and produces intense heat, and it is harmful. Therefore the most pleasant of states is the shade, and for this reason He described Paradise with it, saying: ﴿And an extended shade﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 30]. When this is established, we say: He, glorified is He, has shown that it is among the great blessings and sublime benefits. Then the one who looks at a colored body at the time of shade seems to see nothing but the body and the color. We say: the shade is not a third matter, and it is not known except through this: when the sun rises and its light falls upon the body, that shade disappears. Had it not been for the sun and the falling of its light upon bodies, it would not have been known that shade has existence and quiddity, because things are known only through their opposites. Had there been no sun, shade would not be known, and had there been no darkness, light would not be known. So it is as if, when the sun rose over the earth and the shade vanished, it then became apparent to minds that shade is a quality added to the body and the color. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Then We made the sun its guide﴾, meaning: We created the shade first with what it contains of benefits and pleasures, then We guided the minds to knowledge of its existence by making the sun rise, so the sun became a guide to the existence of this blessing. Then ﴿We withdrew it﴾, that is, We removed the shade not all at once but little by little, for as the sun's height increases, the shade's decrease on the western side increases. And since local motions do not occur all at once but gradually, so too the removal of shading does not occur all at once but gradually. Also, if the withdrawal of shade happened all at once, the interests would be disrupted, but its gradual withdrawal brings with it various interests of the world. The meaning of "withdrawal" is removal and annihilation. This is one of the two interpretations.

The second interpretation: when God, glorified and exalted is He, created the earth and the heavens, and created the stars, the sun, and the moon, the shade fell upon the earth. Then He, glorified is He, created the sun as a guide to it, because according to the movements of the lights the shades move; they are alternating and mutually concomitant with no intermediary between them, so that as one increases the other decreases. Just as the one who is guided follows the guide and keeps close to him, so too the shades are, as it were, guided by and close to the lights, and for this reason He made the sun a guide to them.

Page 78

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Then We withdrew it to Us with an easy withdrawal﴾, either the meaning is that the shades end little by little until they reach the limit of their diminution, so the removal of shades is called withdrawing them; or the meaning of withdrawing it easily is withdrawing it at the establishment of the Hour, through withdrawing its causes, which are the bodies that cast shades. His saying "easy" is like His saying: ﴿That is a gathering easy for Us﴾ [Qaf: 44]. This is the summarized interpretation.

The fourth issue: the way of reasoning from it to the existence of the Creator, the Benevolent, is that the occurrence of shade is a beneficial matter for living beings and rational beings. As for the occurrence of pure light or pure darkness, it is not among benefits. So the occurrence of this shade is either obligatory or permissible. The first is false, for otherwise it would not be subject to change, since what is obligatory does not change. Therefore it must be permissible, and so for its existence after non-existence, and its non-existence after existence, it needs a capable, governing, benevolent Creator who determines it in the beneficial manner. And this is none other than one who is able to move the upper bodies and arrange the celestial bodies in the best description and the most perfect order, and that is none other than God, glorified and exalted is He. If it is said: shade is an expression for the absence of light from what is capable of shining, so how does one reason from a privative matter to its own existence, and how is it counted among blessings? We answer: shade is not pure non-existence, but rather lights mixed with darknesses, and the verification is that shade is an expression for the second light, which is an existential matter, and on its verification and elaboration there is a subtle discussion, which is to be referred to in our rational books.

"Subat" is rest, and He made sleep a subat because it is a cause of rest. Abu Muslim said: subat is rest, and from it comes the name of Saturday (yawm al-sabt), because of the rest customarily taken on it. And it is said of the sick person when he gets relief from the fatigue of the illness: masbut. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: subat is death, and the masbut is the dead, because he is cut off from life. He said: this is like His saying: ﴿It is He who takes you back [in death] at night﴾ [al-An'am: 60]. We have said that interpreting it as death is preferable to interpreting it as rest, because "resurrection" (nushur) in opposition to it rejects that. Abu Muslim said: ﴿and made the day a resurrection﴾ means in the sense of dispersal and movement, just as God, exalted is He, named a person's sleep a death (wafah), saying: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died in their sleep﴾. Likewise He reconciled rising from sleep and rising from death through the naming "resurrection." This verse, together with its indication of the Creator's power in it, is a manifestation of His blessings upon His creation, for the concealment by the cover of night holds many religious and worldly benefits for many people. He likened sleep and wakefulness to death and life. It is reported from Luqman that he said to his son: "Just as you sleep and are awakened, so you die and are resurrected."

**The third type: His saying, ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good news before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf 7:57 has been explained earlier]. Then in it there are issues:**

**The first issue:** It is read as "al-rih" and "al-riyah" (the wind and the winds). Al-Zajjaj said: In "nashran" there are five readings: with a fatha on the nun and with a damma on it; with a damma on the nun and the shin; with the ba' (with one dot) and an alif; and in the feminine; and "bushran" with tanwin. Abu Muslim said: Whoever reads "bushran" intends the plural of *bashir* (bearer of good news), like His saying, ﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of good news﴾ [al-Rum 30:46]. As for the reading with the nun, it has the meaning of His saying, ﴿And by those that scatter, scattering﴾ [al-Mursalat 77:3], and it means the winds. And *al-rahmah* (mercy) means the rain, the water and the downpour.

**Page 79**

**The second issue:** His saying, ﴿And We send down from the sky pure water﴾, is explicit that Allah sends down water from the *sama'* (sky), not from the clouds. And the saying of one who says "the cloud is a *sama'*" is weak, because that is according to *al-ishtiqaq* (derivation of the word). But according to the convention of the language, *al-sama'* is the name of this known ceiling, so turning the word away from it is abandoning the apparent meaning.

**The third issue:** They differed about what *al-tahur* is. Many scholars said: *al-tahur* is that with which one purifies oneself, like *al-fatur* is that with which one breaks the fast and *al-sahur* is that with which one takes the pre-dawn meal. This is also narrated from Tha'lab. The author of *al-Kashshaf* rejected this and said: *fa'ul* is not from *taf'il* at all, and *tahur* has two forms in Arabic: an adjective and a noun that is not an adjective. The adjective is your saying *ma'un tahur* (pure water), like your saying *tahir* (pure). The noun is your saying *tahur* for that with which one purifies oneself, like *al-wada'* and *al-waqud* for that with which one performs ablution and that with which fire is lit. The argument of the first view is his saying (peace be upon him): "Dust is the *tahur* of the Muslim, even if he does not find water for ten years." If the meaning of *tahur* were *tahir* (pure), its meaning would be "dust is pure for the Muslim," and then the sentence would not be coherent. Likewise his saying (peace be upon him): "The *tahur* of the vessel of one of you, when a dog licks it, is that he wash it seven times." If *tahur* were *tahir*, its meaning would be "the vessel of one of you is pure," and then the sentence would not be coherent. Also, He (Exalted) said: ﴿And He sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you by it﴾ [al-Anfal 8:11]. He thus made clear that the purpose of the water is only purification by it, so it is necessary that what is meant by its being *tahur* is that it is that by which one is purified, because He mentioned it in the context of blessing, so it is necessary to take it to the more perfect description. And there is no doubt that *al-mutahhir* (that which purifies) is more perfect than *al-tahir* (that which is pure).

**The fourth issue:** Know that Allah (Exalted) mentioned two benefits of water:

The first: what relates to plants.

The second: what relates to animals.

Concerning the matter of vegetation, His saying: ﴿That We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾. On this there are questions.

The first question: Why did He say ﴿a dead land﴾ (baldatan maytan) and not "dead" in the feminine form (maytatan)? The answer: Because "baldah" carries the meaning of "balad," as in His saying: ﴿So We drive it to a dead land﴾ [Fatir: 9].

The second question: What is meant by the life and death of a land? The answer: People call land that has no cultivation mawat (dead land), and watering it, which entails its cultivation, is giving it life.

The third question: The group of the Naturalists (al-Tabi'iyyun), and likewise al-Ka'bi of the Mu'tazilah, said: Vegetation arises by the nature of the earth and water and by the influence of the sun upon them. They held to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾, for the preposition ba' in (bihi, "thereby") requires that water have an influence in that. The answer: Although the apparent meaning indicates this, the theologians (al-mutakallimun) set it aside, because there is evidence establishing the corruption of the doctrine of natural nature.
* * *
As for the matter of animals, His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And to give drink to what We have created, cattle and many humans﴾. On this there are questions.

The first question: Why did He specifically mention humans and cattle here, to the exclusion of birds and wild beasts, although all benefit from water? The answer: Because birds and wild beasts range far in seeking water, so drinking does not distress them, unlike cattle; for cattle are the property of humans, and most of their benefits are tied to them. Thus, bestowing favour upon them by giving drink to their cattle is like bestowing favour upon them by giving drink to themselves.
Page 80
* * *
The second question: What is the meaning of indefiniteness in "cattle" and "humans," and of describing them with multitude? The answer: Its meaning is that most people gather in the lands near valleys, rivers and places of water, so they are self-sufficient in drinking water apart from rain. But many of them dwell in the deserts and find no water for drinking except when rain falls. This is His saying: ﴿That We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾, meaning some lands of those who are far from the places where water is expected. It may also in many cases be taken as referring to His saying "and to give drink" (nusqiyahu), because a living being needs water moment after moment, unlike vegetation, which is sufficed by a fixed amount of water; indeed, if more is added after that, it would be closer to harm, whereas an animal needs it moment after moment for as long as it is alive.
* * *
The third question: Why did He place the giving of life to the land and the watering of cattle before the watering of humans? The answer: Because the life of humans is by the life of their land and the life of their cattle. So He mentioned first what is the cause of their life and livelihood before their own watering; for when they attain what serves as watering for their land and their livestock, they have thereby also attained their own watering. Also, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them﴾ means that He turns the rain each year to another side; and if that is so, it does not water everyone from it, but each year it waters many humans from it.
* * *
The fourth question: What are the "anasi" (humans)? The answer: al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "insi" and "anasi" are like "kursi" and "karasi" (chair and chairs). He did not say "kathirin" (many), because the form fa'il has come singular while intending multiplicity, as in His saying: ﴿And generations between them, many﴾ [al-Furqan: 38], and ﴿And excellent are those as companions﴾ [al-Nisa': 69].

Know that the jurists have derived the rulings on waters from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We sent down from the sky water, pure﴾. We will point to the foundations of those issues, so we say: Here there are two considerations:
One of them: that water purifies.
The second: whether other than water is purifying or not.

The first consideration: We say: Water either does not change or changes. The first category, which does not change, is pure in itself and purifies others, except used water (al-musta'mal). According to al-Shafi'i it is pure but not purifying. Malik and al-Thawri said: ablution with it is permissible. Abu Hanifah, in the narration of Abu Yusuf, said it is najis (impure). Here there are issues:
The first issue: To show that it is not purifying. Our evidence is his saying, upon him be peace: "Let none of you bathe in standing water while in a state of major impurity." Had the water remained as it was, pure and purifying, there would be no meaning in prohibiting it. And by way of analogy: the Companions used to perform ablution on journeys and did not collect that water, though they knew they would need water afterward; had that water been purifying, they would have carried it for the day of need. Malik argued from the verse, the report and analogy. As for the verse, it is on two grounds:
The first: His saying: ﴿And We sent down from the sky water, pure﴾, and His saying: ﴿And He sends down upon you from the sky water to purify you thereby﴾ [al-Anfal: 11]. The verse indicates that the attribute of purifying has been established for water, and the basis for what is established is its continuance; so it is necessary to rule that this attribute remains for water after it becomes used. Also, His saying "pure" (tahuran) requires that one may purify with it time after time.
The second: He commanded washing absolutely in His saying: ﴿Then wash﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and using any liquid is washing; for there is no meaning to washing except passing water over the limb. The poet said:
"How beautiful it is, when tears wash its kohl!"
So whoever bathes with used water has performed washing, and so it must be sufficient for him, because he has done what he was commanded, and thus must be discharged of the obligation. As for the Sunnah: it is reported that he, upon him be peace, "performed ablution and wiped his head with the remainder of what was in his hand," and from him, upon him be peace: "that he performed ablution and took from the moisture of his beard and wiped his head with it," and from Ibn 'Abbas that he, upon him be peace, "bathed and saw a bare spot on his body which the water had not reached, so he took a hair which had moisture on it and passed it over that spot." As for analogy: it is pure water that has met a pure body, so it resembles when it meets a stone or iron; and likewise water used in the fourth washing, and water used for cooling and cleaning. And because there is no disagreement that if one places water on the top of his face and the obligation of that place is discharged by it, then that same water descends to the rest of the face, it suffices him, although that water has already become used on the top of the face.
* * *
The second issue: The evidence that used water is pure is His saying: ﴿And We sent down from the sky water, pure﴾, and from the Sunnah that he, upon him be peace, "took from the moisture of his beard and wiped his head with it, and said: 'Water was created pure; nothing makes it najis except what changes its taste, smell or colour.'" Al-Shafi'i said: he, upon him be peace, performed ablution, and there is no doubt that some of what dripped from him reached his garment; it is not reported that he changed his garment or washed it, nor did any of the Muslims do so; so it is established that they agreed it is not najis. Also, it is pure water that has met a pure body, so it resembles when it meets a stone.
* * *
The third issue: Used water is either used on the limbs of ablution or in washing garments. As for that used on the limbs of ablution, it is either used for what was obligatory and an act of worship, or for what was obligatory and not an act of worship, or for what was an act of worship and not obligatory, or for what is neither obligatory nor an act of worship.

As for the first category: that used for what was obligatory and an act of worship, it is non-purifying by the agreement of al-Shafi'i's companions.

As for the second category: it is like the water used by a dhimmi woman under a Muslim husband, namely in washing her menstruation so that intercourse with her becomes lawful for the husband.

As for the third category: it is like water used in the second and third washings, water used in renewing ablution, and water used in recommended baths; al-Shafi'i's companions have two opinions regarding these two categories.

As for the fourth category: it is like water used in the fourth washing, and for cooling and cleansing; that is by the agreement of al-Shafi'i's companions not used water, and it is pure and purifying.

As for water used in washing garments: if one washes a garment from najasah and it becomes clean with one washing, it is recommended to wash it three times; the water separated off in the second and third washings is purifying according to the more correct view.

The second category: water that changes. We say: when water changes, either it changes by itself or by something else. As for the first, it is like water changed by long standing, and it is permissible to perform ablution with it; for he, upon him be peace, used to perform ablution from the well of Qudha'ah, whose water was as if it were an infusion of henna. As for water changed by the cause of something else, that other thing is either not joined to it or is joined to it. As for what is not joined to it: it is like when a carcass falls near the water and the water becomes foul-smelling because of it; this too is purifying. As for when it changes because of something joined to it, that joined thing is either pure or najis.

The first category: if it is pure, it either does not mix with it or mixes with it. If it does not mix with it, it is like water changed by the falling into it of oil, perfume, aloes-wood, ambergris, or solid camphor; this too is purifying, just as when a carcass is near the water, and because purifying was established by His saying: ﴿And We sent down from the sky water, pure﴾, and what is established has its continuance. As for water changed by something that mixes with it: that mixing thing either cannot be kept away from the water or can be. As for what cannot be kept away, it is like water changed by dust, silt, leaves that fall into it, or the algae that grows in it; this too is purifying, for purifying was established by the verse, and avoiding that is difficult, so it is lifted by His saying: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. Likewise if water flows in its course over a mine of arsenic, or lime, or antimony, or some of these fall into it, or it wells up from their mines. As for when water changes by mixing with what the water can dispense with, one considers: if the change is slight, such that the water is not described by it, as when saffron falls into it and it becomes slightly yellow, or flour and it becomes slightly white, ablution with it is permissible according to the sound view of the school; for it has not stripped it of the name of water. As for when the change is great: if it acquires a new name, like broth, ablution with it is not permissible by agreement; and if it does not acquire a new name, then according to al-Shafi'i ablution with it is not permissible, and according to Abu Hanifah it is permissible.

The proofs of al-Shafi'i are of several kinds:
First: "He, upon him be peace, performed ablution and then said: 'This is an ablution with which God does not accept prayer except with it.'" If that ablution was made with changed water, it would have to be impermissible except with it; but by agreement this is not the case; so it is established that it was with unchanged water, which is what was sought.
Second: when rosewater mixes with water and then a person performs ablution with it, it is possible that some of the limbs were washed with rosewater rather than water; and if that is so, doubt has arisen regarding the attainment of ablution, while the certainty of the minor impurity remains, and doubt does not override certainty; so it must remain in the state of minor impurity. This differs from when it is slight and its effect does not appear, for then it is as if non-existent; but if its effect appears, we know it remains, and what we have mentioned applies.
Third: ablution is an act of devotion whose meaning cannot be understood; for if one performed ablution with rosewater, his ablution would not be valid, and if he performed it with turbid, rotten water, his ablution would be valid. And what whose meaning cannot be understood must be confined to the place of the text and abandon analogy.

The proofs of Abu Hanifah are several:
First: His saying: ﴿And We sent down from the sky water, pure.﴾ The verse indicates that water is purifying, and what is established has its continuance, so this attribute must remain after change by mixing.
Second: His saying: ﴿Then wash﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6] is a command to washing absolutely, and he has done it, so he must be discharged of the obligation; and we have already explained the statement of this point earlier.

**[Page 82 continues]**

Third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you find no water, then perform tayammum﴾ [An-Nisa': 43]. He made the permissibility of tayammum (dry ablution with clean earth) conditional on not finding water. Whoever finds this changed water has found water, because changed water is water with the attribute of change, and the qualified thing exists while its attribute exists. Therefore it is not permissible for him to perform tayammum.

Fourth: His saying, peace be upon him, concerning the sea: «Its water is pure (al-tahur)». Its apparent meaning requires that purification with it is permissible even if something else has mixed with it, because the Prophet (ﷺ) stated it without restriction.

Fifth: He, peace be upon him, permitted ablution with the leftover of a cat and with the leftover of a menstruating woman, even if some of their saliva had mixed with it.

Sixth: There is no disagreement about performing ablution with rainwater and torrent water whose colour has changed by the mixing of clay and of the grass and plants found in the open country. Because of such mixing, it is sometimes seen as changed to blackness and at other times to redness or yellowness. This became a principle for everything that mixes with water, provided it does not overpower it so as to strip it of the name "water."

**The second section:** If what mixes with the water is something ritually impure (najis), some people claim that water does not become impure unless it is changed by the impurity, whether it is little or much. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Nakha'i, Malik and Dawud, and Shaykh al-Ghazali inclined to it in his book "al-Ihya'." Abu Bakr al-Razi said: The position of our companions (the Shafi'is) is that whenever we are certain that some part of an impurity is in it, or it is considered likely, its use is not permissible. This rule does not differ between sea water, well water, a pond, still water or flowing water. For if an impurity falls into sea water, the water in which the impurity is located may not be used, and likewise flowing water. As for our companions' consideration of a pond in which, if one edge is moved, the other edge does not move, it is only a discussion about the direction of probable reaching of the impurity that falls into one edge to the other edge. It is not our discussion that some waters containing an impurity may be used while others may not. This is all the words of Abu Bakr.

I say: Some people distinguished between little and much water. From Abdullah ibn Umar: «If the water is forty qullahs, nothing makes it impure.» From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: «A pool in which a junub (one in major ritual impurity) bathes is not to be used unless it contains forty ghurub.» This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. Masruq and Ibn Sirin said: If the water is abundant, nothing makes it impure. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Still water is not made impure by anything if it is the amount of three qullal. Al-Shafi'i said: If the water is two qullatayn by the qullal of Hajar, only what changes its taste, smell or colour makes it impure; and if it is less, it becomes impure because the impurity appears in it.

Know that it is possible to support Malik's position with several arguments:

First: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We sent down from the sky pure water﴾. Its application was abandoned in water that has changed in colour, taste or smell because of the appearance of impurity in it, so it remains in other cases on the original basis.

Second: His saying, peace be upon him: «Allah created water pure; nothing makes it impure except what changes its taste, colour or smell». This is a clear text on the matter.

Third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So wash your faces﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 6]. One who performs ablution with this water has washed his face, so he does what he was commanded and is discharged of the obligation.

Fourth: Whenever two mixed things exist and one of them predominates over the other, the overpowered thing takes on the quality of the dominant one. For example, if a drop of vinegar falls into abundant water, the quality of vinegar is lost from it and it takes on the quality of water. The predominance of one over the other is known only through the sensible properties and effects, namely taste, colour or smell. Therefore, whenever the taste, colour or smell of the impurity appears, the impurity is dominant over the water, the water is annihilated in it, and the ruling of impurity prevails. But when none of that appears, the dominant thing is the water, the impurity is annihilated in it, and the ruling of purity prevails.

Fifth: What is narrated from Umar: that he performed ablution from a jar of a Christian woman, although the impurity of Christian vessels is known with a probability close to certainty. This indicates that Umar relied only on the absence of change.

Sixth: The determination of water by a known measure, even if it were considered, as two qullatayn according to al-Shafi'i or ten by ten according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, would make Makkah and Madinah the most suitable places for purity, because water is not abundant there, neither flowing nor large still water. From the beginning of the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) to the end of the time of the Companions, it is not reported that they debated the determination of water by fixed measures, nor that they asked about how to keep water from impurities. Their water vessels were handled by children and female slaves who did not guard against impurities.

Seventh: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lowered the vessel for the cat, and they did not prevent cats from drinking from their vessels, although they used to see that the cat eats the mouse. And there were no pools in their lands from which cats lap, and they did not descend to the wells.

Eighth: Al-Shafi'i stated explicitly that the washing water of impurities is pure if it does not change, and impure if it changes. What difference is there between the water touching the impurity by coming upon it or by it coming upon the water? And what meaning is there to the claim that the force of the flow repels the impurity, given that the force of the flow did not prevent mixing?

Ninth: They used to relieve themselves (istinja') at the edges of little flowing water, and there is no disagreement that al-Shafi'i's school holds that if urine falls into flowing water and does not change it, ablution with it is permissible, even if it is little. What difference is there between flowing and still water? I wish I knew whether reliance on non-change is better, or reliance on the strength of the water due to its flowing.

Tenth: If urine falls into two qullatayn, then they are separated, every cup taken from it is pure according to al-Shafi'i. It is known that the urine is spread in it, and it is little. So what difference is there between this little falling into that amount of water initially, and between it reaching it when another thing is joined to it?

Eleventh: Bathhouses have not ceased in past ages, where the ascetics perform ablution and dip hands and vessels into that little water from those pools, while knowing that pure and impure hands kept coming upon them. Had the determination by two qullatayn been considered, that would have become well known and would have reached the level of tawatur (mass transmission). Because a matter on which the masses have a great need must have its transmission reach the level of tawatur. Since that is not the case, we know that it is not considered.

Twelfth: If we rule that water is impure, then we cannot rule that water is impure when it is in the extreme of abundance, like the water of great valleys and large pools. For that is by consensus false, so a determination by a specific measure is necessary. We have transmitted different determinations from people, and none of them is preferable to another, so they conflict and cancel each other out. As for Abu Hanifa's determination of ten by ten, it is known to be mere arbitrariness. As for al-Shafi'i's determination by two qullatayn, based on his saying, peace be upon him: «When the water reaches two qullatayn, it carries no impurity», it is also weak, because when al-Shafi'i narrated this report he said: "A man informed me." So the narrator is unknown, and the hadith is mursal (with a missing link), and this is not a proof according to him. Also, many hadith scholars claim that it is mawquf (stopping at a Companion) on Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. Even if we grant the soundness of the narration, it is referring an unknown matter to another unknown, because the qullah is not known, as it suits a cup, a jar, and everything carried in the hand; and it is also a name for the top of a man's head and the peak of a mountain. Even if we grant that the qullah is known, there is disturbance (idtirab) in the text of the report, for it has been narrated as "when the water reaches two qullatayn," and narrated as "when it reaches a qullah," and narrated as "forty qullahs," and narrated as "when it reaches two qullatayn or three," and narrated as "when it reaches two cups." Even if we grant the soundness of the text, it abandons its apparent meaning, because his saying, "it carries no impurity," cannot be applied to its apparent meaning, for when an impurity falls into it, it has carried it. Even if we grant that it can be applied to its apparent meaning, impurity is of two types: legal impurity and real (physical) impurity. When a term is between its linguistic meaning and its legal meaning, carrying it on the linguistic meaning is preferable, because the term is literal in the linguistic meaning and figurative in the legal meaning, to avoid homonymy and transfer. When this is so, it must be carried on that. The linguistic meaning of impurity is what is naturally disgusting, and he, peace be upon him, said: «What the Arabs find disgusting is forbidden.» Having established this, we say: the meaning of his saying "it carries no impurity" is that it does not become naturally disgusting. We say in accordance with its implication. But why do you say that it is not made impure in the legal sense? Even if we grant that the intended meaning of impurity is legal impurity, his saying "it carries no impurity" means that it is too weak to carry it, and weakness means being affected by it, so this would be evidence that it becomes impure, not that it remains pure.

It may be said: The answer to these objections is that although al-Shafi'i did not mention the name of the narrator in some places, he mentioned it in other places, so it is no longer mursal. Also, the other hadith scholars have specified the name of the narrator. As for his saying that it is mawquf on Ibn Umar: we say we do not accept this, for Yahya ibn Ma'in said: "Its isnad is good." It was said to him: "Ibn 'Ulayyah stopped it at Ibn Umar." He said: "If Ibn 'Ulayyah stopped it, Hammad ibn Salamah raised it." As for his saying that the qullah is unknown: we say we do not accept this, because Ibn Jurayj said in his narration: "by the qullal of Hajar." Then he said: "I have seen the qullal of Hajar, and the qullah would hold two qirbahs or two qirbahs and something." As for his saying that there is disturbance in its text: we say we do not accept this, because we and you agree that all other measures are not considered, so what we have mentioned remains considered. As for his saying that it abandons its apparent meaning: we say if we carry it on legal impurity, this objection is removed, and that is preferable, because carrying the words of the Law on the legal benefit is preferable to carrying them on a rational meaning, especially since carrying them on a rational meaning entails nullification. As for his saying that the intended meaning is that it is too weak to carry it: we say it is authentic in some narrations that he said: «When the water is two qullatayn, it does not become impure», and because he, peace be upon him, made the two qullatayn a condition for this ruling, and what is conditioned on a condition is absent when the condition is absent. According to what they have said, the two qullatayn would have no benefit. We say: There is no doubt that this report, if authentic, requires the specification of the general meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We sent down from the sky pure water﴾, and the general meaning of His saying: ﴿But He wants to purify you﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 6], and the general meaning of His saying: ﴿So wash your faces﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 6], and the general meaning of his saying, peace be upon him: «Water was created pure; nothing makes it impure.» This specifier must be far from possibility and confusion, and the qullal of Hajar are unknown. As for Ibn Jurayj's saying that the qullah holds two qirbahs or two qirbahs and something, it is not a proof, because just as the qullah is unknown, so the qirbah is unknown, for it may be large and it may be small. Also, the narrations differ: at times he said "when the water reaches two qullatayn," at times "forty qullahs," and at times "two cups." So when they conflict…

[Page 85]

Having established the argument in support of Malik's view, we now turn to the arguments of those who ruled that water becomes impure when an impurity falls into it. They offered several proofs.

The first is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He makes lawful for them the good things and makes unlawful for them the impure things﴾ [al-A'raf: 157]. Impure substances (najasat) are among the impure things (khaba'ith). Allah also says: ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion and blood﴾ [al-Nahl: 115], and about wine He says: ﴿It is an abomination from the work of Satan, so avoid it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90]. The Prophet (peace be upon him) passed by two graves and said: "Indeed, they are being punished, and they are not being punished for a major sin. One of them did not protect himself from urine, and the other went about spreading slander." Allah has therefore prohibited these things absolutely, and He did not distinguish between their existing alone and their being mixed with water. Hence it is obligatory to prohibit the use of any water in which some part of the impurity remains. At most, the proofs showing that water is a purifier entail that it is permissible to purify with it. But those proofs are permissive, whereas the proofs we have cited are prohibitive, and when the permissive and the prohibitive conflict, the prohibitive takes precedence. Do you not see that if a slave-girl is owned jointly by two men, one of whom owns a hundredth part of her and the other a single part, the aspect of prohibition is stronger than the aspect of permission, and it is not lawful for either of them to have intercourse with her? The same applies here.

The second is the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "None of you should urinate in standing water and then bathe in it from a state of major impurity (janabah)." He stated it without qualification, making no distinction between a small and a large quantity.

The third is the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "When one of you wakes from his sleep, let him wash his hand three times before he puts it into the vessel, for he does not know where his hand spent the night." He commanded the washing of the hand as a precaution against an impurity that may have touched it from the place of istinja' (cleaning after relieving oneself). It is known that if such a hand is put into water, it does not change it. Had the impurity not corrupted the water, the command to take precaution against it would have no meaning.

The fourth is the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "When the water reaches two qullahs (qullatayn), it does not carry impurity (khabath)." By its implication, when water does not reach two qullahs, it must carry impurity.

Malik answered the first argument by saying: There is no dispute that it is prohibited to use an impurity. But a small part of a liquid impurity, when it falls into water, shows no effect in its colour, taste or smell. Why do you say that the impurity remains? Why is it not possible to say that it has been transformed out of its former attribute? The explanation of this is what we have already presented. As for the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him), "None of you should urinate in standing water," why do you say that this prohibition is only for the reason you have mentioned? Perhaps the prohibition was only because a person might drink it, and that is something the natural disposition finds repugnant; but the discussion is not about natural repugnance. As for the words, "When one of you wakes from his sleep, let him wash his hand three times," we are agreed that this command is recommended (istihbab). How then can what is consequent upon it be a command of obligation? Furthermore, even supposing it were a command of obligation, why do you say that it was directed at that obligation only for the reason you have mentioned? As for the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him), "When the water reaches two qullahs," the discussion of it has already preceded. Then, having conceded everything we have said, this is an appeal to the implication and to the texts we have mentioned in their explicit form, and the explicit takes precedence over the implicit. And Allah knows best.

The second inquiry: whether other than water is purifying (tahur). Al-Asamm and al-Awza'i said that ablution is permissible with all liquids. Abu Hanifa said that ablution with date-wine (nabidh) is permissible while travelling, and he also said that the removal of impurity is permissible with all liquids that remove the substance of impurities. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the quality of being purifying (tahuriyyah) is restricted to water absolutely. His proof, in the case of ritual impurity (hadath), is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and if you find no water, then perform tayammum﴾ [al-Nisa': 43]. He made tayammum obligatory when water is absent, and if ablution were permissible with vinegar or date-wine, tayammum would not be obligatory when water is absent. As for the case of impurity (khabath), it is because if vinegar were effective in removing impurity, it would be purifying, for "purifying" (tahur) means nothing but that which purifies. And if it were purifying, it would be permissible to use it for removing ritual impurity, by the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Allah does not accept the prayer of any one of you until he places the purifier (tahur) in its proper places." The word "until" (hatta) denotes the endpoint, so the non-acceptance ends when the purifier is used. And the non-acceptance ends when acceptance is achieved. Hence, if vinegar were purifying, the prayer would be accepted by using it. Since it is not accepted, we know that being purifying in the case of impurity is also restricted to water.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verses 50–52:**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly varied it among them that they may take heed, but most of the people refused except disbelief﴾ ﴿And had We willed, We would have sent into every town a warner﴾ ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it, a great striving﴾. And in this are several issues:

The first issue: Know that they differed concerning what the pronoun in His statement ﴿And We have certainly varied it﴾ refers to, and they mentioned three possibilities:

The first, which is the view of the majority, is that it refers to the rain. Among these, some said: the meaning of "varied it" (ṣarrafnāhu) is that We made it flow in the rivers, so that they benefited from it for drinking, for crops, and for all kinds of livelihood. Others said: its meaning is that He, glorified is He, sends it down in one place and not another, and in one year and not another; then in the second year it falls differently from what it did in the first year. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "No year is more abundant in rain than another, but God varies it across the earth," and then he recited this verse. Ibn Masʿūd narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no year with more rain than another, but when a people act in sinful ways, God turns it away from them to others, and when they all disobey, God diverts it to the wastelands."

The second is the view of Abū Muslim: that His statement ﴿varied it﴾ refers to the rain, the winds, the clouds, the shades, and the rest of the proofs that God, exalted is He, has mentioned.

The third: ﴿And We have certainly varied it﴾ means this statement (i.e., the Qur'an) among the people, and in the rest of the Books and scrolls that were sent down to the messengers. It is the mention of the formation of the clouds and the sending down of the rain, so that they may reflect and infer from it the existence of the Creator. The first view is closer, because it is the nearest of the things mentioned to the pronoun.

The second issue: al-Jubbāʾī said: His statement, ﴿that they may take heed﴾, indicates that He, exalted is He, wills for all of them that they take heed and give thanks. Had He willed that they disbelieve and turn away, this would not be valid. This refutes the view of those who say that God wills disbelief from whoever disbelieves. He said: His statement ﴿but most of the people refused except disbelief﴾ also indicates their capacity to perform this taking heed; for if they had no capacity, it would not be correct to say, "They refused to do it," just as one does not say of a lame person, "He refused to walk." Al-Kaʿbī said: His statement ﴿And We have certainly varied it among them that they may take heed﴾ is a proof against those who claim that the Qur'an is a burden upon the disbelievers, and that He did not intend by sending it down that they should believe. For His statement "that they may take heed" is general over all of them, and His statement ﴿but most of the people refused﴾ requires that this "most" be included in that general reference; for it is not correct to say, "We sent it down to the Quraysh that they may believe, but most of the Banū Tamīm refused except disbelief." Know that the discussion of this has already preceded several times.

The third issue: His statement ﴿but most of the people refused except disbelief﴾: the intended meaning is ingratitude for the blessing and denial of it, in that they do not reflect upon it or infer from it the existence of the Creator, His power, and His beneficence. It has also been said: the intended meaning of "disbelief" (kufr) here is unbelief itself, and that unbelief occurs because they say, "We were given rain by such-and-such a star-mansion (nawʾ)." For whoever denies that blessings come from the Bestower, and attributes some part of this blessing to the spheres and the stars, has disbelieved. Know that the verified position is that whoever holds that the spheres and the stars are independent in producing these things, there is no doubt of his disbelief; but as for whoever says that the Creator, exalted is He, has created them with properties and attributes which bring about these events, his error may perhaps not reach the level of disbelief.

The fourth issue: They said: the verse indicates that the opposite of what God knows is within His capacity. For the word "law" (lau) indicates that He, exalted is He, did not will to send into every town a warner; then He informed of His being capable of that. This indicates that the opposite of what God knows is within His capacity.

[Page 87]

As for His statement, exalted is He, ﴿And had We willed, We would have sent into every town a warner﴾, the strongest view is that its purpose is the exaltation of the Prophet (ﷺ). This is for several reasons:

The first: It is as if He, exalted is He, made clear to him that, although He has the power to send a messenger and a warner into every town, He specified him with the messengership and preferred him above all by it. For this reason He followed it with His statement: ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾, that is, do not agree with them.

The second: The intended meaning is: "Had We willed, We would have lightened from you the burdens of the messengership to all the worlds, and sent into every town a warner. But We restricted the matter to you, honored you, and preferred you over the rest of the messengers. So respond to this honor with firmness in the religion."

The third: The verse requires combining gentleness with severity. For it indicates the power to send into every town a warner like Muḥammad, and that there is absolutely no need in the Divine Presence for Muḥammad. His statement "had" (law) indicates that He, glorified is He, does not do that. Thus, by considering the first, discipline is achieved, and by considering the second, honor is achieved.

As for His statement: ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾, the intended meaning is the prohibition of obeying them. This verse indicates that a prohibition against something does not require that the one prohibited be occupied with it.

* * *

As for His statement: ﴿and strive against them with it, a great striving﴾, some of them said: the intended meaning is exerting effort in conveying and calling to the message. Others said: the intended meaning is fighting. Others said: both. The closer view is the first, because the surah is Meccan, and the command to fight came after the Hijrah by a period of time. He said, ﴿a great striving﴾, because if He had sent into every town a warner, it would have been obligatory upon every warner to strive against his own town. Thus those strivings would have gathered upon the Messenger of God, and his striving would have multiplied and become great because of that. So He said to him, "and strive against them" by reason of your being the warner of all the towns, ﴿a great striving﴾, comprehensive of every striving.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is He who released the two seas, one sweet and palatable, and the other salt and bitter; and He placed between them a barrier and a forbidding partition.﴾

Know that this is the fourth type of the proofs of Tawhid (Divine Oneness). His saying: ﴿released the two seas﴾ means He let them go free and sent them forth. It is said: "I released the animal (marajtu al-dabbah)" when you let it graze freely. The root of al-maraj is release and mixing, and from it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they are in a confused matter﴾ [Qaf: 5]. He named the two great, vast bodies of water "two seas."

Ibn Abbas said: "maraja al-bahrayn" means He sent them forth in their courses as horses are sent forth in the pasture (al-marj), and they meet. His saying: ﴿this is sweet and palatable﴾ — by "furat" is meant the one that is extremely sweet, to the point of being sweetest. Ujaj is its opposite. He, glorified is He, by His power separates them and prevents them from intermingling, and as part of His great power He made a barrier, a hindrance, from His might. Here there are questions.

The first question: What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and a forbidding partition (hijran mahjuran)﴾? The answer: it is the phrase that one who seeks refuge says, and we have explained it. Here it is used in a figurative sense, as if each of the two seas seeks refuge from its companion and says to it, "hijran mahjuran," just as He said: ﴿They do not transgress against each other﴾ [al-Rahman: 20], meaning neither of them oppresses the other by mixing. So the absence of transgression is like seeking refuge. Here He made each of them in the form of one who transgresses against its companion, so it seeks refuge from it, and this is among the finest of metaphors.

[Page 88]
The second question: There is no existence of a sweet sea, so how did God, exalted is He, mention it here? It is not said: this is refuted in two ways:
First: that what is meant by it is the great rivers, such as the Nile and Jayhun.
Second: perhaps He placed in the seas a place where one of its two sides is sweet and the other salty.

We say: As for the first, it is weak, because these rivers do not contain salt, and the seas do not contain sweet water, so there is absolutely no place for wonder. As for the second, it is weak, because the place of argument must be known, and by mere supposition an argument is not good. We say: what is meant by the sweet sea is these rivers, and by the bitter one the great seas. And He made between them a barrier, that is, a barrier of land. The point of the argument here is clear: for if sweetness and saltiness were due to the nature of the earth or the water, there would necessarily be uniformity; and if it is not so, then there must be a wise, powerful Agent who assigns to each of the bodies a specific, determined property.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verse 54:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who created from water a human being and made him [a line of] lineage and marriage. And your Lord is ever Competent.﴾

Know that this is the fifth type of the proofs of Tawhid (divine oneness), and it contains two discussions.

The first: they mentioned two opinions regarding this water.

One of them: it is the water from which the origins of living beings were created, and this is what He meant by His saying: ﴿And Allah created every moving creature from water﴾ [al-Nur: 45].

The second: that what is meant is the sperm-drop (nutfah), by His saying: ﴿created from a gushing fluid﴾ [al-Tariq: 6], and ﴿from a despised fluid﴾ [al-Mursalat: 20].

The second discussion: the meaning is that He, exalted is He, divided mankind into two kinds possessing lineage (nasab), that is, males to whom descent is traced, so it is said: "So-and-so, son of so-and-so," and "So-and-so, daughter of so-and-so," and possessors of marriage relations (sihr), that is, females with whom people become related by marriage, and the like. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He made of him two mates, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39]. And ﴿your Lord is ever Competent﴾, in that from a single drop He created two kinds of humankind, the male and the female.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verse 55–58:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they worship besides Allah that which neither benefits them nor harms them, and the disbeliever is ever an assistant against his Lord.﴾ ﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner.﴾ ﴿Say, "I do not ask you for it any wage, except that whoever wills may take to his Lord a way."﴾ ﴿And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die, and exalt [Him] with His praise. And sufficient is He as Knower of the sins of His servants.﴾

Know that when Allah, Exalted is He, had explained the proofs of tawhid (divine unity), He returned to condemning their conduct in worshipping idols. There are several issues in this verse:

The first issue: It has been said that what is meant by "the disbeliever" is Abu Jahl, because the verse was revealed concerning him. But it is better to take it in its general sense, because the specificity of the cause (sabab al-nuzul) does not detract from the generality of the wording, and because it is more consistent with the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿And they worship besides Allah﴾.

The second issue: They have mentioned several meanings for "ẓahīr" (assistant):

The first of them: that ẓahīr is in the sense of muẓāhir (one who backs up), like ʿawīn in the sense of muʿāwin (helper), and the form faʿīl in the sense of mufāʿil is not uncommon. The meaning is that the disbeliever backs up Satan against his Lord with enmity. If it is asked: how is it valid for the disbeliever to be a helper of Satan against his Lord with enmity? We say: Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned Himself and meant His Messenger, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 57].

The second: It is permissible that by ẓahīr is meant a group, as in His saying: ﴿And the angels thereafter are a supporting group﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4], just as ṣadīq and khalīṭ are used (in the plural sense). According to this interpretation, what is meant by "the disbeliever" is the category, and that some of them back up others in extinguishing the light of the religion of Allah, Exalted is He. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿and their brothers extend them in error﴾ [al-A'raf: 202].

The third: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: ẓahīr derives from the expression "ẓahara fulān bi-ḥājatī" when he cast it behind his back (ignored it), and it is from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and you have taken Him behind your backs, disregarded﴾ [Hud: 92]. It is said of one who holds a thing in contempt: "he cast it behind his back." The analogy of Arabic would be to say maẓhūr (one who is cast aside), i.e., held in contempt and left behind the back. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 25, verses 59–60:**

Allah's saying: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne, the Most Merciful; so ask about Him one who is informed.﴾ And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to whatever you command us?" And it increases them in aversion.

Know that when Allah, glorified is He, commanded the Messenger to put his trust in Him, He described Himself with several attributes:

The first: that He is Living and does not die, as in His saying: ﴿And rely upon the Living who does not die﴾ [al-Furqan: 58].

The second: that He is Knowing of all that is known, as in His saying: ﴿And sufficient is He as one informed of the sins of His servants﴾ [al-Furqan: 58].

The third: that He is Capable of all possible things. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth﴾. His saying ﴿He who created﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿the Living who does not die﴾, because since He, glorified is He, is the Creator of the heavens and the earths and of everything between them, it is established that He is the One capable of all forms of benefit and of repelling harm, and that all blessings come from Him. Therefore, it is not permissible to rely upon anyone except Him. There are questions regarding the verse:

**The first question:** Days are an expression for the movements of the sun in the heavens, and before the heavens there were no days. So how does Allah say, "He created them in six days"? The answer: it means in a period whose measure is this period. It is not said that a thing which is measured by a limited quantity and accepts increase, decrease and division cannot be pure non-existence, but it must be existent; thus its existence entails the existence of a duration before the existence of the world, and that requires the eternity of time. We say: this is countered by time itself, because the imagined duration that can contain ten days cannot contain five days, and the imagined duration that can contain five days cannot contain ten days, so it would follow that the duration has another duration. Since this does not follow, what you have said does not follow either. Based on this we say: perhaps Allah, glorified is He, first created the duration and then created the heavens and the earth within it, in a measure of six days. Some people said: "in six days of the days of the Hereafter, each day being a thousand years," but this is far-fetched, because definition must be by a known matter, not by an unknown one.

**The second question:** Why did He determine the creation and bringing into existence with this measure? The answer: according to our view, will and power are sufficient for specification. The Mu'tazilah (a theological school that emphasized human reason and divine justice) said: rather, there must be a motive of wisdom, namely that specifying the creation of the world with this measure is better for those who are obligated. This is far-fetched for two reasons:

The first: the realization of that wisdom is either necessary in itself or possible. If it is necessary, it must not change, so it would be realized at all times, and therefore it is not suitable to be a cause for specifying a particular time. If it is possible, then the realization of that wisdom at that time requires another specifier, and this entails an infinite regress (tasalsul).

The second: the difference between each of these is something the mind and reasoning of the one who is obligated cannot reach. So when the realization of that difference is not perceived, how can it impair the realization of the benefits?

Know that it is obligatory upon the one who is obligated, whether according to our view or the view of the Mu'tazilah, to cut off the desire for such questions, for it is a sea with no shore. Among these are: the determination of the angels who are the companions of the Fire as nineteen, the bearers of the Throne as eight, the months of the year as twelve, the heavens as seven, and likewise the earth; and likewise the statement regarding the number of the prayers, the measures of the niṣāb (the minimum threshold) in zakat, and likewise the measures of the hudud (fixed punishments) and expiations. So affirming that everything Allah, exalted is He, has said is true is the religion, and abandoning inquiry into these matters is what is obligatory. Allah, exalted is He, has indeed stated this in His saying: ﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire except angels, and We have not made their number except as a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those who were given the Scripture may be certain and those who believe may increase in faith, and those who were given the Scripture and the believers will not doubt, and that those in whose hearts is disease and the disbelievers will say, "What does Allah intend by this as an example?"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. Then He said: ﴿And none knows the soldiers of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. This is also the answer regarding why He did not create them in an instant, although He is capable of that. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that He created them in six days, although He is capable of creating them in an instant, as a teaching to His creation of gentleness and deliberation. It is said: the creation was completed on Friday, so Allah, exalted is He, made it a festival for the Muslims.

**The third question:** What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿then established Himself upon the Throne﴾? It is not permissible to interpret it as "dominion" and "power," because dominion and power are attributes of Allah that have never ceased, and the particle "then" (thumma) cannot be applied to it. The answer: "settling" (istiqrar) is not permissible, because it requires change, which is the proof of being created, and it requires composition and partition, and all of that is impossible for Allah. Rather, what is meant is: "then He created the Throne and raised it, and He is dominant," as in His saying: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know﴾ [Muhammad: 31], for what is meant is "until those who strive strive, and We know them."
