**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 25, verses 59–60:**

Allah's saying: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne, the Most Merciful; so ask about Him one who is informed.﴾ And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to whatever you command us?" And it increases them in aversion.

Know that when Allah, glorified is He, commanded the Messenger to put his trust in Him, He described Himself with several attributes:

The first: that He is Living and does not die, as in His saying: ﴿And rely upon the Living who does not die﴾ [al-Furqan: 58].

The second: that He is Knowing of all that is known, as in His saying: ﴿And sufficient is He as one informed of the sins of His servants﴾ [al-Furqan: 58].

The third: that He is Capable of all possible things. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth﴾. His saying ﴿He who created﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿the Living who does not die﴾, because since He, glorified is He, is the Creator of the heavens and the earths and of everything between them, it is established that He is the One capable of all forms of benefit and of repelling harm, and that all blessings come from Him. Therefore, it is not permissible to rely upon anyone except Him. There are questions regarding the verse:

**The first question:** Days are an expression for the movements of the sun in the heavens, and before the heavens there were no days. So how does Allah say, "He created them in six days"? The answer: it means in a period whose measure is this period. It is not said that a thing which is measured by a limited quantity and accepts increase, decrease and division cannot be pure non-existence, but it must be existent; thus its existence entails the existence of a duration before the existence of the world, and that requires the eternity of time. We say: this is countered by time itself, because the imagined duration that can contain ten days cannot contain five days, and the imagined duration that can contain five days cannot contain ten days, so it would follow that the duration has another duration. Since this does not follow, what you have said does not follow either. Based on this we say: perhaps Allah, glorified is He, first created the duration and then created the heavens and the earth within it, in a measure of six days. Some people said: "in six days of the days of the Hereafter, each day being a thousand years," but this is far-fetched, because definition must be by a known matter, not by an unknown one.

**The second question:** Why did He determine the creation and bringing into existence with this measure? The answer: according to our view, will and power are sufficient for specification. The Mu'tazilah (a theological school that emphasized human reason and divine justice) said: rather, there must be a motive of wisdom, namely that specifying the creation of the world with this measure is better for those who are obligated. This is far-fetched for two reasons:

The first: the realization of that wisdom is either necessary in itself or possible. If it is necessary, it must not change, so it would be realized at all times, and therefore it is not suitable to be a cause for specifying a particular time. If it is possible, then the realization of that wisdom at that time requires another specifier, and this entails an infinite regress (tasalsul).

The second: the difference between each of these is something the mind and reasoning of the one who is obligated cannot reach. So when the realization of that difference is not perceived, how can it impair the realization of the benefits?

Know that it is obligatory upon the one who is obligated, whether according to our view or the view of the Mu'tazilah, to cut off the desire for such questions, for it is a sea with no shore. Among these are: the determination of the angels who are the companions of the Fire as nineteen, the bearers of the Throne as eight, the months of the year as twelve, the heavens as seven, and likewise the earth; and likewise the statement regarding the number of the prayers, the measures of the niṣāb (the minimum threshold) in zakat, and likewise the measures of the hudud (fixed punishments) and expiations. So affirming that everything Allah, exalted is He, has said is true is the religion, and abandoning inquiry into these matters is what is obligatory. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that He created them in six days, although He is capable of creating them in an instant, as a teaching to His creation of gentleness and deliberation. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verse 61–62:

Allah's saying: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky great constellations, and placed therein a lamp and a moon giving light.﴾ ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day alternating for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful.﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, related the excessive aversion of the disbelievers to prostration, He mentioned what, if they reflected upon it, would have made them know the obligation of prostrating and worshipping the Most Merciful. So He said: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky great constellations﴾. As for "Blessed" (tabaraka), its discussion has already passed. As for the buruj (constellations/mansions), they are the stations of the wandering stars (al-sayyarat), and this is well known. They were named buruj after the buruj (lofty palaces), because these stars are for them like dwellings for their inhabitants. The derivation of buruj is from tabarruj (display), because of its manifestness. There is another opinion from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the buruj are the great stars, but the first is more preferable because of His saying: ﴿and placed therein﴾, meaning in the buruj. If it is said: why is it not permissible that His saying "therein" refers to the sky and not the buruj? We say: because the buruj are closer, so returning the pronoun to them is more preferable. The siraj (lamp) is the sun, because of His saying: ﴿and made the sun a lamp﴾ [Nuh: 16]. It was also read as "surujan" (surujan), and it means the sun and the great stars within them. al-Hasan and al-A'mash read: "﴿wa qamaran munira﴾", and it is the plural of a night "qamra'" (moonlit), as if it were said: "and possessor of a shining moon", because the nights are moonlit by the moon, so he attributed it to them. It is not far-fetched that qumr means qamar, like rashad and rushd, and 'arab and 'urb.

As for al-khilfah (alternation), there are two opinions:

The first: it is an expression for the state of two things in which one of them succeeds the other and comes after it. It is said: "So-and-so has khilfah and ikhtilaf (alternation)," when he frequently goes back and forth to his place of relief. The meaning is that He made them two of alternation, i.e., two of succession, where this one follows that one and that one follows this one.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: He made each of them succeed its companion in what one needs to do in it, so whoever neglects a deed in one of them makes it up in the other. Anas ibn Malik said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, when he had missed his recitation of the Qur'an at night: 'O son of al-Khattab, Allah has revealed a verse concerning you.' And he recited: ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day alternating for whoever wishes to remember﴾ — what you have missed of the supererogatory prayers at night, make it up during your day, and what you have missed of the day, make it up during your night."

The second opinion: and it is the opinion of Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Kisa'i. It is said of every two things that differ: "They are two khilfan," so His saying "khilfah" means differing, this one black and this one white, this one tall and this one short. The first opinion is closer.

As for His saying: ﴿for whoever wishes to remember (an yadhdhakkara)﴾, the reading of the majority is with the shaddah (tashdid), and the reading of Hamzah is without it (takhfif). From Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "yatadhakkara". The meaning is that the observer should look at their alternation, and know that in their transition from one state to another there must be a transmitter and a changer. His saying "an yadhdhakkara" refers to all the blessings mentioned earlier. Allah the Exalted explained that those who said, "And what is the Most Merciful?", if they had reflected upon these blessings and remembered them, they would have been guided by them to the great power of Him, and to the gratitude of the grateful for the blessing in them: the tranquility in the night and the activity in the day, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas: 73]. Or they are two times for those who remember and give thanks: whoever misses a portion of worship in one of them performs it in the other. And al-shukur is the verbal noun of shakara, yashkuru, shukran.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verses 63–64:

God the Exalted says: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾ ﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing.﴾ ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, turn away from us the punishment of Hell; indeed, its punishment is ever a lasting torment."﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a place of settlement and residence.﴾ ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever between that a balanced course.﴾

Know that His saying, ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾, is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is at the end of the surah, as if it were said: "And the servants of the Most Merciful, those whose attributes are these, those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber (al-ghurfah)." It is also permissible that its predicate is ﴿those who walk﴾. Know that He, glory be to Him, restricted the title "servants" (ʿibad) to those occupied with servitude ('ubudiyyah), and this indicates that this attribute is among the most noble attributes of created beings. It was also read as ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾. Know that He, glory be to Him, described them with nine kinds of attributes:

The first attribute: His saying, ﴿those who walk upon the earth in humility (hawnan)﴾. This describes their conduct by day. It was read as "yamshūna hawnan," in which hawnan is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a descriptor of the walking, meaning "gentle people," or meaning "walking gently." However, placing the verbal noun in the position of the descriptor is for emphasis (mubalaghah).

Al-hawn means gentleness and softness. From it is the hadith: "Love your beloved gently, for a while," and His saying (ﷺ): "The believers are gentle and soft." The meaning is that their walking is with softness, tranquility, dignity, and humility. They do not stamp their feet, nor do they drag their sandals in arrogance and insolence, nor do they strut out of self-admiration, as He said: ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾ [al-Isra' 37]. It is narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam: "I sought the explanation of 'hawnan' and did not find it, so I saw in a dream that it was said to me: 'They are those who do not desire corruption on the earth.'" Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verses 63–64:

Know that His saying, ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾, is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is at the end of the surah, as if it were said: "And the servants of the Most Merciful, those whose attributes are these, those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber (al-ghurfah)." It is also permissible that its predicate is ﴿those who walk﴾. Know that He, glory be to Him, restricted the title "servants" (ʿibad) to those occupied with servitude ('ubudiyyah), and this indicates that this attribute is among the most noble attributes of created beings. It was read as "yamshūna hawnan," in which hawnan is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a descriptor of the walking, meaning "gentle people," or meaning "walking gently." However, placing the verbal noun in the position of the descriptor is for emphasis (mubalaghah).

The meaning is that their walking is with softness, tranquility, dignity, and humility. They do not stamp their feet, nor do they drag their sandals in arrogance and insolence, nor do they strut out of self-admiration, as He said: ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾ [al-Isra' 37]. It is narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam: "I sought the explanation of 'hawnan' and did not find it, so I saw in a dream that it was said to me: 'They are those who do not desire corruption on the earth.'" And from Ibn Zayd: "They do not act arrogantly or tyrannically, and they do not desire exaltation on the earth."

The first, and it is the strongest: He, exalted is He, described them with moderation, which lies between excess and deficiency, and with the like of this He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) in His words: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely outstretched﴾ [al-Isra': 29]. Then he prepared a second, and he sent to him, and he said: "It is a right; whoever wishes, let him respond, and if not, let him remain seated." They did not eat food for luxury and pleasure, nor wear clothing for beauty and adornment, but they ate what satisfied their hunger and helped them in the worship of their Lord, and wore what covered their nakedness and protected them from heat and cold. Here there are two issues:

The first issue: "al-qiwam." Tha'lab said: "al-qawam" with a fatha means justice and uprightness, and with a kasra means that by which a matter endures and becomes stable. The author of al-Kashshaf said: al-qawam is justice between two things for the uprightness and balance of both sides, and the counterpart of qawam from istiqamah (uprightness) is "sawa'" from istiwa' (equilibrium). It was read "qiwaman" with a kasra, and that is what by which a thing is sustained. It is said: "You are our qiwam," meaning that by which the need is sustained, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it.

The second issue: the two accusatives, that is, "bayna dhalika qawaman," may both be predicates, or "bayna dhalika" may be made a superfluous element (laghw) and "qawaman" a settled predicate, or the adverbial phrase may be the predicate and "qawaman" an emphatic circumstantial accusative. Al-Farra' said: If you wish, you may make "bayna dhalika" the noun of "kana," as you say: "kana duna hadha kafiyan" (what is less than this is sufficient), meaning less than that. Then the meaning of "bayna dhalika" would be: the middle between that is qawaman, that is, just. This interpretation is weak, because qawam is the middle, so the statement would become: "and the middle was a middle," and this is superfluous.

**The Sixth Attribute.**

God, may He be glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And those who do not invoke another god alongside God, nor kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right, nor commit adultery. Whoever does that will meet a penalty.﴾ ﴿The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide in it in humiliation.﴾ ﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds; for those, God will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. God is ever Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ ﴿And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, indeed he turns to God in a sincere return.﴾

Know that He, glorified and exalted, mentioned that among the attributes of the servants of the Most Merciful is their avoidance of associating partners with God, of killing, and of adultery. Then He mentioned the ruling on the punishment for whoever does these things, and then He excepted from them the one who repents. Here there are questions.

**The first question:** Before mentioning this attribute, He declared the servants of the Most Merciful free from trivial matters. How, then, does it fit that He afterwards purifies them from grave matters such as associating partners, killing, and adultery? Would it not be better if the order were reversed? **The answer:** One who is described by those previous attributes may still hold to associating partners out of religious conviction, may commit the killing of the buried infant girl (al-mawda'ah) out of religious conviction, and may commit adultery out of religious conviction. It is as if He said: The servants of the Most Merciful are those who do not invoke another god alongside God, while you do invoke; ﴿nor kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾, while you kill the buried infant girl; ﴿nor commit adultery﴾, while you commit adultery.

**The second question:** What is the meaning of His words ﴿nor kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾? It is known that whoever is lawful to kill does not enter the category of the forbidden soul, so how is this exception valid? **The answer:** The cause for the prohibition of killing is always present, and the permissibility of killing is established only by an opposing factor. So His words ﴿which God has forbidden﴾ point to the underlying cause, and His words ﴿except by right﴾ point to the opposing factor.

**The third question:** On what grounds is killing lawful? **The answer:** By apostasy, by adultery after being married (ihsan), and by killing in retaliation (qawad), according to what is in the hadith. It has also been said: and by waging war (muharabah), and by proof (bayyinah), even if there is no reality to what is testified to.

[Page 97]

**The fourth question:** Some have interpreted His words ﴿nor kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾ as referring to apostasy. Is that valid? **The answer:** The word "killing" is general, so it encompasses all cases. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud: "I said: O Messenger of God, which sin is greatest? He said: That you set up a rival to God while He created you. I said: Then what? He said: That you kill your child for fear that it will eat with you. I said: Then what? He said: That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." So God revealed its confirmation.

The first: al-athām is the recompense for sin (ithm), on the pattern of wabal (ruinous consequence) and nakal (exemplary punishment).

The second, which is the view of Abu Muslim: al-athām and al-ithm are one and the same, and what is meant here is the recompense for al-athām, so the name of a thing is applied to its recompense.

The third: al-Hasan said: al-athām is one of the names of Hell. Mujahid said: ﴿athāman﴾ is a valley in Hell. Ibn Mas'ud read it as "athāman," meaning "severe," as one says: "a day of athām," meaning a grievous day.

* * *

As for His words ﴿The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide in it in humiliation﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** yudā'af (will be doubled) is a substitute for yalqa (will meet), because both have the same meaning. It is recited as yuḍ'af and as nuḍā'if lahu al-'adhāba with nun and the accusative for al-'adhāb. It is also recited with the nominative as a new sentence or as a circumstantial clause (hal). The same applies to yakhlud. It is recited as wa-yukhlad in the passive voice, both lightened and intensified, from ikhlad and takhlid. It is also recited as wa-takhlud with ta' as an iltifat (shift in grammatical person).

**The second issue:** The reason for the doubling of the punishment is that when a polytheist commits sins alongside his polytheism, he is punished for the polytheism and for the sins together, so the punishment is doubled in proportion to what he is punished for. This indicates that the disbelievers are addressed by the particulars of the sacred law (furu' al-shara'i').

**The third issue:** The judge (al-Qadi) said: God made clear that the doubling and increase will have the same status in duration as the original. So His words ﴿and he will abide in it﴾ mean: he will abide in that doubling. Moreover, that doubling was caused only by the punishment for the sins, so it must be that the punishment for these sins for the disbeliever is perpetual. And if that is so, it must be so for the believer as well, because his state regarding what he deserves does not change, whether he committed it with others or alone. The answer: Why should it not be that committing a thing together with another has an effect in increasing the ugliness? Do you not see that two things may each be good in themselves, though combining them is ugly, and each may be ugly while combining them is uglier? So it is the same here.

**The fourth issue:** His words ﴿and he will abide in it in humiliation﴾ refer to the established principle that punishment is pure harm accompanied by degradation and humiliation, just as reward is pure benefit accompanied by honour.

* * *

As for His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds; for those, God will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. God is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The verse indicates that repentance is accepted. The exception does not indicate this by itself, because it establishes that the punishment is doubled, so for the exception to be valid it is enough that the penitent is not doubled in punishment. What indicates acceptance is His words ﴿for those, God will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾.

**The second issue:** It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The repentance of the killer is not accepted. He claimed that this verse is abrogated (mansukhah) by His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾ [al-Nisa': 93]. They said: The severe ruling was revealed a short time after the lenient one. It is also reported from al-Dahhak and Muqatil that it was eight years later. The discussion of this has already been presented in the commentary on Surah al-Nisa'.

**The third issue:** If it is said: Righteous deeds include repentance and faith, so mentioning them before the mention of righteous deeds is superfluous (hashw). We say: He singled them out for mention because of their high status. Since there must be other deeds alongside them, He mentioned righteous deeds right after them.

**The fourth issue:** The scholars differed about the meaning of His words ﴿for those, God will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾, and there are several views:

The first: the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Qatadah: The replacement happens only in this world. God replaces the ugly deeds of their polytheism with the fine deeds of Islam. He replaces polytheism with faith, the killing of believers with the killing of polytheists, and adultery with chastity and marriage (ihsan). It is as if He is giving them good news that He enables them to do these righteous deeds, so that they deserve reward for them.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: An evil deed in itself does not become a good deed. But the interpretation is that the evil deed is erased by repentance, and the good deed is recorded together with the repentance. As for the disbeliever, God nullifies his deeds and records evil deeds against him.

The third: Some said: God erases the evil deed from the servant and records a good deed in its place by the ruling of this verse. This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Makhul, and they cite what Abu Hurayrah (may God be pleased with him) reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Some people will surely wish that they had multiplied their evil deeds." It was said: "Who are they, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Those whose evil deeds God replaces with good deeds." On this view, the replacement is in the Hereafter.

The fourth: al-Qaffal and al-Qadi said: God replaces the punishment with reward. He mentioned the two (the evil deeds and the good deeds) and meant what is deserved by them. If it is understood in this way, then the attribution to God is literal, because reward comes only from God, may He be exalted.

Regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then indeed he turns back to Allah with a (proper) turning back﴾, there are two questions.

The first question: What is the benefit of this repetition? The answer is in two respects:

The first: This is not a repetition, because when the first (mention) was about those traits, Allah, exalted is He, made clear that all sins stand in the same position regarding the validity of repentance from them.

The second: The first repentance is a turning back from polytheism and acts of disobedience, while the second repentance is a return to Allah, exalted is He, for recompense and reward, as in His saying: ﴿Upon Him I have relied, and to Him is my return﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 30], meaning my place of return.

The second question: Is repentance anything other than repentance to Allah, exalted is He? So what is the benefit of His saying: ﴿then indeed he turns back to Allah with a (proper) turning back﴾? The answer is in several respects:

The first: What has preceded, namely that the first repentance is turning back from disobedience, and the second is returning to the judgment and reward of Allah, exalted is He.

The second: Its meaning is that whoever repents to Allah has brought a repentance that is pleasing to Allah, expiating sins and securing a great reward.

The third: His saying ﴿And whoever repents﴾ refers to the past. He, glorified is He, mentioned that whoever performed this repentance in the past, sincerely, has been promised that He will grant him success in repenting in the future, and this is among the greatest of glad tidings.

The seventh attribute.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verse 72:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who do not bear witness to falsehood, and when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity.﴾

On this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-zawr (falsehood) may mean giving false testimony, so the meaning would be that they do not bear false witness. The genitive construction is elided: the governing noun (al-mudaf) is omitted and the governed noun (al-mudaf ilayhi) is put in its place. It may also mean attending places of falsehood, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So turn away from them until they plunge into some other talk﴾ [al-An'am: 68]. It may also mean attending any place where what is unbecoming takes place, and this includes the festivals of the polytheists and the gatherings of the wicked. For whoever mixes with the people of evil, looks at their deeds, and attends their gatherings, has indeed partaken with them in that disobedience, because attending and looking are a sign of approval of it, and indeed they are a cause of its existence and its increase, since what moves them to do it is the admiration of the spectators and their desire to look at it. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: the intended meaning is the gatherings of falsehood in which they speak falsehood against Allah, may He be exalted, and against His Messenger. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: al-zawr is singing. Know that all of these interpretations are possible, but its use for falsehood is more common.

The second issue: The most sound view is that al-laghw (vain talk) is everything that must be disregarded and left aside. Some have defined al-laghw as everything that is not obedience, but this is weak, because permissible things are not counted as vain talk. So His saying, ﴿and when they pass by vain talk﴾ means: by people of vain talk.

The third issue: There is no doubt that His saying, ﴿they pass by with dignity﴾ means that they keep themselves dignified above the state of vain talk, and their dignifying themselves in this way can only be by turning away, by disapproval, and by refraining from assisting and supporting it. This includes polytheism, vain talk concerning the Qur'an, insulting the Messenger, and delving into what is unbecoming. The root of the word is from the saying of the Arabs: a "generous" (karima) she-camel is one who, at milking, turns away out of nobility, as if she does not care about what is milked from her because of her abundance. So this was borrowed for pardoning a sin. Al-Layth said: it is said, "So-and-so behaved with dignity regarding what disgraces him," when he stays far from it and honours himself above it. A parallel to this verse is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it and say: "For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds; peace be upon you; we do not seek out the ignorant."﴾ [al-Qasas: 55]. From al-Hasan: sins did not make them foolish. It has also been said: when they hear insults and harm from the disbelievers, they turn away. And it has been said: when marriage is mentioned, they speak of it by allusion.

The eighth attribute.

﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall down upon them deaf and blind.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall down upon them deaf and blind.﴾

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: His saying, ﴿they do not fall down upon them deaf and blind﴾, is not a negation of falling down; rather it is an affirmation of it together with a negation of deafness and blindness, just as one says: "Zayd does not meet me greeting [me]," which is a negation of the greeting and not of the meeting. The meaning is that when they are reminded of them, they throw themselves upon them eagerly to listen to them, and they turn toward the one who reminds them of them. And in their throwing themselves upon them, they are hearing with attentive ears and seeing with watchful eyes, unlike those who are reminded of them and you see them bent over them, turning toward the one who reminds them of them, showing intense eagerness to listen to them, while they are like the deaf and the blind, in that they do not understand them and do not perceive what is in them, like the hypocrites.

The Ninth Attribute.

﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and our offspring the delight of our eyes, and make us a leader for the righteous."﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and our offspring the delight of our eyes, and make us a leader for the righteous."﴾ In it are several issues:

The first issue: Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim recited ﴿wa-dhurriyyatina﴾ with the alif of the plural (dhurriyyat), while the rest omitted it and read it in the singular (dhurriyyah). The word dhurriyyah may be used as both singular and plural.

The second issue: There is no doubt that the intention is for them to be the delight of their eyes in religion, not in worldly matters such as wealth and beauty. Then they mentioned two possibilities regarding this:

The first of them: they asked for spouses and offspring in this world who would share with them, so they wished to be together with them in holding fast to the obedience of Allah, so that their hope of attaining Paradise together with them would grow stronger, and their joy in this world would be complete through this hope, and in the Hereafter upon attaining the reward.

The second: they asked that Allah join their spouses and offspring with them in Paradise, so that their joy in them would be complete.

The third issue: If it is asked, "What is the 'min' (from) in His saying, ﴿from among our spouses﴾?" We say: it may be explanatory (bayaniyyah), as if it was said, "Grant us the delight of our eyes," then the delight was specified and explained by His saying, ﴿from among our spouses﴾, and this is from their saying, "I saw from you a lion," meaning, "You are a lion." And it may be initial (ibtida'iyyah), in the sense of "Grant us, from their side, that which will delight our eyes of obedience and righteousness."

If it is asked, "Why did He say ﴿delight of eyes﴾ indefinitely and in a diminished form?" We say: as for the indefiniteness, it is because the qurrah (delight) is indefinite, since an annexed noun cannot be made indefinite except by making the noun it is annexed to indefinite; as if he said, "Grant us from them joy and happiness." As for saying "a'yun" (eyes) rather than "uyun," it is because he intended the eyes of the righteous, and they are few in comparison to the eyes of others. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba, 13].

The fourth issue: Al-Zajjaj said: "Allah cool your eye," meaning: your heart encounters what it loves. Al-Mufaddal stated three opinions regarding "the coolness of the eye":

The first: it returns her tear, which is the one that accompanies laughter and joy, whereas the tear of sorrow is hot.

The second: her sleep, because it occurs with the departure of sorrow and pain.

The third: the presence of contentment.

The fifth issue: His saying: ﴿and make us a leader for the righteous﴾. The closest meaning is that they asked Allah the Exalted to bring them in obedience to the level at which they would be pointed to and taken as examples. Some said that the verse contains an indication that leadership in religion should be sought and desired. Khalil (peace be upon him) said: ﴿And grant me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations﴾ [al-Shu'ara, 84]. It was also said that these verses were revealed concerning the ten who were given the good news of Paradise.

The sixth issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued from this verse that the act of the servant is created by Allah the Exalted. They said: because leadership in religion can only be attained through knowledge and action, and this indicates that knowledge and action occur only by the making and creation of Allah the Exalted. The Qadi said: what is meant by the request is the divine favours (alutaf) which, when they increase, make them choose these things, and so they become leaders. The reply: those favours are necessarily already done, so asking for them would be pointless.

The seventh issue: Al-Farra' said: He said "imaman" (a leader) and did not say "a'immah" (leaders), just as He said regarding two persons: ﴿Indeed, I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Zukhruf, 46]. It is also possible that the meaning is: make each one of us a leader, just as He said: ﴿He brings you out as a child﴾ [Ghafir, 67]. Al-Akhfash said: "imam" is a plural whose singular is "amm," like "sa'im" and "siyam." Al-Qaffal said: In my view, when "imam" is treated as a noun of genus, it takes the singular form, as if it was said: make us a proof for the righteous; and similarly "bayyinah" (clear proof), as one says: "These are the proof of so-and-so."

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, enumerated the attributes of the righteous and sincere ones, He then explained after that the kinds of His favour to them, which are gathered under two matters: benefits and honour.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 25, verses 75–77:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber for their patience, and they will be met therein with greeting and peace﴾.

As for the benefits, it is His saying: ﴿Those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber for their patience﴾. The intended meaning is that they will be rewarded with the lofty chambers (ghurufat). The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿and they will be secure in the lofty chambers﴾ [Saba': 37], and He said: ﴿For them are chambers, above them are chambers built high﴾ [az-Zumar: 20]. The ghurfah in the language is the elevated place, and every high building is a ghurfah, and what is meant by it is the lofty ranks. The exegetes said: ghurfah is a name for Paradise, so the meaning is: they will be rewarded with Paradise, and it consists of many gardens. Some of them read: "Those will be rewarded in the ghurfah." As for His saying ﴿for their patience﴾, there are two discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: Those who held that Paradise is by merit argued from this verse, saying: the particle "bi" (for, because of) in His saying ﴿for their patience﴾ indicates this, and if its attainment were by promise, this would not be true.

The second discussion: He mentioned patience without mentioning what one is patient against, so that it encompasses every kind, and it includes their patience over the hardships of reflection and reasoning in the knowledge of God Exalted, over the hardships of acts of obedience, over the hardships of abandoning desires, over the harm of the polytheists, over the hardships of jihad, poverty and the training of the self. There is therefore no basis for the view of those who say that what is meant is patience over poverty specifically; for these qualities, when they are present together with wealth, entitle the one who possesses them to Paradise just as they entitle him by means of poverty.

( 30 ﴿And they will be met therein with greeting and peace﴾ ﴿Abiding therein; excellent is it as a place of settlement and residence﴾ ﴿Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication. But you have denied, so there will be (punishment) inseparable﴾.
The second of the two is glorification: it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they will be met therein with greeting and peace﴾. It has been read "yulaqqawna" (they will be met), like His saying: ﴿And He gave them radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insan: 11], and "yalqawna" (they will encounter), like His saying: ﴿he will meet penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]. The tahiyyah (greeting) is the supplication for long life, and the salam (peace) is the supplication for safety; so the outcome of the tahiyyah returns to the bounty of Paradise being lasting and not cut off, and the salam returns to that bounty being pure, free of any admixture of harm. Then this greeting and peace may come from God Exalted, by His saying: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]; and it may come from the angels, by His saying: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, [saying]: Peace be upon you﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 23–24]; and it may come from some of them to others.

As for His saying: ﴿Abiding therein; excellent is it as a place of settlement and residence﴾, the meaning is that He, glorified is He, when He promised the benefits first and the glorification second, explained that among their attributes is permanence, which is the meaning of His saying ﴿abiding therein﴾, and among their attributes is also purity, which is the meaning of His saying ﴿excellent is it as a place of settlement and residence﴾. This is in contrast to His saying: ﴿evil is it as a place of settlement and residence﴾; i.e., how bad that is and how good this is.

As for His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication. But you have denied, so there will be (punishment) inseparable﴾, know that He, glorified is He, when He described the attributes of the God-fearing and described the state of their reward, commanded His Messenger to say: ﴿Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication﴾. Thereby it indicates that He, Exalted, is free of need of their worship, and that He Exalted only imposed obligations upon them so that they might benefit by their obedience. There are issues concerning this:

First issue: al-Khalil said: "ma a'ba' bi-fulan" means: I do not do anything with him, as if he considers him insignificant and contemptible. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "ma a'ba' bihi" means: his existence and his non-existence are equal to me. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: you have no weight with your Lord. The 'ib' in the language is weight. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "ma yubali bikum rabbi" means: my Lord does not care for you.

Second issue: Concerning "ma" there are two views:

One of them: it includes the meaning of interrogation, and it is in the position of the accusative, and it refers to the verbal noun, as if it were said: What weight would there be to you before your Lord were it not for your supplication.

The second: that "ma" is a negating particle.

Third issue: They mentioned two possibilities concerning His saying ﴿were it not for your supplication﴾:

One of them: were it not for His calling you to the religion and your obedience; the "du'a'" here is a verbal noun added to the object.

The second: that the supplication is added to the agent, and on this assumption they mentioned several meanings:

One: "were it not for your supplication": were it not for your faith.

Second: were it not for your worship.

Third: were it not for your supplication to Him in times of hardship; like His saying: ﴿So when they board the ship they call upon God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 65].

Fourth: your supplication, i.e., were it not for your thanks to Him for His kindness; by His saying: ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful?﴾ [an-Nisa': 147].

Fifth: I did not create you, and I have no need of you, except that you ask Me and I give you, and you seek My forgiveness and I forgive you.

As for His saying: ﴿But you have denied﴾, the meaning is: when I informed you that My judgment is that I do not regard My servants except for their worship, then by your denial you have opposed My judgment, so there will necessarily befall you the effect of your denial, which is the punishment of the Hereafter. Its parallel is that a king says to one who has disobeyed him: "My custom is to show kindness to whoever obeys me, and you have disobeyed, so you will see what I will bring upon you because of your disobedience." If it is asked: to whom is this address directed? We say: to people in general, among them are believers who worship and deniers who disobey, so they are addressed with what is found in their kind of worship and denial. It has been read: "fa-qad kadhdhaba al-kafirun, fa-sawfa yakunu al-'adhab lizaman," and it has been read "lazaman" with a fatha, in the sense of necessity, like "al-thabat" and "al-thubut." The preferred view is that the omission of the name of "kana" unpronounced, after it is known that it is among what was threatened, is for the sake of vagueness, and it encompasses what description does not encompass. Then it was said: this punishment is in the Hereafter; and it was said: it was on the day of Badr, and this is the view of Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him. And Allah knows best.

The tafsir of this surah is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and blessings and peace upon our master Muhammad, the Unlettered Prophet, and upon his family and companions, all of them.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "ma a'ba' bihi" means: his existence and his non-existence are equal to me. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: you have no weight with your Lord. The 'ib' in the language is weight. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "ma yubali bikum rabbi" means: my Lord does not care for you.

Second issue: Concerning "ma" there are two views:

One of them: it includes the meaning of interrogation, and it is in the position of the accusative, and it refers to the verbal noun, as if it were said: What weight would there be to you before your Lord were it not for your supplication.

The second: that "ma" is a negating particle.

Third issue: They mentioned two possibilities concerning His saying ﴿were it not for your supplication﴾:

One of them: were it not for His calling you to the religion and your obedience; the "du'a'" here is a verbal noun added to the object.

The second: that the supplication is added to the agent, and on this assumption they mentioned several meanings:

One: "were it not for your supplication": were it not for your faith.

Second: were it not for your worship.

Third: were it not for your supplication to Him in times of hardship; like His saying: ﴿So when they board the ship they call upon God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 65].

Fourth: your supplication, i.e., were it not for your thanks to Him for His kindness; by His saying: ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful?﴾ [an-Nisa': 147].

Fifth: I did not create you, and I have no need of you, except that you ask Me and I give you, and you seek My forgiveness and I forgive you.

As for His saying: ﴿But you have denied﴾, the meaning is: when I informed you that My judgment is that I do not regard My servants except for their worship, then by your denial you have opposed My judgment, so there will necessarily befall you the effect of your denial, which is the punishment of the Hereafter. Its parallel is that a king says to one who has disobeyed him: "My custom is to show kindness to whoever obeys me, and you have disobeyed, so you will see what I will bring upon you because of your disobedience." If it is asked: to whom is this address directed? We say: to people in general, among them are believers who worship and deniers who disobey, so they are addressed with what is found in their kind of worship and denial. It has been read: "fa-qad kadhdhaba al-kafirun, fa-sawfa yakunu al-'adhab lizaman," and it has been read "lazaman" with a fatha, in the sense of necessity, like "al-thabat" and "al-thubut." The preferred view is that the omission of the name of "kana" unpronounced, after it is known that it is among what was threatened, is for the sake of vagueness, and it encompasses what description does not encompass. Then it was said: this punishment is in the Hereafter; and it was said: it was on the day of Badr, and this is the view of Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him. And Allah knows best.

The tafsir of this surah is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and blessings and peace upon our master Muhammad, the Unlettered Prophet, and upon his family and companions, all of them.
